items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

MOTIONS
Queen Elizabeth II—Diamond Jubilee

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave that th is House congratulates
Her Majesty the Queen on the occasion of the diamond jubilee of Her Majesty’s
accession to the Throne.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Prime Minister is seeking leav e. Is there any objection to that
course of action being followed? There is no objection.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House congratulate Her Majesty the Queen
on the occasion of the diamond jubilee of  Her Majesty’s accession to the throne . On 6
February 1952—60 years ago yesterday—Queen Elizabeth II ascended to the throne
and became New Zealand’s monarch. She was only 25 years old—younger, in fact, than
any member of our Parliament today. In her speech as she ascended to the throne she
promised to follow the example of servic e and devotion provided by her father, King
George VI. For six decades the Queen has kept that undertaki ng. These have been
decades during which the concept of the Brit ish Empire has receded and the importance
of the Commonwealth has come to the fore . The realms over which Queen Elizabeth
reigns have had their times of prosperity, al ong with times of tur bulence and challenge.
And over 60 years New Zealand has orientated  itself on the world map differently: less
the Antipodes and all that that implies, more a modern and assertive nation with a
central role in the Pacific. We have developed our own dist inct sense of identity. We
value the things that make us unique, that  make us Kiwis. We are a nation of many
different peoples sharing a common belief in peace, progress, and a fair go.
The dignity, wisdom, and assurance that the Queen brings to her role as New
Zealand’s head of State supersedes maps and distances. Throughout the changes of the
past 60 years her status as our  Sovereign has given many of us a sense of stability and
confidence. Her role is a link with syst ems of constitutional government that have
histories much longer than our own, and with traditions that move and inspire us.
In my time as Prime Minister, I have been  fortunate enough to meet Her Majesty on
a number of occasions, and I can say to memb ers of this House, and, indeed, to New
Zealanders, that she has a great care, concern, and passi on for, and intimate knowledge
and love of, this country, and, in my view, has done a wonderful job as the monarch of
New Zealand. I know that in this Parliament there are a ra nge of views on the future of
the monarchy in New Zealand. I respect thos e views are sincerely held, while at the
same time maintaining my own belief as bot h Prime Minister of New Zealand and as a
80 Motions 7 Feb 2012
citizen of this realm that the monarchy con tinues to be both relevant and meaningful.
Sixty years of service, and counting—let us warmly congratulate the Queen of New
Zealand.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: On behalf of th e Labour Party, I
join with the Prime Minister and other members of this House in paying tribute to, and
thanking, Queen Elizabeth II, who marks the 60 th anniversary of he r ascension to the
throne. New Zealand stands alongside many other Commonwealth countries in
congratulating Her Majesty on  this, her diamond jubilee. I also welcomed the Prime
Minister’s announcement earlier that New Zealand will host the Prince of Wales and the
Duchess of Cornwall later on, in November this year, and I know that will be welcomed
by many New Zealanders.
I understand that Queen Victoria was the only other queen to have reigned as long as
Queen Elizabeth II, so it is appropriate that Parliament marks this occasion. Her reign is
perhaps best described by the United Nati ons Secretary-General, Ban Ki-moon, who
said that “in a churning and ch anging world” she is “an anchor for our age.” Her reign
has been one of an unwavering commitment and dedication to service. It is a
commitment that has spanned the service of 14 New Zealand Prime Ministers and 12
British Prime Ministers, and, as the Prime Minist er just remarked, it is sobering that the
weight of responsibility of the monarchy fell on her at the age of only 25. Perhaps most
famously for New Zealand is our link to that coronation 60 years ago, when Sir Edmund
Hillary conquered Everest and said that that feat was, in fact, a coronation gift. No one
can doubt her dedication to Commonwealth countries. In our darkest hours she has
stood by us. Her words of support, for example,  in Canterbury were very well received,
and her grandson’s visiting and saying the words “kia kaha” to Cantabrians perhaps best
acknowledged the stoic resolve of Cantabrians at that particular time. She is the first
monarch, in fact, to have ever visited New Zealand, and she has visited 10 times in her
60-year reign.
I had the privilege of meeting Queen Eli zabeth at Buckingham Palace some 15 or 16
years ago, and it is an honour I will not forg et. I have enormous respect for her work
and her service.
We acknowledge, of course, that over the last 60 years much has changed in New
Zealand, and there will inevitably be some discussion about our future constitutional
arrangements. But that is a debate for anothe r day. Today is a day to  mark her reign of
service, commitment, and dedication, and on behalf of the Labour Party I congratulate
Her Majesty.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Green Party pays tribute to our head of
State, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth of Ne w Zealand. As the sec ond - longest serving
Sovereign, the Queen has played a most si gnificant and important role in the world
through an extraordinary 66 years of tumultuous world history. She has honoured the
institution of the monarchy th rough the natural dignity of her person and the grace with
which she has discharged her duties. She has honoured this country in the genuine
interest she has displayed in our history, our  culture, our sporting prowess, our military
sacrifices, our changing demographic charac ter, and our hopes and aspirations for the
future.
When the Queen was crowned in 1952, Sir Edmund Hillary was yet to conquer
Mount Everest. Back home, ha lf of New Zealand homes did not have a fridge, and one
in five did not have a flus hing toilet. No home had televi sion. The idea of standing on
the moon remained in the realm of heroic pla nning, if not science fiction. So times have
changed considerably sin ce our Queen ascende d the throne as a young woman. We
celebrate her 60 th anniversary with a respectful me ssage of gratitude and personal
affection shared by all New Zealanders.
7 Feb 2012 Motions 81
No discussion about the New Zealand m onarchy occurs today without attention
being naturally given to the nature of the institution of the head of State. We remain in a
small minority of nations that share the same head of State with others. There are many
who advocate a transition soone r or later to a republican institution—one based here in
our own soil. There are others who are comfor table with the status quo and wish it to
continue. Her Majesty will not be unaware of  the somewhat desultory debate in the
country along these lines. The Green Party does not have a formal position on this
matter, and now is not the time to explore it. But equally it is inappropriate, even as we
pay tribute to our respected monarch, not to  acknowledge the future  challenge we face
as a nation on this matter. Let us send a message from this Parliament of Aotearoa New
Zealand to Her Majesty thanking her for he r gracious service and wishing her a long
and fruitful life ahead.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand First wishes to be
associated with the previous sentiments and to say that we agree with them in their
entirety. New Zealand is one of only nine countries with an unbroken line of democracy
these last 150 years, and the Queen being our head of State may be one of the
significant reasons why we have that proud cl aim, which so few countries can boast as
we do. Hence we send her our heartfelt congratulations.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Huri rauna t ēnā
tātou katoa. E tautoko ana i ng ā mihi atu ki te Kuini. I te mea hoki ka huri au ki te reo
Pākehā, kia mōhio tūturu ai tātou, he aha pū ngā whakaaro kai roto i taku ngākau.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker, and to us throughout. I endorse the accolades to the
Queen and immediately turn to English so that we understand fully  what the thoughts
within me are.]
On behalf of the Mana movement I congrat ulate the Queen on achieving this historic
milestone, and I urge this Gove rnment to invite her to reaffirm her commitment to Te
Tiriti o Waitangi as a guide to how this Gove rnment might act in all matters pertaining
to the indigenous people of Aot earoa and the lands and resources  that it holds on behalf
of all New Zealanders. Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: The ACT Party is glad to be associated with
this motion. This weekend marked the 172 nd anniversary of the sign ing of the Treaty of
Waitangi. Rather than a day of national celebr ation, it has continue d to be a time of
angst and controversy. We contin ue to be lost in a mire of conflicted identity. The last
time I attended Waitangi was in 1990, the year  the Queen suffered an offensive affront
to her dignity as our head of State when  she was assaulted on the Treaty grounds. I
vowed that day that I would not return unt il the behaviour improved. Two decades later
the behaviour of many of those remains the same. It is my hope that 6 February can
become a day when all of us can peacefully  celebrate the greatness of our country and
can recognise the important ro le that both the Crown and M āori have played in the
development of our nation.
The sixth of February also marks the 60th anniversary of the Queen’s ascension to the
throne. Today offers an opportunity for this  Parliament to celebrate the Queen and
everything her reign has meant to the country over the past six decades. Her
commitment to the Commonwealth and the sense of duty with which she has carried out
her role is to be applauded. Her reign ha s brought a common thr ead of stability and
unity to our young country, and as a nation we  should not be in any great haste to
change such an important link to our past . The Queen has kept her solemn coronation
oath to govern the people of New Zealand ac cording to our laws and customs. Fourteen
New Zealand Prime Ministers have served her, and she has always fulfilled her duty
without becoming embroiled in the politics of  the day. She embodies the principle that
82 Motions 7 Feb 2012
constitutional monarchy is power constrai ned and upholds democratic government in
New Zealand through the notion that policy is determined, finally, in this House.
Today this Parliament—this country—gives praise and thanks, congratulations, and
warmest best wishes to Queen Elizabet h II, Queen of New Zealand, on her 60 th year on
the throne. Long may she live in good health, happiness, and contentment.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: On behalf of United Future I
want to join with others who have spoken in tribute to Her Majesty the Queen on the
occasion of the 60th anniversary of her ascension to the throne.
It is sobering to realise that when that event occurred very few members of this
House were actually alive, Winston Churchil l was the Prime Minist er of Great Britain,
Harry Truman resided in the White Hous e, and Stalin was still carrying on his
murderous ways in Russia. Sidney Holland wa s our own Prime Minister. So much has
changed, when one reflects upon those people and the character of their times, and yet
the one thing that Queen Eliz abeth has been able to provi de through thos e intervening
60 years to the present has been a sense of continuity, a huge measure of dignity, and, in
many senses, that portrayal of common sens e and common wisdom that has held her
own country together in times of great crisis, and, I think, has been a beacon of hope for
many around the world. It never ceases to  amaze me that republics like the United
States, for instance, give the Queen perhaps the warmest welcome of all when she visits
there, and I think that says a lot about her and her character.
As a republican, I acknowledge this is not the occasion to delve into that debate in
any sense; this is the occasion to mark 60 years of service, commitment, and dedication
to her people by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, and to wish her and her family well as
they celebrate this occasion and look forward to the future.
Motion agreed to.
Economy—Government Priorities and Challenges
1. SIMON BRIDGES (National—Tauranga) to the Minister of Finance: What are
the Government’s priorities for the economy in its second term?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government intends to get back
to surplus and manage the Government’s fina nces very well. We in tend to continue to
develop a more competitive economy, because we  have to earn a living in the next 10
years, rather than borrow it as we did in the last 10 years. The Government intends to
rebuild Christchurch, and our final top prior ity is to improve public  services across the
board so New Zealanders get better service for the same or fewer resources.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: What challenges does New Zealand’s economy face?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The fundamental challenge is the same now as it was 2 or 3
years ago, which is to rebalance this ec onomy from excessive resources in the non-
tradable sector to the tradable sector. Much of the growth of the last 10 years was built
on borrowed money going into an uncompe titive domestic economy. In the next 10
years we have to earn our living by investing in a competitive export sector.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: How does the Government intend to tackle the economic
challenges?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the same considered and balanced way as it did in its first
term of office. But I think New Zeala nders share with the Government the
determination to make real progress over the next few years so that we can have more
jobs and higher incomes.
7 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 83

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Did the briefing he received as incoming Minister from his chief
economic advisers in Treasury project that under his Government’s economic settings,
New Zealand’s net international liabilities would increase by nearly 10 percent of GDP
over the next 5 years—an increase of approximately $25 billion?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That may have been their projection; I would have to go and
check. We, of course, want to continue with the significant improvement in recent years
in our net international liab ilities. I am somewhat more optimistic than Treasury
because I think New Zealanders have learnt the lesson that more borrowing and
excessive borrowing are not the way for them to  get better incomes, and if they refrain
from excessive borrowing and get into higher savings, the prospects of that projection
coming to pass are less.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: What signs of progress has he seen in the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Just to give a couple of signs, the economy has grown for
nine of the last 10 quarters, and the forecas ts for growth in this economy are stronger
than in the US, Europe, and quite a numb er of other develope d countries. Secondly,
some of the more detailed changes the G overnment is making are bearing fruit. For
instance, on 1 April there will be a $600 million reduction in ACC levies because the
Government in the last 3 years applied itself to turning ACC round. That is an example
of what can be achieved with public services.
Economy—Prime Minister’s Statements and Relationship with Māori Party
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement “National will deliv er a strong, stable government—and build a
stronger economy with less debt and more jobs”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he take seriously th e question of whether the M āori Party will
continue to be bound to his G overnment for confidence and supply; and if so, is he
confident that they will?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I am confident they will.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Has he discussed with M āori Party co-leader Tariana Turia her
comments in relation to section 9 of the Stat e-Owned Enterprises Act that she is “not
one prone to idle threats”; and if so, what was the result of that discussion?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, not specifically in relati on to that comment, but I think
what the co-leader of the M āori Party was saying is that they take that issue seriously.
The Government is going through a 2-week  consultation process, and I am very
confident we will come out with an elegant solution at the end of it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: In the negotiations for the formation of the Government,
did the Māori Party raise that issue in those discussions—yes or no?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement of  this morning that “they are bound
with us for confidence and supply, which is  effectively the Budget, and the mixed-
ownership stuff doesn’t flow through the Budget”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I do, insomuch that they are not bound by the mixed-
ownership model legislation, which will fall outside of the Budget.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did he read the Government’s B udget papers, which show that the
next 5 years’ capital budgets rely on the sale of public assets?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and that is probably one of the reasons why we have 59
MPs and the Labour Party has very few. And that is because New Zealanders want less
debt, more productive assets, and an economy that is going to function, not a load more
debt, as Phil Goff was promising and, I have no doubt, David Shearer is, as well.
84 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Feb 2012

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: How will he make a Treaty clause apply just to the Crown’s share of
the State-owned enterprises, when the actions  of the privatised State-owned enterprises
will affect both the Crown and private shareholders alike?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Treaty is a compact between the Crown and M āori, and
what the Government will be aiming to do is to  spell out that very clearly in the section
that will then apply to the mixed-ownership model.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he accept that his determination to push ahead with asset sales
is creating instability in his Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Not in the slightest. I accep t what it will do is deliver a
country that has less debt than it would under Labour, a Government that will deliver
for New Zealanders something to invest in other than failed finance companies—which
were overseen by the previous Labour Government—entities that will deliver well. I say
to that member the same thing I used to say to Phil Goff: “If you don’t like the mixed-
ownership model, put up your policy to buy b ack the bit of Air New Zealand we don’t
own.”

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I ask the Prime Minister, if the M āori Party campaigned
against asset sales, and if United Future was committed to ensuring that water was
regarded as a strategic asset, then where does he get his majority from to make the
assertions he is making around the country of having public support?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the right honourable Prime Minister, obviously he is
not responsible for what either the M āori Party or ACT campaigned on. But the latter
part of the question can be answered.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As part of the confidence and supply agreements put together
between National, ACT, and United Fu ture, we secured support for the mixed-
ownership legislation. That is 61; that is a majority.
State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Ownership of Shares
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister for State Owned

items.speaker: Enterprises
items.text: What steps, if any, has he taken to  ensure that should the Government sell
49 percent of Mighty River Power, Meridia n, Genesis and Solid Energy, “New Zealand
investors will be at the front of the queue  for shareholding, and that there will be
widespread and substantial New Zealand share ownership”?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.role: Minister fo r State Owned Enterprises
items.text: Ministers have
made this requirement of widespread New Zealand investment a fundamental part of
every step of the process to date. Both th e scoping studies and Crown advisers have
confirmed that there is sufficient domestic demand to meet the Government’s
objectives. As part of any share float the G overnment has the ability to determine what
type of investors are allocated shares, and we will use this ability to ensure widespread
and substantial New Zealand shareholding. These proposed share floats are important to
ensure public debt remains under control, a nd we certainly do not want to reach the
level of debt as in some countries such as Britain, where they are having to lay off
700,000 public servants.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How will he ensure that New Zealanders are at the front of the
queue when New Zealand’s trade and invest ment agreements state that New Zealand
investors cannot be given preference over foreign investors?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government is quite clea r that those agreements do not
override the Government’s ability in respect  of the allocation policy to make those
decisions.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: What advice has he received regarding the ability of the
Government to give preference to New Zealand investors, and advice that the
agreements we have do not prevent him doing that?
7 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 85

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: We have received advice that those agreements do not prevent
the Government from ensuring widespread and substantial New Zealand ownership of
the mixed-ownership model companies.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: What is he going to put in place, if anything, to stop buyers
of shares from onselling those shares to overseas interests?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think what is quite clea r is if you look at the mixed-
ownership model as it applie s at the Port of Tauranga, which is a mixed-ownership
model type approach, we have actually got  New Zealanders buying out foreigners. I
think the fact that we have  good quality investments will give New Zealanders that
opportunity—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. That was a specific
question. It simply asked—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear the member. To save time, the honourable member may
repeat his question.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: What actions, if any, is he goi ng to put in place that would
stop buyers of shares in these State-owned enterprises from onselling those shares to
overseas interests? What specific actions will he take, if any, to stop that happening?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government is not proposing that it would take any
action that would stop ordinary people having a right to decide to whomever they sell
their shares. The problem is that the part y opposite does not think working people are
good enough to own shares, and on this side of the House, we think they are.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will the Minister release the advice he has received, as stated in
his earlier answer, that the Government has no restrictions on giving preference to New
Zealand buyers of shares in these companies?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The member is entitled to ma ke an Official Information Act
request for that information, and I am sure we will consider it in due course.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was not asking whether I
could make an Official Information Act request; I was asking whether the Minister
would release the advice.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think, in fairness to the honourable member, the Minister made it
clear that without such a request he proba bly would not, but with such a request it
would be looked at. I think that is a reasonable answer to the question asked.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table an Offici al Information Act request from
Professor Jane Kelsey seeking that advice, which was declined by the Minister in full.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: Kia ora to the Minister. What  is the Government’s position
regarding the united call from Mana, the New Zealand M āori Council, iwi leaders,
Māori organisations, and Māori people all around the country for the Treaty of Waitangi
clause to be retained in legislation being drafted for the sale of our power companies, or
does the Government feel that it has a greater obligation to remove the clause to make it
easier for foreign investors to buy those companies?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Kia ora to the member. The Government’s view is that we are
about to enter quite a lengthy consultation process wi th iwi around the country in
respect of how those rights and interests can best be protected in the legislation.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: Kia ora anō e te Minita. What reports has the Government received
about the Māori Party being willing to stay with the Government even if it pushes ahead
with its plans to remove the Treaty of Waita ngi clause from legisl ation as long as the
clause can be rewritten to sound very important even if it is completely meaningless?
86 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As Minister for State Owned Enterprises, I have not asked for
any specific reports on that matter.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In the advice that the Minister has received regarding the
implications of New Zealand’s trade agreemen ts for the ability of the Government to
give preference to New Zealand investors, did officials raise any concerns about the
Government’s ability to do that?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As I recall, no.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How are New Zealanders to know  what is actually the case
here—the ability of the Government to give preference to New Zealand buyers of these
shares or not—when the Government refuses to release the advice and keeps it secret?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think New Zealanders can take assurance of the fact that the
Government has made it very clear that it  is our intent ion to mainta in strong and
widespread New Zealand interest in these companies, and we would not have made that
commitment unless we were able to do so. A nd I have got to say there are a lot of New
Zealanders who are very interested in what is to come.
National Certificate of Educational Achievement—2011 Results
4. NIKKI KAYE (National—Auckland Central)  to the Minister of Education :
What reports has she received on the 2011 NCEA results?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā
tātou. I have received a report with some  early results from the New Zealand
Qualifications Authority. These results show  that there has been improvement across
the board. Some highlights in clude the overall result for National Certificate of
Education Achievement (NCEA) level 2 for year 12, which has risen from 76 percent in
2008 to 81.5 percent in 2011; NC EA level 2 for year 12 M āori has risen from 63.1
percent in 2008 to 72.7 per cent in 2011; and NCEA level 2 for year 12 Pasifika has
risen from 54.4 percent in 2008 to 63.2 percen t in 2011. I am also advised that early
indications are that Christchurch students im proved their achievement rates. This is a
great result in the face of a very difficu lt year, and I am sure that the whole of
Parliament joins in offering congratulations to all students who achieved in 2011.

items.speaker: Nikki Kaye
items.text: How will she continue to focus on lifting NCEA achievement rates?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I will have an unrelenting focus on the learner at the centre
and on raising achievement. We cannot truly be a world-class system while we have
groups—that the member opposite has occasionally opined to be interested in—who are

12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister of Customs : What recent

items.text: As this is the first day of
a new Parliament, I cannot say “more good news”, so I will start by saying this is the
first of a number of good-news announcements  along the way this year for customs.
SmartGate has, indeed, already made a bi g difference for people travelling between
Australia and New Zealand. Now, with new technology, we have been  able to change
the age of compatibility from 18 down to 16. Previously, you had to be 18 years or over
to use SmartGate kiosks. SmartGate provides faster processing for eligible travellers
arriving at, or departing from, Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch, and for those
arriving at Australia’s eight international airports.

queuing process. SmartGate has already proces sed over 2 million travellers since it was

be able to use it. I wish that it was not that the facial structures of children under the age
of 16 changed so much, because if that was not the case, we would actually be able to
lower it even further than 16.

KiwiSaver, which has seen the export of  millions and millions of New Zealanders’
dollars and capital into foreign markets to  buy foreign shares, but the same opportunity
being given to New Zealanders to buy blue-chip stock here in New Zealand is somehow
found by them to be abhorrent and unacceptable.
No one should forget that they were the group who presided over the massive losses
suffered by so many New Zealanders—partic ularly elderly New Zealanders—as the
finance sector went out of control in this  country, completely unchecked by Ministers
who failed to understand what those companie s were up to, and repeatedly listened to
their own advice on what needed to be done to stem some of the wild claims that those
companies were making. Their credibility in this area is absolutely zero, and no one
should be moved by the sort of silly “get out in front of a parade and wave a flag”
nonsense that David Shearer appears to be leading the Labour Party towards.
It was interesting to note in his reply to the Speech from the Throne that the first 5 to
10 minutes indicated a new approach, but then straight away there was a slot back into
the old loser politics that saw Labour so well d ealt to in the 2011 election. I want to say
to the Labour members, who repeatedly say th ey want to act in a more bipartisan way,
to start acting that way if you want to be respected for that decision. At the moment
what we are seeing essentially is a knocki ng at the door, a pressing at the window, a
demand to be let into the room, to be part of the decision making, so that they can run
outside and work out how to attack you even better.
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 95
It is not our job to be the Opposition; it is their job. And if they want to be the
Opposition, then they should be. If they want to  be the Government, or if they want to
be part of Government decisi on-making, then they need to behave in a far better way
than we have seen not only before the election but post it as well. I speak about some of
the issues in Christchurch in that regard as well.
There is no doubt that New Z ealanders have an expectation that a Government will
do what it can to make their lives better. Th is Government is not in any way shirking
from that. One of the things that is sort of fascinating is that the Labour Government—
the Labour Party, I should say—is saying that if they were in G overnment, they could
achieve all sorts of things without making any hard decisi ons. We, for example, have
recognised that if young New Zealanders are to have the very best education system in
the world, then they need to have the very be st of facilities in which to be taught. That
means that over the next few years facilitie s in schools are going to have to massively
improve. It is no good just putting in the br oadband, which I will sp eak about in a few
minutes; there has to be a capacity to take full advantage of that.
We have committed in the Speech from the Throne to $1 billion from the Future
Investment Fund being put into not only building new schools but modernising all
schools so that they are fit to deliver 21 st century education to our young people. But if
you listen to the other side of the House, they believe that you just pluck that out of the
sky somewhere and put it into place at ab solutely no cost. If it comes to a choice
between holding 100 percent of a particular a sset and choosing to have greater quality
schools for our young people, and therefore a great er investment in the future of this
country, then I know which side of the fence I sit on.
The Government is also committed to increasing or improving the infrastructure for
our transport in this country. We have said that over the next 10 years the State highway
network, the local roads network, etc. need to have some $12 billion worth of
investment. That is a huge amount and it will make a difference to those economies.
Anyone who goes to Auckland will know that  the Waterview Connection is a very
smart piece of infrastructure that will massive ly improve traffic flows in that city. We
have also got the problem of  KiwiRail, and I say “the pr oblem of KiwiRail” because it
does not operate at the maximum of its potential at the present time. But the
Government is committed to the KiwiRail Tu rnaround Plan, and that also has to be
funded from somewhere.
Then there is the very, very big commi tment of $5.5 billion—up to this point—for
the rebuild of Christchurch. Christchurch is around about 15 to 20 percent of the New
Zealand economy, with a massive potential to increase in the future. Although there will
be huge stimulus that comes in from the to tal $20 billion that will be spent there over
the next few years, there is no doubt that be yond the growth that comes from that initial
rebuild input there is a need for greater levels  of economic activity in that area. In that
regard, there is the Government’s commitment  to irrigation and to assisting people to
put up those projects. Then there is our commitment to ensuring that the resource
management project, taking full consideration of all environmental matters, does deliver
the opportunity to build those sorts of projects to get the sort of growth that the province
needs and, frankly, that this country desperately needs.
I want to just mention the consequence, I guess, of the earthqua kes in Christchurch,
the biggest being the way in which New Zeala nd prepares itself for future events of a
catastrophic nature. In New Zealand, they say, you live with  your risk. Some parts of
the country are very eart hquake-prone; others are flood-prone. Auckland has the
potential for a volcanic erupti on as well as being considerab ly exposed in the event of
any tsunami. And we can sit and laugh about th at, as they are doing on the other side of
96 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
the House, and say: “Well, it may never happ en.” or “It probably will never happen.”
Well, I would hope it does not—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Don’t be so crass!

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, I was not talking to you, Mr Cosgrove; you
show very few emotions at any time. I was talking to Mr Mallar d, who is behind you,
who is finding these things somewhat amusi ng. What I would say is  that no one can be
certain in saying that we should just put these things on the long finger.
But it is going to mean change for a lot of  New Zealanders. It is going to be a big
cost to our economy. You cannot escape the fact  that changes to the way in which an
insurance market views Christchurch will filt er through to the rest of the country as
well. So we are going about things down th ere in a very considered fashion—not being
knee-jerked into fast decisi ons, but at the same time not  taking so long as to be
unreasonable—in making sure that the province and the capital city of that province do
have a future.
I think that the Government’s programme is  comprehensive; I think it very clearly
points towards the sort of growth New Zeal anders would expect. New Zealanders will
also be able to see in a very short time that the continuation of the National-led
Government will be very much to their advantage and will make sure that their lives are
better for the future.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: There is a rumour going
around, actually, that Gerry Brownlee is th inking of changing his name to Gerry
Dotcom in order to get access to National’s economic plan, which I understand is in a
cyber-locker somewhere, caught up in the Me gaupload debacle. I sa y that because we
have once again seen from the Prime Minister in the state of the nation speech—the so-
called state of the nation speech—the absence of an economic plan.
We also saw that in his response in the Address in Reply debate. I am not sure
whether the Prime Minister is a fan of Rona n Keating, the Irish singer who was in town
last week, but in outlining his vision for Ne w Zealand the Prime Minister seems to have
adopted the words of one of  Ronan Keating’s favourite s ongs: “You say it best when
you say nothing at all.” That is the Prime Mi nister’s approach—nothing at all. There
was nothing at all in the stat e of the nation speech, and nothi ng at all in the Address in
Reply speech—nothing at all, that is, except for one thing: sell it off. The pathway to the
PM’s heralded brighter future is paved with “For Sale” signs.
Well, the message for Mr Key is that you cannot sell your way to a brighter future.
The Prime Minister is getti ng that message loud and clear from the 70-plus percent of
New Zealanders who do not want their assets sold. He  heard the message from M āori
loud and clear this past weekend. From those at the flax-roots through to the iwi leaders,
they do not want these assets sold.
You would have thought that for something that is the centrep iece of National’s
programme for this year there might have been a little bit more  thought given to the
removal of the single most significant legislative clause for M āori in this area: section 9
of the State-Owned Enterprises Act. Goodness, I was in form 4 in 1986 and I knew
about the Lands case and the genesis of section 9. Mr Key was at Elders Merchant
Finance at the time, I think—too busy selli ng things, I suspect, to actually notice the
significant political action. To claim, as Mr Key has done, that section 9 is symbolic and
not relevant is not only a slap in the face to M āori but symptomatic of the shambles that
now surrounds this asset sales process.
Mr Key is looking for an elegant solution to the problem he has created. Well, I have
got an elegant solution for Mr Key: do not se ll the assets. That is the elegant solution:
do not sell the assets, listen to New Zealanders, and keep Kiwi assets in Kiwi hands.
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 97
But there is a very good reason why this Government is so determined to press ahead
with asset sales: it is that it is all they have got. The plan to lift our  economic sights
comes down to selling off our future, hoping  someone will dig up some wealth, and
cutting public services. Now, wh atever the merits of cuts to  the public sector, I can say
this to the Government: it will not provide the answer to the lack of a plan for the
economy.
That is what the Government has in store for New Zealand: sell , cut, hope. That is
the plan. That is the total of the strategy: sell, cut, hope. It is a tired, old theory and it
fails to grasp one of the core opportunities that lie in front of New Zealand: the
opportunity to base our futu re on ideas and po licies that see th e economy and the
environment as two sides of the same coi n. The notion that in order to grow our
economy we must compromise our environmen t comes from another century. It comes
from the same century as the trickle-down economics practised by the party opposite.
For Labour, we recognise that our future li es in the development of companies and
people who are smart, clean, and green. Da vid Shearer has alre ady talked about
LanzaTech in this debate. In  universities, Crown research  institutes, and businesses
throughout this country there are people w ho have the ideas that will propel our
economy forward. We must invest  in those people, and we know that this can happen
only if the economy and the environment go together, hand in hand. That is Labour’s
vision, and we will continue to promote positive ideas in that space over this term.
New Zealanders’ passion for our environment is something that I believe truly unites
us as a nation. The horror that  greeted the grounding of the Rena and its impact on
birdlife, the coastal environment, and our  beaches and oceans resounded throughout
New Zealand. Was it not interesting to hear Nick Smith today? Despite telling New
Zealanders that he was going to throw the fu ll force of the law at those responsible for
the grounding of the Rena, it turns out that that amounts to a hope that the Bay of Plenty
Regional Council might take a case. That is the full force of the law from Nick Smith.
That is how much protecting the environment seems to mean to him. That is how much
of a priority he wants to make it.
In the wake of some of what happened at Waitangi it could be easy to focus on issues
that divide us, but I believe that the protec tion of our waterways and our coastlines is
something that all New Zealanders—M āori and P ākehā alike—want to see made a
priority, and Labour will certainly be doing this. In the environmental space that priority
must be seen in the management of fresh water. The M āori Council has a right to put a
claim to the Waitangi Tribunal, and we will awa it the court process, as is the right thing
to do with that. But let us be absolutely clear: this would not be happening if the
Government was not selling assets. This woul d not be needed if the Government was
not selling assets, and the solution, which the M āori Party knows, which the M āori
Council knows, and which this Government s hould know, is that this  could all stop if
the sale of those assets stops.
There was an absence from Mr Key’s stat e of the nation speech—and, indeed, from
his contribution to this deba te—of the environment, but there was also an absence of
discussion on the pressing social issues of our time: inequality and child poverty. If
Gerry Brownlee wants to find evidence of a bi partisan approach, I say that three times
in the last term of Government Annette King wrote to the Gove rnment and said we
would cooperate on child poverty. David Sheare r said straight after being elected as
leader that we want to be part of a par liamentary committee that deals with issues of
poverty, and this year Jacinda Ardern has rep eated the call. That is  bipartisanship, Mr
Brownlee. That is where the opportunity is in  this House for us to work together and
address child poverty, and it ha s been rejected by the Nati onal Government, not by the
Labour Party.
98 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
When we look at child poverty, the one reacti on we have seen from this Government
was its trying to stop New Zealanders hearing about it. It is outrageous that the showing
of a documentary on child poverty just befo re the election would generate from Mr
Key’s electorate chair a complaint and an a ttempt to stop it. The problem with the
broadcast of that documentar y was that it was the only on e on those sort s of issues
before the election. What we need prior to an election in New Zealand is more
information for the public, not less.
Public broadcasting in this country is in  serious danger. We need quality public
broadcasting. It is good for democracy, it is good for accountability, and it is good for
public participation. This Government is starving Radio New Zealand of funds and
dismantling one of the few remaining pieces of public broadcasting, in the form of
TVNZ 7. It is not good enough, and it is es pecially not good enough for New Zealand
On Air to be used in such a political way.
What that documentary on child poverty highlighted was the huge damage being
done to New Zealand and the loss of the potential of those involved. It is simple stuff. If
you live in a cold, draughty, damp home, you will get sick. If you do not have food in
your cupboards, your kids will go to school hungry and they will not learn as well. If it
costs too much to go to the doctor, you just will not go. Child poverty is a moral issue.
It is, as David Shearer has said, a human ri ghts issue for those ch ildren, and it is a
shame on this Government that the Prime Mi nister in his state of the nation speech
failed to even mention these issues.
Six billion dollars a year is lost to the New Zeala nd economy through child poverty,
but of similar importance to our society is the loss of em pathy that goes with growing
inequality in our country. When the salaries of chief executive officers grow 14 percent
in a year but the salaries of those on the fact ory floor grow by only 2 percent, we have a
growing problem. As gated communities grow  around us, we have a problem. We need
answers that are sensible but that are also visionary. We must invest in our people.
Many New Zealanders are f acing tough times, and when that happens we know that
New Zealanders will come together and pitch in. We have got to us e our brains and we
have got to invest in people, get them into  education, give people a chance to achieve
their potential, and allow them to live live s that will allow them to achieve their
potential. We need sensible solutions; we need positive solutions. What we do not need
is sell, cut, and hope, and that is all we have seen from this National Government.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: At least Labour members are
looking a bit thoughtful now, because after the 2008 election they all sat there thinking
“Haven’t the public made a dreadful mistake?  They didn’t really mean to vote us out;
they put in that flaky John Key and the Na tional Government.” They sat there puzzling
about how the public could have made that mistake. In 2011 they came back after the
election and they are thinking “How did the public do it again? How did they make the
same mistake again?”.
You see, Labour members still do not understand that it is the public that is right, and
Labour that is wrong. It is not a mistake that they lost seat s and vote share in the last
election; it was the deliberate intent of  the New Zealand public to send one more
message—because the last one had not arrive d—that the nasty, stale Labour Party was
irrelevant. Until they start talking about what matters to New Zealanders instead of what
matters to the Labour Party, nothing is going to change. I welcome this new
thoughtfulness. They are sitting there, scra tching their heads, thinking “How did the
public get it wrong again?”. Well, the public did not get it wrong; it got it right.
In listening to the deputy leader of the Labour Party, I can only say that I am sure his
colleagues hope that he does not disappear as quickly as he did when he became the
tertiary education spokesman, never to be heard from again. I am told—because I was
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 99
not aware of this—that apparently he was the health spokesman. Is that not meant to be
one of Labour’s strongest issu es? Apparently he was the h ealth spokesman; well, he
disappeared quickly from that. Now he is the environment spokesman. I just say to
Labour that the Greens do it a lot better. Th ey do it a lot better. The way they think
about the environment and the economy is mo re sensible and more sophisticated—well,
more sophisticated but not that sensible—than what Labour will ever come up with.
With the old arrogance of the Labour Part y, the deputy leader is saying there is a
balance between the economy and the environmen t, as if that is some new idea. No one
has thought of that before! Well, if he come s to my electorate to see people who would
never think of voting Labour, but vote National,  he will see that they are spending
hundreds of thousands of dollars of their ow n money finding exactly that balance, and
changing their farming practices trying to find that balance.
They know what Labour means when it says  a balance between the environment and
the economy. It means bigger government, ma king more rules, taking more tax, and
borrowing more money. That is actually what that means, whereas what they will get
from this Government is strong support for the competitive export economy. That is one
of the priorities of the Government through this term of office. Our first priority is to get
back to surplus—to manage the Government finances prudently to get back to surplus
by 2014-15. To continue the process of re building New Zealand’s international
competitiveness is our second priority. The thir d one is to deliver better public services,
and the final one is to rebuild Christchurch.
I want to refer to the need to continue  rebuilding the competitive economy. I think
few New Zealanders understand just how da maging the custodianship  of the previous
Labour Government was—to be fair, they we re part of a movement across developed
economies around the world—where our export sector actually shrank in the first
decade of this century. Even though the wo rld economy was growing faster than ever,
our ability to earn income by selling to that world actually shrank. However, our ability
to spend what we were not earning grew fa ntastically well. The gap, of course, was
filled by borrowing. A more competitive econo my has to be about the movement of
resources—that is, people and capital—into the tradable sector.
We want to see in the next 5 years somethi ng we did not see in the last 10 years, and
that is job growth in the e xport sector. Today there are ha rdly any more jobs in the
export sector than there were 10 years ago, so very little of the job growth of the last 10
years actually occurred in the income earni ng side of our economy. The prospects for
that are pretty good, as long as Government gets behind and pushes hard. Those
prospects are good because the markets into  which we are sel ling increasingly are
growing reasonably fast and our export sector has become remarkably resilient.
In this context I want to pay a particular tribute to the manufacturing sector, which in
recent years has continued to grow when, fo r instance, the Australian manufacturing
sector has been shrinking. That is because they have worked out how to be adept, fast-
moving, adaptable organisations finding their niche in a very competitive world.
The Government will be focusing on this rebalancing of the economy. The sources of
growth over the next few years, I think, ar e reasonably clear now. Our continued high
export prices are actually as high as they ha ve been since the late 1960s, and if those
prices can hold up even somewhere near wher e they are now, that will continue to add
wealth and jobs to the New Zealand economy.
Another source of growth will be the Ch ristchurch rebuild. There is roughly $20
billion that needs to be spent in Christchurch; only $2 billion has been spent so far. It is
already having an impact on New Zealanders ’ incomes. We see in the labour market
figures coming out today the growth in cons truction wages in Christchurch of around 8
percent in the last year—more than double the average wa ge increase across the rest of
100 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
the economy. Of course, we will have to watc h out for inflationary effects of a wage
blowout, but there will be t housands of new jobs and huge  investment going on in
Christchurch. Whatever discussions they might be having among themselves about their
local council, they have shown remarkable resilience and persistence about the recovery
of that city.
I want to make a few remarks about another of the Government’s objectives, and that
is to deliver better public services. I think the Public Service has now understood that
this is not just a passing phase  of fiscal restraint; it is now  permanent. It will never go
back to the days it enjoyed in the first decade of this century when, because of the
economic situation, it had money pouring in th e door. I want to pay tribute here to the
leadership of the Public Service. Across Government departments they have got to grips
with the new reality, and worked with the G overnment through a co nsidered process of
getting ready for significant change. Some of  them have already executed significant
change. Almost all of them are planning sign ificant change in the delivery of public
services.
The Government will be focusing very strong ly on ensuring that the service to the
public is the same or better as we reduce the costs of delivering that service. But it will
be a challenge. Over the next 3 or 4 year s most Government departments will get no
new money. So we would not want to  underestimate the challenges and the
discussion—vigorous discussion, I am su re—that is going to flow from the
Government’s ambition to deliver better public services despite the fact that the budget
is very tight.
The Prime Minister set out the objectives for the Government in his state of the
nation speech. We expect to get on with that  agenda in this Parliament and through
Cabinet, and we also expect that the New Zealand public have had to, in a pragmatic
frame of mind, go through their own process of  making change in their households and
their businesses because of the economic circumstances. They can look forward to
reasonable and moderate growth over the next few years, the opportunity for wage
increases and better incomes—many of them have not had wage increases in recent
years—and a Government that is strongly suppo rtive of their aspira tions and is willing
to do the hard work now necessary to fulfil  those aspirations in a world where it has
become a lot more difficult than it was in the last 10 years.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: That speech spent 50
percent of the time criticising Labour in Opposition. Unbelievable. A speech from the
Minister of Finance spent 50 percent of the time on crit icism of Labour in Opposition,
rather than on telling New Zealanders what the Government’s plan is for the future.
[Interruption] OK, so the last 50 percent was an attempt to do that, but it is unbelievable
that we are attacked in O pposition and the Government is not standing up for what it
believes in. That is why I am pleased to be able to support the amendment to the
motion, as moved by David Shearer, to add the following words: “and the National-led
Government will sell New Zealand’s asse ts against the will of the public; the
Government has no ideas to create jobs or a clean and innovative New Zealand; that the
Government is widening the gap between the very rich and the rest  and therefore this
House has no confidence in the National-led government.”
I am pleased to be able to speak today. As I went through the Speech from the
Throne, there were three key things that  the Government highlighted that would
underpin its way of doing things  in this term. The first wa s a confidence and supply
agreement—a strong one—with Un ited Future, ACT, and the M āori Party. Well, less
than 2 months later we see that that c onfidence and supply agreement is under threat.
The one opportunity the M āori Party had to hold this Government to account in
question time was not utilised by the M āori Party, and we should be concerned about
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 101
that. In fact, it forebodes that the Government is on shaky ground and the Māori Party is
probably poised to pull the plug.
The second pillar of the Government’s age nda, or strength going fo rward, is that it
claimed that it would operate in an effective,  inclusive, and stable manner. What have
we seen? There are already claims from within its ranks that the Government has not
been inclusive, and that it is not creating st ability, by not being upfr ont in its coalition
arrangements with its parties. Well, either the M āori Party is not telling the truth about
National or the Government is fudging the truth on the Māori Party. Which one is it?

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: Both.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: It probably is both, as my colleague points out.
We should be really concerned about this. The country deserves a stable Government
that is inclusive and consults with communities in a real way—not a rushed consultation
of 2 weeks, 3 weeks, or maybe a month, if we are lucky, but real, genuine consultation,
and not predetermined outcomes, as we have seen is the case on asset sales and the
Government’s consultation with M āori, but genuine opportunities for people to give
feedback. But what we see here is that the M āori Party itself, a coalition member of this
arrangement, is highlighting some very real cracks in its arrangements with National.
The third pillar to the relationship of this  Government going forward is to build a
more competitive and internationally focuse d economy. But we have already seen, in
less than 2 months, the Crafar farms sold offshore to the highest bidder when there were
New Zealand interests on the table and many people throughout the country were
hoping there would be a real oppo rtunity for Kiwi lands to stay in Kiwi hands. That did
not happen. I think the Government is really underestimating the level of sentiment that
is out there in provincial New Zealand, in  our communities, amongst a wide range of
people who say we should be looking for ways to keep Kiwi lands in Kiwi hands.
What else have we seen? We have seen the Government steamrolling ahead with its
plan to sell State-owned enterprises. Granted, it was a ke y election platform of National
going forward at the last election. But to say that this Government has a mandate to sell
State assets, I think, is clearly overrepresenti ng the truth. In fact, if  the Government on
that question alone was to put the moral mandate for the sale of State-owned enterprises
to the House—and I would challenge the House and seek leave of the House to put that
vote, certainly in terms of the M āori mandate to the M āori electorate MPs, to see
whether the Government has any support at all to sell State-owned assets. You know,
the Iwi Leaders Forum should not be a defa ult for a parliamentary mandate of people
who have been elected to represent the views of their communities on issues like this. It
is just too important to fritt er away New Zealand assets where there is strong public
sentiment that we should be keeping them and reinvesting in them to benefit all
Kiwis—all New Zealand families.
Again, this question of moral mandate is some thing I want to focus on a little bit,
primarily because the Government will tell you again and again that the election result
in itself was a mandate to sell State-owne d assets. But what we have in the House,
clearly, is the fact that the Greens do not support the sale of St ate-owned assets, New
Zealand First does not s upport the sale of State-owned assets, the M āori Party does not
support the sale of State-owned assets, and neither does Mana. And Labour campaigned
on this issue as a core policy: we believe d selling State assets was not a long-term
investment in the future of this countr y. Rather, it was short-sighted and would not
deliver gains.
So how is it, in a parliamentary majority  like the one we see here—those 61—that
the great views of all New Zeal anders will be represented? We have diversity in this
House. MMP clearly delivered an opportunity for all Kiwis to represent that diversity in
the parliamentary make-up, and I accept the ou tcome. But to say that one vote in this
102 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
House then shifts the moral mandate of the Government to sell State-owned assets? I
would caution: “Think again.”
In 2 short weeks the Government will be undertaking a consultation round,
particularly with iwi, on this  issue. At Waitangi we saw ev idence of the fact that there
are very strong views amongst M āori and amongst iwi on this particular issue, and on
removing section 9 from the State-Owned Ente rprises Act. I support the opportunity for
Māori to contribute to the decision and think about what is on the table, but 2 weeks for
a consultation? Come on! To call that co nsultation, I think, is  a big disingenuous. We
did hear the Minister for State Owned Ente rprises in question time today almost imply
that that was ample time for consultation on this very important issue.
There is probably going to be a lot more water to go under th is bridge before
decisions can be made with some convi ction that the Trea ty interests of M āori and of
iwi will be protected. But La bour will watch this process ve ry carefully. We will be
seeking feedback of our own on the process, as  we believe, and continue to assert, that
State asset sales will not deliver long-term bene fits to the country or to Kiwi families.
We are convinced that there is no future in selling State assets. We all own those assets,
and we do not want to be tenants in our own c ountry. If this is the brighter future that
National promised, then someone had better sh ine some more light down the hole it is
sitting in.
Labour believes that there is no greater investment in the fu ture of this country than
ensuring that all of our children get the ve ry best from a quali ty public education
system. The Government seems determined to push ahead with national standards, even
though they were not supported by the sector. They seem determined to increase class
sizes for efficiency’s sake but not for the value of the learning outcomes of our children.
They want to push ahead with charte r schools when the evidence overseas is
inconclusive. How it will be applied to the New Zealand context will further lead to
greater concern amongst the education professionals; they are saying that now.
Education is just far too important to push along with blatan t ideology. What we
need is a high performing education system that invests in all our children and their
learning capability. When I went to listen to  Sir Paul Callaghan he said that at the
foundation of the New Zealand education syst em we must recognise that we are a
unique country, and that the language, culture, and identit y of all our people must
underpin a strong education system. I believe that is the case—not larger class sizes, not
charter schools, not national standards, a nd certainly not shifting more money into
private schools.
An export-led economy can be guaranteed on ly if we have a high-skilled population
where all our children can thrive, not a sy stem where there are winners and losers.
National has very few plans on this front . The high rate of underachievement of
vulnerable children, of children living in poverty, and of M āori and Pacific children is
something that we should all be concerned about, because if this continues in our
education system, the export-led economy th at National is talking about cannot be
realised to the full value of every Kiwi livi ng in this country. Far too many of them are
missing out. The Government should be very accountable to those who are most in need
and those who are vulnerable—not losers, as Gerry Brownlee put it, but those most in
need and most vulnerable. If we can see the benefits of that in education, then we will
see a great investment in the future of this country.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.role: Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector
items.text: I
begin my address this afternoon by saying that I am heartene d to hear some words from
the other side of the House th at, in fact, are words that—[ Interruption] There are some
common ideas here about protecting the vulne rable—that is what we did during the
recession—and, in fact, about improving the ability of those who are vulnerable to
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 103
actually get a good education. That is what this Government is actually doing. An
export-led recovery—we heard that several times. It is just th at here in th is Parliament
this Government is delivering it in a totally different styl e from the style that was under
the Clark Government, where I believe th at member was a Minister. So on 26
November the people of New Zealand spoke, and as in all elections the mood of the day
in the months leading up to the election wa s reflected in the vot e. The people of New
Zealand voted an increased percentage for this the National Government led by John
Key. You know, in elections in times gone by it was most unusual for a second-term
Government to have an increased percenta ge of the vote—most unusual, indeed. But
that, in fact, is what the people of New Z ealand delivered on elect ion day last year. I
would like to spend a bit of time rehearsing why I think that happened.
As a nation we have had a pretty tough tim e of it. In fact, you know, the vulnerable
of this nation have had the toughest time of it. Unfortunately, New Zealand actually
beat the gun into recession, and that was again because of the policies of the Clark
Government. So having settled into the real ms of recession, with job losses occurring
and youth unemployment getting higher and higher , and given the fact that the tradable
sector had not actually started to shrink sinc e the recession but had started that very
early, back in 2004, I believe, way before th e recession, the State sector had been
allowed—no, not allowed, perhaps; nay, en couraged—to gobble th rough the healthy
surpluses as if there was no tomorrow. Bu t then, of course, hang on, there was no
tomorrow for the Clark Government come N ovember 2008. So we added to that toxic
mix of tax and spend devastating earthquak es, and a raft of other challenges. New
Zealand was facing down the barrel of many gloomy tomorrows.
But John Key, his Ministers, and MPs were up to the challenge. Really, was there a
choice? They had to step up to the mark, and they did. So after years of tax and spend,
this Government certainly set out, knowing th at was not the way to a brighter future in
New Zealand. We had the sobering respons ibility of managing the economy and the
country through tough times, protecting those who were the most vulnerable, and all the
while there were additional vul nerable people being added to  that group. That is what
happens in a recession. The trust and th e goodwill that the public of New Zealand
conferred upon us on election day—26 Novemb er—was, in fact, a solemn challenge.
Our status as a First World nation has come under threat from the policies of old, the
policies of the last Government under Clark. Now, in order to further protect vulnerable
New Zealanders, we have to challenge the policy settings. We have to change those
policy settings to enduring and sustaina ble policies so, in fact, we lessen our
vulnerability. Strong, continue d, and stable Government is  the way forward, but the
stability has to be with a purpose—the purpos e to grow our economy, so we all have a
brighter future.
The plan is a comprehensive one, and that  action plan was announced in policy prior
to the election. It is not a one- liner. It is not about tax and sp end; it is about a brighter
future. There is a fair heap of work in there that needs to be  done. But it is worth
working hard for; it is worth striving for. We have four prioritie s, and those priorities
lay down the challenges that we must achieve to have a brighter future.
The finance Minister spoke  in the House today about New Zealand earning an
income, not borrowing it. There has never been a truer word spoken. New Zealand
families who are making ends meet at this pa rt of the year, when it is so tough for
families in the post-Christmas and getting-in to-school time, are making ends meet with
their finances, so they are very pleased to h ear that our No. 1 prior ity is to responsibly
manage the Government’s finances. You see, as I often reassure my constituents, it is
not the Government’s money. That is the way the Clark Government treated it, but it is
not the Government’s money. It is taxpayers’ money. They worked hard to earn it, and
104 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
they want us to make very good use of it. Our second priority is about building a more
productive and competitive economy, and that is a pathway to a brighter future. The
third priority is about examining public se rvices under this tight  fiscal setting and
making our public services better. Lastly, and one that resonates very much with me and
with the other Canterbury MPs, is our pr iority to rebuild our second-largest city,
Christchurch. I will say something I have said  in speeches over the last year or so: you
know, I just do not think the majority of Ne w Zealanders even knew it was our second-
largest city until we started describing it as that, as we identified the magnitude of the
task ahead. So I am heartened that the re build is amongst the top four. As Canterbury
MPs we respect the work that  has already been done by the Government. We are very,
very pleased that there is money in the bank for that rebuild.
New Zealand’s future economic stability is going to be best served by our being
returned to surplus by 2014-15, but it needs a firm and steady hand on the tiller to
achieve that. Well, there are lots of analogies around the place about making the boat go
faster, and I would like to remind the House of the spectre of a combination of the
parties opposite steering our boat, “New Zealand” . With their combined policies, I
believe we were looking at a potential Costa Concordia. Being fiscally responsible is
not just about balancing the Government’s books; the flow-on to the people of New
Zealand will also mean it will be keeping pre ssure off interest rates, which is the single-
biggest cost to our households. We need to  reverse, as a nation, the downward spiral
that the Clark Government thrust New Zealan d into when the tradable sector was not
growing. New Zealand was always going to be living beyond its means and its
productive capacity under setti ngs such as that. We want  to see an export-focused
economy, built on a solid base of innovation, selli ng more of what the world wants, at a
competitive price. That is actually quite a big ask; that is quite a comprehensive goal to
be setting.
Our economic action plan will follow through on the progress we have actually made
in the last 3 years. We have prioritised bett er public services, a nd we have made some
good progress already. We have found the phant om trainees in the industry training
organisation sector; we have actually found them, and we know that money was going
to waste. We are reforming Government pur chasing of supplies such as vehicles and
information technology hardware, and, you know, the first four joint procurement
projects alone are expected to save around $115 million over the next 5 years. There are
many more examples. The programme of acti on is comprehensive. Now, we are also
looking at the State sector, right across it, at  how it is organised. We need to streamline
and improve the way it works, for New Zealand’s sake.
Lastly, I want to touch again on that fourth  priority, of rebuilding Christchurch. We
are getting on with the challenge. It is a monstrously big challenge. Much of the
demolition has taken place, and I want to pay tribute to the former Timaru District
Council chief executive, Warwick Isaacs, who is handling some of the overseeing of the
demolition projects. Empty spaces create opportunities for rebuilding. There will be
grief and there will be loss at what those empty spaces mean—the memories. But
Christchurch deserves a Government that is purposefully going to commit to rebuilding
it. The people of Canterbury deserve that. We  have put in 4,500 places for construction-
related training in Canterbury and around the country, and we have also put a temporary
17,000-seat stadium in there for the Cantabrians who love sport. It is a bit like saying
“Is the Pope Catholic?”—of cour se they love spor t down in Canterbury. So it is very
much one of our high priorities: $5.5 bil lion committed to the Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery Fund. That is this Government ’s share of that money—that is, this
Government’s share of rebuilding local in frastructure—and to repair Crown-owned
assets.
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 105
We have a big challenge ahead  of us as a Government. T hose four priorities say it
all. They are part of a wider economic de velopment plan that will build a stronger
economy for New Zealand. It is a big challenge, but this Government is up to it.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: In December last year in the Speech from the
Throne delivered by the Gove rnor General, the Prime Mi nister did two things: he
identified what he called the “driving goal” of  his Government, and he laid out what he
called a “comprehensive agenda” and a s ubstantive legislative programme to
accomplish that goal. I thank the Prime Mi nister for setting out a rational and
systematic, if rather visionle ss, exploration of the Governme nt’s approach to the 50th
Parliament. His comments were repeated toda y by the Minister of Finance, and, just
most recently, by Jo Goodhew. They summarise it in terms of four priorities as they see
it: returning to surplus, ensuring a compe titive economy, cutting the Public Service and
making it efficient, and rebuilding Christchurch. As she said, and they said, that is part
of a broader programme for the rede mption—the economic redemption—of this
country.
So let me assess the Prime Minister’s driv ing goal that underlies his Government’s
political agenda and legislative programme, and then I shall offer, on the same basis, an
alternative goal, agenda, and legislative pr ogramme of a Green Government. The Prime
Minister explained that the driving goal of this Government is “to build a more
competitive and internationally-focused econom y with less debt, more jobs and higher
incomes.” This was to be pursued, he said, within the challenging context of an ongoing
global financial crisis; the euro debt crisis ; recovery from a series of devastating
earthquakes in Canterbury; and a difficult recovery from a major national recession.
The Prime Minister then outlined a comp rehensive policy agenda: a blow-by-blow
account of oft-repeated lines of around 20 ite ms. The environment and climate change
did not make the agenda until over halfwa y through. His comprehensive policy agenda
is a rational, if rather pede strian, plan by a practical, if rather visionless, Government.
Where, for example, is this Government’s vi sion for a brighter future for the people—
for a more inclusive and harmonious New Zealand society? Where is this Government’s
vision to make New Zealand a responsible global citizen? A strong economy certainly
enables financial resources with a view to returning to surplus, but it does not, on its
own, buy social and environmental justice and responsibility. These must be envisioned
and enacted.
So what is to be found in the political agenda and the legisla tive programme of the
Government? As I said, we can count 20 in  the Speech from the Throne. First, and
presumably most important, it seeks to return into operating surplus by 2014-15. Of
course, that is laudable e nough, although there is huge scep ticism over the prospects of
this occurring. Secondly, it plans to ensure a lower cap on core Government staff. This
is, of course, an ideological twitch on the part of a National Government. Brilliantly the
Prime Minister says that his Government will be focused on achieving results! Now
there is a statement and vision and practical determination! There is not a Government
in the 155 years of responsible government in this country that has not assured the
voting public that it is intent  on the Public Servi ce achieving results. It  simply begs the
question of how we go about doing that.
Then there is the policy for what is mellifluously known as the mixed-ownership
model. What that means is selling off our State assets overseas. It means the
socialisation of the losses and the privatisation of the profits, as we saw during the
financial crisis the Prime Minister cited as one of the problems his Government is
encountering. There are other policies on welfare, on education, on innovation for
entrepreneurship, and on strengthening infrastructure through building roads of national
106 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
insignificance. There are changes ahead for housing and health, the ACC, and tougher
law and order policies. There is a stray reference to the so-called constitutional review.
Then the Government purports to cover fo reign policy, defence, and trade. It will
focus on Pacific aid and run for a seat on the UN Security Council. It will maintain a
bipartisan foreign policy. It will implement the Defence Capability Plan and continue to
pursue high-quality trade agreements. This G overnment’s chances of securing a seat on
the Security Council will be enhanced if it acts as a responsible global citizen through
genuine multilateralism rather than crabbi ng its way back to the mid - 20th century,
searching for military security through be ing very good friends with selected powers—
panting, tongue hanging out.
The Government trumpets a bipartisan foreign policy, thereby displaying its
ignorance of the multiparty nature of MMP, which has been in force for nearly two
decades, or it betrays a sublim inal preference for first past the post. Because the foreign
policy of this Government cannot be descri bed as globally resp onsible it is not
bipartisanly shared by the Green Party.
We need an alternative vision of how this country can develop—how it can act in the
wider world. Let me describe today a Gree n vision for a sustai nable, richer New
Zealand—a New Zealand that is a responsible global citizen, that recognises the need to
be integrated globally, not just in economic terms but in environmental and social terms,
as well. The Green vision for a strong economy is one that  is fully entwined with
environmental sustainability and social responsibility. It is a vision that lives within our
means, and lives up to our clear, clean, green  image. The Green economic vision has an
expanded and more comprehensive measure of what success is. A Green Government
would draw on measures such as the genui ne progress indicator, which would benefit
those who must inherit this economy from us . In political terms, in New Zealand the
distinction is this: National believes that economic growth has a horizon, and that that
horizon can be progressively pushed back th rough human ingenuity, provided a decent
respect is paid to the environment. La bour has bought into th at belief, though not
