without some anxiety. The Green belief is that economic growth has a limit, and that
that limit is natural, immutable, and non-negotiable, requiring humanity to live
harmoniously within its parameters, and at a certain material point to develop along
cultural and spiritual lines rather than through simply further economic growth. There is
a natural end point to economic growth.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: When?

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The member says “When?”. When there is a Green
Government; you are invited to vote accordingly. There are qualitatively different world
views here. There is no deeper distinc tion between National and Labour thought, and
Green thought, than this: the Green social vi sion is compassionate. Economic growth is
not progressed if it occurs at the expense of social equality. The Green vision recognises
that research and development are integral  to progress. Where the Prime Minister
repeats again that his Government intends to build more roads and get ultra-fast
broadband, the Green vision sees research as invaluable to realising an innovative and
sustainable future that does not further our reliance on finite and harmful fossil fuels. I
call on this Government to re view its own Speech from the Throne, and introduce into
its driving goal, its agenda, and its legislative programme at least part of the Green
vision. The people may have voted this Gove rnment in—just—but the people also want
the Green vision that I have described.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I want to
spend my time in this Address in Reply debate addressing just the one issue, and that is
to do with the sale of land to foreigners. I want to start by just putting a bit of my
personal credentials on the table. I am  a sixth-generation New Zealander. The
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 107
Williamson family came here in the mid-1800s  from Scotland and settled, and have
been farmers along the way. So I do not thi nk that anyone could say I am some great
desirer of new foreigners taking over, because I have a family history of being from this
country. My 89-year-old mother lives peacef ully in Matamata, where I was brought up
in a dairy-farming town, and I must say that  I think probably 97 pe rcent of the people
there will disagree with the decision that I have taken recently. I think I said to her that I
have now got 97 percent of New Zealanders who hate me, and she said: “Is that down
from 98, beforehand?”, so who knows?
What I want to make clear in this debate is that Ministers have some discretion when
there are issues of doubt, but it is very clear from the Act, and it was very clear from the
advice that was given to Mini sters from Crown Law that no discretion exists if the
applicant meets every one of the criteria that  are in the current Overseas Investment Act
2005, passed by the Labour Government, and the corresponding regulations that go with
it. Ministers cannot just say: “Well, I don’t care what the law says; I’m just going to
exercise discretion and say no.” I have to tell members that there is such a thing as a
judicial review and you would simply lose the case. If the Minister was taken to judicial
review, he or she would lose the case if they were not able to say: “Mr Judge, I declined
this because…”. Now, in the case of the Na tural Dairy bid to buy th ese Crafar farms, I
am happy to say that I put my signature to the decline. It failed to meet a number of the
criteria under the Act. Some members of  this House have claimed: “Oh yeah,
Williamson just rubber-stamps them.” I did not rubber-stamp that application. I declined
it, because it did not meet the requirements.
In the case of Kim Dotcom wanting to buy the Coatesville mansion, again, it got a
decline. It got a decline that was able to be substantiated based on character and, as
members will have seen from what has been playing out in the media in recent days,
there may have been quite a good decision taken. But in the case of Shanghai Pengxin
looking to buy these farms, it met every one of the criteria that are laid down in the Act
passed by the Labour Government, and it met ev ery one of the criteri a laid out in the
regulations—and remember that National even  added two more criteria to try to
strengthen the Act and the regulations, so that  we did have a little bit more say, and all
of those were met as well. So my frustration first, today, is with any one of the members
of this House or of the public who say: “Oh, you just should have said no.” When David
Shearer and David Parker from the Labour Part y said that they would have said no, my
very first question to them is on what grounds they would have said no. Remember, you
do not just have the final say in this; there are courts, and Governments have been found
by the courts to have acted inappropriately  on a number of things, and they have
overturned Ministers’ decisions. Take Chris Carter and the Whitianga waterways—

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: Whangamata.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: —or the Whangamata whatever it is. The
Minister got overturned by the courts, because he did not follow the proper procedure.
The next thing that I find really diffi cult—because I do know there are some
absolutely genuine people who do not want fo reigners buying land in  this country. I do
understand that. I do not think there are many, but I actually fully respect those
individuals who truly are cons istent all along the way and sa y: “I do not want foreign
ownership of our land.” But I think they are few and far between. The first one I do not
understand is from those who were born in another country and sp ent the vast bulk of
their life in another country. Russel Norman, for example, was born in Brisbane, grew
up in Australia, and was an Australian all his life until he came here to write his PhD on
the Alliance, yet he is getting up in this House and saying he does not want foreigners to
buy land, and he is going on Breakfast saying he does not want foreigners to buy land. I,
first of all, want to question his definition of what a foreigne r is, because if he says it is
108 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
as long as people come here to live, what about those ones like  Shania Twain, who
came here, bought a huge high-c ountry estate, and had the Prime Minister Helen Clark
walking with her across it for the photo opportunity? New Zealande rs celebrated that.
We celebrated Shania Twain’s purchase of th is beautiful, big South Island high-country
estate, saying: “Wasn’t it wonderful?”. I ne ver heard a mutter, not a murmur, not a
whisper from anybody about how dreadful that was—not one, and I have checked all of
the newspaper articles. I have checked all of the speeches in this House—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: All the newspapers?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, I am sorry; I got the research unit to go
through them, and I have found not a mutter, not a murmur, not a whisper of how evil
that was.
There have been lots and lots of others to the point, and let me give you some
figures. First of all, I want to give a ster n warning to the news media, which used so
many figures during this debate that we re wrong. And I will tell you why. There is a
whole range of different numbers that you can use. For example, there is gross sale to
foreigners, or there is net. Now gross, in  my view, does not matte r, because gross is
where a German sells the land to a Swiss, a Swiss sells it to a French person, and a
French person sells it to an American. Thos e do not really matter, because they were
already owned by foreigners; they were al ready in foreign ownership. For me, the
number that I think does matter is net,  because net is where the land has been
transferred from the ownership of a New Zeala nd entity to that of a foreigner. That, I
think, matters, because it makes a difference; the other one did not. You may think there
is a difference between a Swiss and a Germ an owning the same piece of land, but I do
not think there really is. Here are the nu mbers. During Labour’s 9 years in office it
approved the sale—and this is net; I will stick with net figures for the rest of this
debate—of 660,000 hectares of land, net, to foreigners.
One of my favourite years was the year 2006, when Winston Peters was the Minister
of Foreign Affairs in the then  Government. He was the Mini ster of Foreign Affairs in
the then Government and it approved the sale  of 375,000 hectares of land to foreigners
that year, and not a mutter, not a murmur, not  a whisper. So I ha ve to say there is
something funny going on here. It is one of these sorts of “Mahareyisms”: “Oh, that was
then but this is now. It is a ll right when we did it but it is all wrong now.” I have to say,
the public have woken up to that sort of dua l view of the world—I think I can call it
that; I cannot call it the “h” word—of “When we were doing it, it was all right.”
Then the next one is the fact  that if they were Canadi an, Swiss, or German—or the
United States is a big buyer of land here—a gain, there was not a mutter, not a murmur,
not a whisper. Not a mutter, not a murmur, not a whisper. And I have checked again
through the news media. They have been happening on a regular basis. I do two or three
of these a week, and suddenly it is the Chinese. If you think it is so wrong—if you think
it is so wrong—why did the Labour Party not make such a hue and cry? Why did Helen
Clark walk the track with Shania Twain a nd look at the beautiful  high-country estate
that was sold to—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Nothing was sold, he said. No sale was stopped, he said.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: We are actually talkin g about farmlands here,
Mr Goff. We are talking about  farmlands, and Labour did not  have a problem with it.
Labour did not—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Why doesn’t the member tell the full story?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: I am telling the full story; I am most certainly. I
will tell the full story again, for the bene fit of this House. Under Labour, 660,000
hectares were approved for sale—that is, of  land to foreigners—a nd the Crafar farms
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 109
with 7,000 hectares. So let me give the fi gure again—I will try to do it graphically—
there were 660,000 hectares under Labour, and 7,000 with the Crafar farms.

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: You’re being generous, mate.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: Well, no, I cannot get my fingers close enough
to get the graphics looking good. I want to ma ke it clear: I would much prefer that New
Zealanders had bought those farms. I would much prefer it. It is everybody’s preference,
I would have thought, but in the end the Government has to abide by the law of the
land. And did Labour campaign at the last election on changing the Overseas
Investment Act to block foreigners from buying?

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, it did not. No, it did not.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Oh yes, they did.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: No, it did not. No, it did not—not a mutter, not a
murmur in their policies of blocking fore igners from buying land in New Zealand. No,
it did not. No, it did not. So I want to se nd a clear message to everybody that we should
welcome the investment that comes from foreign investors, and the growth that they can
create for our economy. We should welcome it as long as they are quality investors of
high character who are going to benefit this country.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: I want to go back to a comment that Bill English
made, because I think it bears repeating. It was just one of thos e off-the-cuff comments
that he made when he was doing his little routine after my colleague Grant Robertson’s
very good speech. He said that Grant Robertson had spent all his speech talking about
issues that “don’t matter to New Zealanders ”. Now, what did Grant Robertson spend
most of his speech talking about? Child poverty—child poverty. What a telling
statement from the Minister of Finance that  the National Government  thinks that child
poverty is an issue that does not matter to New Zealanders.
Then we had the new Minist er Jo Goodhew. She spent a large part of her speech
talking about how National spent the last 3 years protecting the vulnerable. Well, I
would like to know what Jo Goodhew’s defini tion of “vulnerable” is, because I cannot
think of any vulnerable New Zealanders who were better off at the end of the last
National Government than when National was elected in 2008. Maybe she was talking
about vulnerable National Party donors, because they were ce rtainly looked after in the
last 3 years of the National Government . Maybe she was talking about all those
vulnerable foreign multinational companies, because they certainly were looked after
under the last 3 years of a National Govern ment. Maybe she was talking about those
poor, vulnerable Australian insurance compan ies that are about to benefit from the
privatisation of accident compensation. Na tional is certainly doing a good job of
protecting them over the next 3 years. They also fall into the category, I suspect, of
vulnerable National Party donors, but we wi ll never know, because the National Party
refuses to disclose who donates to its election campaigns.
When you look at what National did in the last 3 years, you see unaffordable tax cuts
that overwhelmingly went to those who did not need them—those who needed them the
least. How can the Minister Jo Goodhew sta nd up in this House and say that National
protected the vulnerable, when to pay for t hose tax cuts the Government cut funding for
Women’s Refuge? Mr Ardern is a very sensible member. How is cutting the funding for
Women’s Refuge protecting vulnerable New Zeal anders? It was all to  pay for tax cuts
that went to the least vulnerable New Zeal anders. How are cuts to early childhood
education protecting vulnerable New Zeala nders? How is it good for children in this
country that National has now told us it will increase class sizes? How is that protecting
the most vulnerable New Zealanders? How doe s rising child poverty in this country fit
with National’s claim that it has protected vulnerable New Zealanders?
110 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
Is it not interesting that the reaction from the National Party to a TV3 documentary
on child poverty was not “Oh my God, we should do something about child poverty.”; it
was “Oh my God, we should stop New Zeal and On Air from funding documentaries
about child poverty, and we should not let them  be played in the week of an election
campaign.”? God forbid that we talk about an issue like child pove rty in an election
campaign! It is very telling that their reaction to that documentary was not “Let’s do
something about child poverty.”; it was “Let ’s shut down talking about child poverty,
because we know it’s worse under our watch and we know we have absolutely no plan
to deal with it.”
I remember John Key’s Speech from the Th rone after the 2008 election. This was
when he was aspirational for New Zealand, he was going to be turbocharging the New
Zealand economy, and we were going to be ag gressively coming out of recession very,
very soon—of course, failing to mention the fact  that in large part he would have been
able to do that because Labour left the books in a good state. The International
Monetary Fund said that if it had not been for Labour paying off our Government debt
and saving that money for a rainy day, New Zealand would not have been in the good
situation that it was in to d eal with the global recession. Th e National Party likes to say
that, you know, New Zealand went into recessi on before the rest of  the world. Yes, we
did, because we had droughts—because we ha d droughts. That is why we went into
recession early.
In fact, New Zealand was in a very good position after the 2008 election because of
the resilience that Labour had built into the economy. Unfortunately, that was
squandered by a Government that had no plan to deal with the major issues facing our
country over its 3 years in Government. Bu t that was the idea: John Key was going to
deal to unemployment, close the gap w ith Australia, and bring New Zealand
aggressively out of recession and back into su rplus. He was going to be straight up with
voters; he was not going to mince his words.
What happened? Well, he fa iled on every single count—e very single count. He is
almost like a child waiting for Santa Claus at  Christmas. I suspect he woke up every
morning just hoping that the free market had fixed the problems overnight and he would
not have to do anything because a free market  fixes everything. Well, it has not, and we
have gone backwards comparatively in the world because we have had a do-nothing
Government for 3 years. The only thing it ha s done is protect those people who support
it—protect its mates and its cronies. They are the only people who were protected under
the National Government over the last 3 years.
Instead of being straight up with voters, John Key now says that we have to accept
that we live in a dynamic environment—we live in a dynamic envi ronment. He is not
straight up with voters any more. In terms of Australia, last year saw the highest ever
net migration to Australia. Unemployment is up by 50 percent; 157,000 New
Zealanders are now out of work. And for the first time in 13 years not only did we get a
credit downgrade but we got a double dow ngrade—a double downgrade. So much for
turbocharging the economy, so much for being aspirational, and so much for
aggressively coming out of recession.
In last year’s Speech from the Throne, af ter the recent election, what I could see was
that the Prime Minister had learnt the le sson of making these commitments and then
actually being held to account for them. What he did in this one was not make any
commitments. He did not make any comm itments and did not make any kinds of
promises that he could actually be held to account against. There is still no plan for the
economy; that was evident in the Speech fr om the Throne. If you consider today, we
had the very first question time since the election—the very first question time. The
Government had the opportunity to ask itself lots of questions that highlight all the great
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 111
policies and plans and exciting new ideas that it has because it is  recharged and ready
for the next 3 years. What did we have ? Another question for Maurice Williamson on
SmartGate. That is normally a question that we get in the third week of a sitting session,
when the Government is struggling to come  up with questions. The first question time
of this new Parliament and already they have to bring out the Maurice Williamson
SmartGate question. That tells you something.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: It was impressive.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Well, he did have a new angle on it this time, which was
adolescent facial features. It was a new angle. I am not saying it was not interesting. But
the reality is—with all due re spect to the wonderf ul people at the Customs Service—
that there are slightly more pressing issu es facing this country than whether 16-year-
olds’ faces are still developing and whethe r we can let them use SmartGate at our
international airports.
This was an opportunity for the Government to tell us what it is going to do over the
course of this year and to highlight its plans. But, of course, it does not have a plan.
The reality is that the opportunities are there. The oppor tunities are there for the
Government to do what it said it was going to  do 3 years ago, but has failed to do: to
aggressively bring our economy out of recessi on, to get people back into work, and to
improve our education system—not destroy it, which is, quite frankly, where this
Government’s policies are going. But again, in  the Speech from the Throne, there was
nothing. There was no plan, and—this ti me the Prime Minister has learnt—no
commitments that he could actu ally be held accountable fo r at the time of the next
election. He failed to meet any of the comm itments he made in his last 3 years of
Government, so this time we heard absolutely no commitments.
I invite members to look at the plan that Labour put forward at the last election,
because our tax package would get New Zealand back to surplus at the same time as the
National Party was promising without selling our assets—without selling our assets. But
it requires tough choices to be made.
The Government says it has a mandate on asse t sales; it actually does not. When you
add up the percentage of the vote that was ga ined by all those parties that opposed asset
sales, including those that did not make it into this Parliament because they failed to
reach the 5 percent threshold, more than 50 pe rcent of New Zealanders voted for parties
that had policies opposing asset sales—opposin g assets sales—so there is no mandate
for it.
The Government talks about its Future Investment Fund. I had a school principal in
Gisborne say to me that 21 st century education is not a one-off cost. Saying that we are
going to sell off our assets to put a bit of  money into schools on a one-off basis just
shows how little the Government unde rstands about education, because 21 st century
education is an ongoing cost  and you can sell t hose assets only once. Once they are
gone, they are gone. Assets built up by gene rations of New Zealanders, which this
Government has no mandate to sell—once they are gon e, they are gone. Particularly in
the case of the power companies, we will s ee power prices going up. People are already
struggling to pay the power bi ll, and we will see power prices going up when those
assets are privatised.
It is short-changing future generations. Future generations are asking where the
National Government’s plan is to deal with the cost of an ageing population. Where was
that plan in the Speech from the Throne? The f act is we cannot keep putting it off. It is
all right for John Key—he will get his superannuation—but what about younger New
Zealanders now, who are look ing and thinking that there is no way, given the ageing
population, that New Zealand superannuation at it s current level is sustainable if we do
not make those tough choices? There were no tough choices made about that, about
112 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
child poverty, or about any of  the other issues facing New Zealand. It is about time the
National Party members, when they get up, act ually started outlining what their plan is
for New Zealand.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Thank you, Mr
Assistant Speaker Robertson. Th at is a very wise call. Ca n I congratulate you also on
your reappointment to the job. This is my first opportunity to do so. Can I say that in my
time in this place I think it would be fair to  say there has never been a more qualified
team—that is, all of the Speak ers that occupy the role you do—in regard to knowledge
of the Standing Orders and process in th e House. I am sure you will maintain the
standards that we have become accustomed to from you. Congratulations on that.
It is always a privilege to follow my fellow Commonwealth Parliamentary
Association group co-chair in one of these A ddress in Reply debates. She touched on a
range of child poverty and social issues. I was once asked what I would consider it to be
if I were considered as rich. My answer to that—and to her—is that providing I have
three reasonably nutritious feeds a day, have a dry bed to sleep in, am able to pay the
phone and power bills and the rent, and have a car that will pass the warrant of fitness
every 6 months, I would consider myself to  be rich. Of course, if you look at our
colleagues on the other side of the House, by comparison, that is not what they consider.
Those things that I spoke of, which are basic needs, they see as the minimum or
poverty. Actually, if you do not have Sky TV now, something needs to be done about it,
and social welfare should stump up!
Let us have a look at the comparison unde r the National Government led by John
Key. In the last term of Parliament, we f aced more crises, I think you could say, than
any Government in modern history when you look at everything that went wrong during
that period. The one that is, I guess, the mo st understated—and certainly completely
ignored by the Opposition—is that fact that  we have gone th rough what has been
termed by international commentators the biggest economic meltdown or depression
since the 1930s. I think we should reflect on th at. Back at home, sure, there have been
some companies and some individuals that  have suffered during these economic times,
but overwhelmingly we are in a better position economically than most of our trading or
competing nation colleagues. When you ask the question of why that is, there is only
one conclusion: because of the solid, sensible , considered economic policies of the Key
Government. The Key Government intends to have New Zealand back in surplus by
2014. That is no mean feat. In fact, some woul d say it is an unrealis tic goal, but all of
the forecasts at this stage suggest that that is possible.
I want to touch on something I think has been the No. 1 driver in that, and that is the
outstanding achievements within our agricultu ral industries. It is  often overlooked, I
have to say—by economic commentators,  political commentators, and our
Opposition—just what role the agricultural sector plays in the New Zealand economy.
What has happened in the agricultural sect or? At a time when markets have shrunk,
when discretionary spending has shrunk, and wh en we have faced some of the toughest
economic circumstances internationally, our market exports have continued to grow,
particularly in the dairy i ndustry. I want to congratulat e the Hon Tim Groser on the
work that he and others have done in making that possible, in opening up markets where
markets did not exist, and in doing trade deal s with countries we have historically had
difficulty trading with. When you look at that, you see that the Key-led Government has
achieved more in the previous 3 years, a nd has a programme going forward to achieve
more, than anything we have seen before.
New Zealand has always been a proud exporter of agricultural products. I have heard
comment from the new Labour leader recently—quite recently, actually—about how we
need to spread our horizons and expand into  non-commodity trading. I could not agree
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 113
more. I think the Leader of the Opposition ha s absolutely nailed it with that comment.
We must do that. But what that does not men tion is the fact that about 60 percent of
what Fonterra exported last year did not exist 5 years ago. Those who are suffering from
asthma use inhalers. To suggest that that inhaling product, if you like, or carrier for
those inhalers—it is a lact ose-based product developed in the New Zealand dairy
industry—is a bulk commodity is simplistic an d childish in the extreme. We need to
look at where our opportunities exist.
If you go through the basket of products we export from that industry, you will find
that we have nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals,  high tech protein-based capsules for
pharmaceuticals—the list goes on. As I said, 60 percent of what was exported from our
biggest company last year did not exist 5 years ago, and I challenge the Opposition to
have a look at some of that stuff.
What are the big issues facing the Gove rnment going forward, and what does this
new National Government need to address in partnership with its support parties? The
first thing that we need to address is responsibly managi ng the Government’s finances.
If you look at the growth in the public sector  through the whole 9 y ears of the previous
Government, at how sustainable that is in  the current economic environment, and at
what the National Government has done to ach ieve a higher level of service from our
public sector with the same level of finance, then you would have to conclude, as would
the rest of New Zealand, that that has been managed reasonably well.
Building a more competitive and productiv e economy does not mean throwing up a
whole lot of cost of compliance and re gulation, whether it be under the guise of
environmental protection, or whether it be und er the guise of fair ness and equality in
terms of who pays what tax where and in terms of depreciation. Wherever you look, the
rhetoric that came out of the Opposition in the last term of Parliament, and prior to that,
was to place more costs. In fact, in the la st term of Parliament it was suggested that
dairy farmers in New Zealand do not pay enough tax and something should be done
about that. Well, I have some dairy-farming colleagues this year who are not that happy
that they are paying, you know, six and seven fi gures in tax in some cases. I challenge
others in the House or in the economy to  step forward and demonstrate how they
believe that dairy farmers paying a higher ta x burden than they are already would be
beneficial for New Zealand.
I heard the previous speaker say that givi ng tax cuts to the rich is not the way
forward in a struggling environment. I could not agree more, if that is, in fact, what
happened. But it is actually middle-class New Zealand that benefited the most from the
last Government’s tax cuts, and I would ha ve to suggest to you that there are large
cross-sections of New Zeala nders now who do not pay any tax at all if they have a
family, given the tax rebates that they get.
Delivering and rebuilding on the Christchurch circumstance that we find ourselves in
is something that no Government would ever want or could plan for. It is the No. 1
priority for this Government, and huge amount s of capital are comm itted to that. I do
not think there is a single person in Parliament who woul d get up and claim that we
should not be doing that. It is  a question of how quickly we  can do it, how we fund it,
how New Zealand can benefit from that, and, going forward, once that has happened,
how we can sustain the economy in the area.
Introducing irrigation to the Canterbury Pl ains—and across the rest of New Zealand
where that is possible, where it is feasible , and where it will gi ve an economic return—
is one of the key platforms that the Ke y-led Government has announced as a policy
going forward. This will be hugely beneficial  to the New Zealand economy. It does not
mean 100 percent conversion of the Canterbury Plains to dairy. What it could mean is
that we diversify the land use into a range of other developments. In fact, right at the
114 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
moment lamb fattening would re turn a higher return on investment than conversion to
dairy. Markets internationally  are opening up for that as well, along with everything
else.
The Key-led Government has a dynamic plan going forward, has shown strong
leadership up to this point , and will manage the New Z ealand economy, I think, better
than any other group or combination in the future. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It is a great pleasure to speak in
the Address in Reply debate this afternoon. I would just like to follow on from the
previous speaker who made a very good point  about New Zealand agriculture and the
strength that New Zealand agriculture displa ys as the main income producer for New
Zealand. Following on from that I think not only do we have to be proud of the
industries that are involved ther e and the history of investment and hard work that has
gone into making those industries so successful, but we also need to look at the attitude,
I think, that those industries display. It is an  attitude of hard work, resilience, backing
themselves, being prepared to take risks,  and also looking for challenges and meeting
those challenges and accepting them. Those are common fundamental principles of any
economy where there is success. If you look at  the industrial grow th of China, for
example, you see that they have a very similar success story. They have met the
challenges of producing products and have done it in a wa y that has exceeded their
competition, and many other countries have failed to keep up with them and paid a dear
price economically.
That leads on to the situation that New Zealand faced and most of the Western World
faced in the last few years. There is a d eep recession in Europe. New Zealand was in
recession before the rest of the world, thanks to our previous Labour administration, and
the US is struggling to get through the recessionary pressures that are in the world at the
moment. I challenge this Parliament to look at it in terms of an East-West divide.
Maybe on the Eastern side of the political equation or the world they may have actually
looked at things in a more long-term and reflective manner than the West has. Maybe
the East has got something that  the West needs to learn, an d that is that government is
not about promises for one election to the ne xt. Government is a bout building futures,
and futures are long term. We in  the West tend to think an  election is a time when we
can go and buy votes. You have parties going out there, promisi ng all these things—
promising to people who may be seen as vu lnerable that they will change that;
promising that their policies are the way to solve the problems—when maybe, just
maybe, we need to take a more Eastern pe rspective and look at it with a long-term
vision and actually look at government as a long-term driver, and look not at our
individual gain per election, but at our long-term gain over time.
That, I think, is the thing that the Europ ean countries have not done. They still face
countries that go from election to election and from promise to promise. Can we buy the
votes of those voters to stay in power? Th is is something the Labour Party was very
good at doing in the previous administrati on. But the world has moved on. The world
needs stable government, the world needs government that is long term in focus, and the
world needs government that has a strong economic base. Those economic
fundamentals are something that we as a country may not pick up explicitly, but
implicitly the people of our country know that. In their day-to-day lives they know that
they can lose their job if the company th ey are working for doe s not perform. They
know that the services they will get from the Government depend on the ability of the
Government to earn revenue and deliver thos e services. The days of borrowing just to
deliver services are gone. The days of a c ountry having to earn its way are the future.
That is a very strong driver that our pe ople understand, but often our politicians do not
understand, and the Labour Party did not unders tand it at the last election. It did not
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 115
understand what people were actually going through on the street, and that is why it did
not connect with the people on the street. We as a Governme nt and as a country need to
have a much longer-term vision. We need to look forward at what our country needs to
deliver. I see the Green members shaking their heads—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: In disbelief.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: No, in support. They understand and they advocate that in an
environmental context. It is a shame they do not do it in an economic context and also a
social context. But in an economic context, which is one of the major issues that we as a
country have to deal with at the mome nt—environmental as well, but economic as
well—that requires long-term planning that in vests in infrastructure, that makes the
right commercial decisions so that New Zeal anders can grow their economy, grow their
businesses, provide those jobs, and provide th e environment for us as a country to then
afford to deliver the social services we all treasure and want to see enhanced. That is the
challenge for this Government and for future  Governments. The challenge of the past
has been in terms of what we can promise for a 3-year cycle; the challenge of the future
is to look forward to what we need to do to deliver a stronger economy and a country
and environment going forward. The National Party is committed to long-term growth,
we are committed to long-term planning, an d we are committed to making sure this
country takes advantage of its opportunities. That is the difference between us and the
Opposition.
The Opposition, I bet, will sta nd in this room for the next  3 years, looking at short-
term things. It will be looking at short-term issues with a short-term vision. We do not
have a short-term vision; we have a vision  that is the right vision in the current
economic environment. It is one where we are investing in the infrastructure that this
country needs. We are building the roads, we are putting the broadband in, and we are
giving those assets to our people so that long term they can grow. That is very much the
economic model you see in successful countri es. Whereas the Chinese at the moment
are building roads and building infrastruc ture, the Russians are building roads and
building infrastructure, and the Indians are building roads and infrastructure, the
European countries of Italy and Spain are talking about how they can manage their debt.
They are not looking at the economic fundament als they need to, and until the day they
measure themselves and look at those long-ter m interests, they will  not compete in the
modern world and they will fall further down.
But New Zealand has the ability to compete.  As Mr Ardern said, we have got an
agricultural economy that is poised to be in the right place at the right time. We are
beside the major economic market s that this world will have for the next generation or
so. We are close to them. We have never been close to them before. We made our
money in the 50s, but we made it by being far away from those economic markets. Now
they are close, so we have to take advantage of  that. We also have to be able to look at
the transfer of skills and the ability to be  part of that neighbo urhood. We cannot look at
ourselves in isolation. If you want to have an isolated New Zeala nd that does not grow
and does not achieve, well then you are going to hold your people back, and we cannot
afford to do that. New Zealanders need to be  able to invest in things and get that
technology so that they can grow and have th e standard of living that they desire. And
this Government will deliver that through our plan, because we will responsibly manage
the Government finance, we will build a str onger economy, we will look at the delivery
of public services, and also we will rebuild Chri stchurch so that it is  an integral part of
the New Zealand plan. And that is a long-ter m focus, which is something most Western
economies do not realise and do not accept at th e moment. That is what is needed for
this country to grow. It is the success of us going forward, and with good leadership we
will achieve that. Thank you.
116 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker
Robertson. Now I have heard ev erything! Now I have really heard everything! I never,
ever thought I would come to this House and hear David Bennett invoking the great
Eastern philosophers in suppor t of National’s economic polic y, which the rest of us
have come to think of as cut, cut public se rvices; sell, sell our assets; and hope. I never,
ever thought I would hear this, but every da y is a new day and that always makes it
exciting to come to the House. You never know what you are going to hear from
members on that side of the House.
Where is the bold rhetoric? Where is the br ighter future that we heard so much
about? Where is it now? Like a fake suntan th at has worn off, the perennially relaxed
Prime Minister is no longer wearing his permanent smile. In fact, in recent weeks he has
looked decidedly tired and grumpy. And the reason is that National has run out of ideas.
It is all getting a bit hard for the Prime Minister and members on that side of the House.
I looked in vain during the electi on campaign for National’s campaign
advertisements showing Mr Key in the We stpac Stadium, talking about all the New
Zealanders who are heading to Australia. Do you know why we did not see images of
Mr Key in the Westpac Stadium? Why? B ecause there is not a stadium big enough in
this country to signify the sheer volum e of New Zealanders  who are leaving
permanently for Australia: 113,000—113,000—New Z ealanders have left this country
permanently to go to Australia since this Government first took office. Last year 36,900
New Zealanders made up the net migration to Australia—the highe st ever recorded.
Why did they leave? They left, and they are leaving, because they have lost hope in this
Government. The world has changed, but Na tional’s thinking, National’s policies and
its answers, has not changed. This Government has ru n out of ideas. Just like the
definition of a psychotic who keeps on tryi ng the same old thing, National keeps on
hoping that the results will be different.
I want to give the House a couple of ex amples of how National has run out of
ideas—how it has run out of steam and it just keeps on tryi ng the same old things. Last
week the Ministry of Trans port released its briefing to the incoming Ministers, and it
made very interesting reading. What those o fficials in the Ministry  of Transport told
us—their analysis and their data made it very clear—is that the centrepiece of this
Government’s transport policy for the last 3 years, the roads of significance to National,
otherwise known as the RONZ, is tipped to become increasingly insignificant because
the world is changing and National has not wo ken up to that fact. What the briefing
showed us was that this Government is going to be increasi ngly unable to fund the
commitments that it has made to build the roads of national signi ficance. There is a
divergence in the budgeted cost of these seve n gold-plated motorway projects and the
other four that the Government proposes to  add to the list. The divergence is between
the budgeted cost and the Government’s ab ility to fund the construction of those
motorways from the normal sources of transport revenue.
The fact is that with a flat economy and rising oil prices, pe ople are driving less.
They are choosing to take public transport increasingly, and, because they are driving
less, the Government’s transport revenue through road-user ch arges and through the
petrol excise is falling proportionately to the size of the economy and the commitments
that this Government has made to build th e roads of national significance. So on one
hand you have got a growing divergence betw een the Government’s commitments and
its ability to pay for them, and, on the other hand, no one can afford to drive on these
motorways because of the cost of petrol. It is bizarre that at the very time when New
Zealanders are choosing to dr ive less and demand for public transport is growing, this
Government has redoubled its commitment to the so-called roads of national
significance. It shows no sign of wavering fr om its total obsession with building gold-
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 117
plated motorway projects, which rob every other major category in the transport budget,
including local roads, rural roads, road safety, and urba n public transport. They have no
qualms—the members on that side of th e House—about robbing every other budget
category to fund their roads of National Government significance.
Now you would think, at a time of  rising oil prices, that it might be a good thing to
think about the long-term resilience of our  transport sector over the next 10, 20, 30
years. But what this Government is doing is precisely the opposite. By refusing to
support Auckland’s plans and aspirations fo r a modern public transport system, by
refusing to stump up with its share of th e funding needed for the city rail link in
Auckland, and by insisting on going ahead with the discredited P ūhoi to Wellsford
“Holiday Highway”, this Government is ma king the country more and more dependent
on imported oil, at the very time that we s hould be thinking about making our transport
sector more resilient and having a more balanc ed transport policy that  invests in public
transport, in rail, and in coastal shipping. But the Govern ment, sadly, does not see the
logic of that; it is building roads like there is no tomorrow. Even though traffic demand,
traffic volume, has been more or less static for the last 4 or 5 years, it refuses to
recognise the demand for public transport, at a time when more and more people are
getting buses and trains to work.
The second example that I want to  give also relates to transp ort, and it is specifically
about Auckland. It has been really inst ructive in the last few weeks. The New Zealand
Herald has run an interesting series  of stories about some of the big challenges facing
our country’s biggest city. I hope members on th at side of the House have read over the
last couple of days what the New Zealand Herald has said about our unfair tax system
and how it is driving ever-higher levels of so cial inequality. But one of the other really
interesting articles that the New Zealand Herald has had in the last week or two
highlighted last week that Auckland, our c ountry’s largest city, will face midday traffic
jams in the next 20 years—midday traffic jams—because the programme of road
building that had been carried out by Labour when we were in Government, and that has
been continued under this Government, simply will not, on its own, solve the problem
of traffic congestion. The changes, the eff ect of the road-building programme over the
last couple of years, are e xpected, according to the Ministry of Transport, to reduce
congestion by only 14 percent by 2021. Congestion will be reduced by only 14 percent
If there was ever a wake-up call that the National Government’s mantra of roads and
suburban sprawl will not deliver a workable future for our co untry’s biggest city, this is
it. But National is blind to the demands and deaf to the aspirations of Aucklanders, who
want to live in a livable city. They want to  be able to move around their city. National’s
only recipe is to build more and more moto rways and add more and more lanes to the
existing motorway. It will not take on board the idea that we have to build a more
balanced, integrated, intermodal transport sy stem that actually gives people the real
opportunity to leave their cars at home and free up the roads for the rest of us. Spaghetti
Junction, the single-biggest  motorway interchange in the southern hemisphere,
completed only a few years ago, is already at full capacity in peak hour at both times of
the day—and the National Government want s to build more and more motorways
across the city, most of them heading into the central city. Well, you do not need to be a
rocket scientist to know that that simply will not work. We have to invest heavily in
public transport, to ease c ongestion and provide a more balanced transport system.
Unfortunately, National has run out of ideas, a nd all it wants to do is do the same thing
over and over again.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker
Robertson. Thank you for the call, and a very  happy New Year to you. It is a pleasure,
118 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
as always, to follow Mr Twyford, but I would have thought now that he is an electorate
member for Auckland—and with his transpor t role in the diminished Labour Party
caucus—he would be particularly aware th at this Government has made a very
significant investment in rail in his area. It is a very impor tant investment. I would have
thought he would welcome that, not ignore it in his contribution.
I also want to say as a Waikato member how thrilled I am, as we speak about that
roading development, that the Waikato Expr essway is on track. It  is going to deliver
more for our region—and I am sure my colleague the member for Hamilton East will
agree with me—than anything else in recent ti mes. It is the single most important thing
we can do for the economic development and the social development of our region. It
will get people moving, it will get businesses moving, and it will create employment. It
is a great development. Yes, it is important , and that is why we as a Government have
been putting so much emphasis on the roads of  national significance. I look forward to
Mr Twyford coming up to speed, getting to understand what it is all about, and throwing
his wholehearted support behind it.
Mr Assistant Speaker, could I at the outse t congratulate you on your reappointment
to your position, and also Mr Speaker, th e Deputy Speaker, and the other Assistant
Speaker. We are well served by our presidi ng officers in Parliame nt, and I wish you
well. I would also like to thank the electo rs of Hamilton West for the great honour that
they have done me by returning me with an  increased majority. I was very proud to
achieve that result and I am very conscious  of the honour and the responsibility that I
have. I will be doing my best to justify the faith that they have again placed in me, and
will be working as hard as I can for the benefit of our exciting city and our vitally
important region.
On this day, as we marked in Parliament the diamond anniversary of our Sovereign, I
would like to pay my respects to Her Majest y the Queen. I am personally a very strong
supporter of our current constitutional arrangement s. I believe that she, in her role as
head of the Commonwealth, has shown a devoti on to duty and a life time of service that
are admirable and really worth acknowledging.  I do thank her for that. I also pay my
respects to His Excellency and Lady Mateparae as they settle into their new viceregal
responsibilities. I believe that they are off to a very good start and that they will serve us
well over the next 4½ years.
The Address in Reply debate, of course, fo cuses on what we heard from the Crown,
through the Governor-General, at the openi ng of the Parliament. There were no
surprises in it, because it is essentially a re flection of the issues that were very well
canvassed in last year’s general election. What did that election result give us? It gave a
Government that for one of the few times in my lifetime actually saw its share of the
party vote go up and its numbers go up. It saw an Opposition that could not really work
out where it stood on the issu es and did not have any credible policy pay the price for
that disarray and substantially go down. And it saw the return of one party, the
enlargement of another, and a little bit of moving around.  But essentially the most
important thing is that it gave us anothe r strong John Key - led Government and a very
clear mandate to press on with the issues  and the policies that the electorate
unquestionably endorsed at the ballot box.
I want to welcome all new members of this House and congratulate them. It is a very
significant honour; I wish you well. I know that there are very talented people who have
come into the House. You come in, of course , at a time of very c onsiderable challenges
to us as a country and to the whole world. We  are still in the grip of a global economic
downturn that has really had a significant impact—there is no question. For instance, we
need only look at the fact that  in last year’s election we were defending a zero Budget.
If you had told me as I was defending one of the marginal seats in  the country that I
7 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 119
would have to go into an el ection defending a zero Budget, I think I would have gone
pretty white. Some say I have gone pretty white! Nevertheless, it was what the public
understood we needed to do. So I wish the ne w members the very best of luck as you
join us to discharge your responsibilities. I look forward to cons tructive contributions
and I particularly look forw ard to hearing your maiden statements over the next few
weeks.
Because of those challenges that I have ju st mentioned, the critical importance of
having an economic plan that is  appropriate and is going to achieve what we need to do
is patently apparent. There are, of course , no easy answers to the position we are in.
Borrow and hope is clearly not an option. We need only look at what has been
happening in Europe in recent times to realise how dire the position of some previously
admired economies is; we do not want to go down that path. New Zealand is doing
everything it can under the John Key - led Government to get our borrowing under
control and to ensure that we are back in surplus by 2014-15. No twithstanding all those
major challenges, particularly the devastati on in the Canterbury region in the last 18
months or so, we remain on our path to doing that. I salute Bill English and the team
working with him for that significant achievement.
When we are not borrowing, when we are back  in surplus, we have choices. We can
continue to invest in the things we want to, rather than simply being constrained and
having to spend quite a bit of what we earn on interest repayments. We were forced into
that borrowing option by the previous Gove rnment, and let us never forget that.
Wasteful expenditure—incredibly wasteful expenditure—on a whol e range of things
meant that this Government came into offi ce already in a recession, having to rein it in
and get our spending back under control, because you cannot continue spending what
you do not earn without imperillin g future generations. That is what the last Labour
Government did, that is why New Zealanders threw it out of office, and that is why they
are saying to us: “For the sake of future  generations, do what you are doing, National-
led Government, because there is no alternative.”
Tax and spend is not an option. Tax and spend is not an option, because—
[Interruption] I did enjoy seeing The Iron Lady, or “The Iron Maiden” or whatever it is
called. What a wonderful film—a fine performance by Meryl Streep. I have to say that I
think Margaret Thatcher was a pretty impre ssive person. She faced similar challenges.
She rose to that. She rose to that challenge as well, and good on her.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Labour is an alternative —not a good one, but it is an
alternative.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Fortunately, it is not one, Mr Williamson, that New Zealanders
are showing any enthusiasm for opting for at the moment.
What did those members want to offer?  More tax and spend—a failed philosophy
that simply stifles investme nt and productivity and drives anyone of an entrepreneurial
spirit who can do so offshore in search of gr eener pastures. That is the last thing we
want. We know that some New Zealanders have gone. We are a very nomadic country;
we have a very large expatria te population living o ffshore. That is not altogether bad,
because they pick up skills, and as long as th ey come back eventually we benefit from
that. But we must ensure that this is an attractive country with an economy that
welcomes them home and that attracts them to invest here, because that is what we need
for our long-term prosperity.
As a Government we are naturally very focused on the need to care for all our
citizens. There are many who are struggli ng through the recession and there are many
who need the assistance of the State, and we are committed to providing that. But we
cannot do it if we do not have the economy under control.
120 Address in Reply 7 Feb 2012
We are, of course, committed to promoting su stainability of our environment. It is a
topic that has certainly beco me far more popular to talk about in recent times. We are
dedicated to doing it. We are very much focused on lifting educational achievement—
no apologies about that. We are passionate about achieving that, and our dynamic new
Minister of Education is determined to do it. I wish her well. I know that she is off to an
excellent start and she is earning the respect of  people in that area, and I wish them all
well as they lift educational achievement for the good of our country and particularly for
our young people.
Welfare reform is crucial, and as a member of the Social Services Committee in the
last Parliament—we began to l ook at this—I am delighted th at we will be working on
this. If we are going to have a social se curity system that is responsive and is
appropriate it must not trap  people in long-term depende ncy, it must ensure that
everybody who can work is working, and it must ensure that all the right incentives are
there. Those incentives have been whacked o ff balance in recent times; we are going to
get them back on track. There are some important challenges there.
I mentioned Christchurch and Canterbury a short time ago. Time moves on and the
media sometimes shifts its focus, but we are conscious of the fact that Cantabrians have
now faced over 10,000 aftershocks. They had t hose terribly big ones, devastating as
they were, just before Christmas. We re main focused on doing the job. As Mr Bennett
mentioned a minute ago, that is a long-term co mmitment and we will ensure that we do
not let them down.
These are exciting times. These are going to be challenging times, and they will be
difficult times for us as a Government. I am really excited, however, by the plan that we
have got on offer. I know that the count ry has huge confidence in what we are
delivering. Let us get on with it—there is no time to lose.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I move, That the debate be now
