Motion agreed to.

sections.heading: National Animal Identification And Tracing Bill

items.text: In Committee

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I seek leave for all the
provisions of the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill to be taken as one
question.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there
any objection? There is no objection. Members,  we move first to the National Animal
Identification and Tracing Bill. The question is that Part 1 stand part.
Hon Damien O’Connor: Mr Chairman—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: One moment, we have a—[ Interruption]
Just to clarify what the deba te is about, as it is one question, I am  sure the honourable
member knows that it is one debate—
Hon Damien O’Connor: Wide ranging, Mr Chair?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, he did not seek a wide-ranging debate;
he just sought that all parts be taken as one question.
Hon Damien O’Connor: Asset sales?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, you are testing me, Mr O’Connor. So
the question is that Parts 1 to 6, schedules 1 and 2, and clauses 1 and 2 stand part.
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 121
Clauses 1 and 2, Parts 1 to 6, and schedules 1 and 2
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : Thank you, Mr
Chair. I appreciate your guidance there.
I just start by going back. We have starte d the new Parliament. The National Animal
Identification and Tracing Bill has been ha nging around for some time—in fact, since
2004, when the previous Labour Government, in  its wisdom, saw the need to introduce
a tracing system that would not put us at the leading edge of national animal
management, but would actually just bring us up to what has be en occurring in a
number of other countries for a number of years. We pride ourselves on being a nation
of good managers of agriculture, livestock, animal welfare issu es, and, of course,
biosecurity.
Unfortunately, at the time when Labour intr oduced this legislation there was quite a
vicious campaign launched by Federated Farmers against this initiative. I have to get
that on record, because as a result of that it  is now 2012, some 8 years on, and we are
passing this bill through Parliament.
Labour supports the bill because we know it is necessary. We need to know where
animals are, whom they have been sold t o, and what should occur in the terrible and
unlikely event of an outbreak of foot-a nd-mouth, for example. We now trace our
animals for tuberculosis, and many of the dairy animals are traced for breeding
purposes, but we do not have one comprehensiv e scheme. This bill will move us down
that track for cattle and for deer.
Just to reiterate, the countri es that currently have su ch a scheme in place are
Australia, the United Kingdo m, Canada, the USA, South Korea, Japan, the EU,
Argentina, and Brazil. We ar e right behind all our compet itors, and in a world where
consumers are demanding to know where their food comes fr om and how it was
produced, and want an assurance that it can be traced in the event of some
contamination or in the event of some disease—we are not there yet—the sooner we
pass this through the House, the better. The National Government sat around on its
hands, I would suggest. The Primary Produc tion Committee dealt with this bill as
quickly as we could, but it has been sitting around and it is important that we move on.
The select committee dealt with a number of issues in its consideration, and I am
sure the chairman will speak at some stage. There were issues because of that 8-year
period. Technology moves on very, very quickl y. What was, in my view, a political
stance by Federated Farmers to animal tr acing in 2004—to object on the basis that
technology was unsure and all th e rest of it—was ju st an excuse at that point. There
were, however, legitimate questions around the technology that should be used moving
forward to make sure we did not impose a sy stem on farmers, processors, and saleyards
and then realise 2 or 3 years down the track that the technology was obsolete. I think the
select committee did its very best in this area.
The issue comes down to low frequency vers us high frequency. Both frequencies are
used on the farm—less so in processing f actories. Labour has supported and supports a
bill that opens the door for both technologies, but we hope that there will be clear
alignment of them as this moves forward, b ecause as soon as we can tell where all the
beef cattle, the dairy cattle, and the deer in this country are, then we will be better off
and more secure in terms of potential biosecurity threats.
I go back to the bill. I am sure the Minister for Primary Industries will get up and
answer a few queries on technical points. One of the questions that we have to ask of
the new organisation is about its ability to  communicate with and connect to lifestyle
farmers. As I say, farmers have reluctantl y taken this on boar d. I think they now
appreciate the benefit of this. Lifestyl e farmers—people with few animals—may not
understand the threat that they, if they stay  outside the system, may pose to our whole
122 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
production systems in agriculture. I implor e the officials to take on board some
guidance about how to get out there and how to do some pub lic relations. We are told
that there will be a whole lot of brochures and a whole lot of marketing. We just have to
make sure that that marketing is well targete d, and that it is effec tive in getting out to
those lifestyle farmers.
Can I say, given that we have a broad-rangi ng debate, that there have been assets
sale here as well—and I know that the Minist er smirks. In fact, the Government, in its
enthusiasm for asset sales, actually sold off last year a company that is likely to
benefit—and good luck to them—from th e implementation of National Animal
Identification and Tracing (NAIT). Sirtrack was a subsidiary of the Crown research
institute Landcare Research, and was sold to  a Canadian company. It has actually
developed technology that will be of huge bene fit to the system when it is implemented
in this country. All I say on that—because  I know you are allowing a wide-ranging
debate, Mr Chairman—is that if we see the stupidity of asset sales continue, then once
again we will miss out on potential benefits as we move into the future.
But I come back to NAIT. I just say that the question of sheep is one that I think
should be raised. The sheep farmers out there will be panicking and saying “Oh, not us!
Why should we be involved?”. I am not qu ite sure what a ewe was worth in 2004—that
is, a female sheep, not “you”, Mr Chairman, because we are not allowed to say that, of
course. A ewe was probably worth maybe $30 to $40. Now they are looking at $150 to
$200 for a good ewe. I think that sheep farm ers might now understand the potential
benefits of having their animals included in a traceability scheme so that if we have an
outbreak we can move quickly, protect our export industry, and know where each and
every one of the sheep are. At the mome nt sheep are outside the scheme, and the
Minister may want to get up and explain whet her he intends to move in that direction
and include sheep. At the moment it is cattle and deer, and I think th at is a positive step
forward.
I am not going to say anything more, other th an that Labour supports this bill. It has
been a long time in coming, and this will be a very important step forward for the
credibility, the integrity, and the value of the New Ze aland agricultu ral production
systems.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: Mr Chairman, can I
take this opportunity to congratulate you on your reappoint ment as Deputy Speaker—I
have not had a chance to do that until now. This National Animal Identification and
Tracing Bill, as the previous speaker, the Hon Damien O’Connor, said, came to the
Primary Production Committee, and we spent a considerable amount of time going
through the issues in relation to the detail of this. In doing so we made some
recommendations to the Minister for Primary Industries. I am pleased to say that the
Minister has taken up most if not all of those recommendations.
The previous speaker touched on the need fo r a robust identification system, and that
is absolute. We as members of the Pr imary Production Committee just met with a
Swedish delegation of our counterparts from that country. They were fascinated by the
growth of our primary industries in this country and asked us what it was that we
thought may have differentiated what we do he re as compared with what is happening
in other parts of the world. One of the things that sets us aside when you look forward at
what our opportunities might be  as far as exporting our primary industry products is
concerned is our quality control and the checks and balances and assurances we can
give when we market product to something like 150-odd countries in the world.
One of the things that goes with that is  traceability. How certain are you that the
product you are selling is what you say it is, to  the quality the market is requiring, and
what you are suggesting you are going to mark et it as? That makes it absolutely
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 123
essential that we have in place systems that can robustly check those measures. That
comes down to something as fundamental as be ing able to identify the particular animal
in question. It is important not only from a quality-control  point of view but from a
biosecurity point of view as well.
So the select committee looked at what was being proposed, listened to a wide range
of submissions, and called in a number of  experts, and through that process we
discovered that potentially we were being left behind by emerging technology. We were
not sure—and how will you ever be sure of those things—and so we asked for further
advice on how we could make the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill more
enabling around that. We received some, I gue ss, conflicting information. The Minister
and his officials have been grappling with that for some time. Ultimately, we ended up
in a situation where we have come up with provisions that enable future development in
that area. So the bill is an enabling piece of legislation that doe s not lock in one or
another particular piece of technology.
Some of the opposition that the previous sp eaker spoke of earlier  in the debate on
this issue was around what cost there would be to the individual producer and what
potential benefit there coul d be to the individual produ cer. As our markets have
emerged and developed, and prices have incr eased, there is more and more potential for
this to be used not only for the purposes in tended by the Ministry  of Agriculture and
Forestry and the Government but by farmers themselves in the management of their
farming systems. So to enable a rapid and accurate tracking of an imals from birth to
death is something that is fundamental for our exports. There is nothing more
fundamental than providing information on th e location, the moveme nt, and the history
of animals, and I think it was brought to the attention of the Ministry of Agriculture and
Forestry, under the previous Government , with the Waiheke Island foot-and-mouth
hoax. There were a lot of small lifestyle bl ocks, as you would expect at a location like
that, that were unidentified, or the animals thereon were unidentified, and a lot of time
was spent trying to ascertain what was actuall y there and what the risks were. The real
irony of that is that by the time that in formation was availabl e, news reports and
suchlike were reporting all sorts of things that  were inaccurate. To be able to have an
accurate register of these livestock is abso lutely fundamental to the integrity of our
biosecurity system.
This bill is intended to improve our biosecu rity management. It will help manage
risks around human health. Th ese are often overlooked. With  the whole debate around
the use of 1080 and the eradication of possums , what are we trying to do here? We are
trying to control the spread of  tuberculosis. It has an effect on humans. It is an old
disease. It is not something that is commonl y thought of as a modern-day disease, but it
could be, and the interrelationship between bovi ne tuberculosis and human tuberculosis
is well documented. So there is a lot of opportunity in regard to that.
To improve animal productivity—that is the point, I think, that th e previous speaker
was touching on. There is a range of options in terms of recording the performance of
individual animals within a herd or a flock that ultimately could lead to a profitable use
by the farmer himself or herself of this new technology. That is something that I think is
completely underexplored at the moment. It is probably more advanced in the cattle
industries of dairy and beef than it is in the sheep industry, but there is an opportunity
for all.
The bill also, as I said earlier, allows a higher degree of certainty around market
access. When we are marketing to the world we need to be able to assure those markets
that we are providing a product up to a standard. It also supports a lot of the compliance
issues that Ministers face in international agreements around trading. So there is a range
of opportunities there. Enabling the establishment of the Na tional Animal Identification
124 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
and Tracing governing organisation is going to  be a fundamental part of the whole
process going forward, and, you know, the legisl ation needed to be solid around that. If
there is any further debate to be had I am sure it will be had in  the Committee stage of
this process. Data management systems, th e protection of those, and the information
provider involved in that have the same diff iculty as any other information provider and
data management. So the right regulation, etc., around that needs to be set.
Then, of course, the species of animals that are included is an evolving thing. I
suspect that it will not be l ong before all types of animal s are in there, but obviously
there is some resistance from our sheep-far ming colleagues as to what benefit there
could be and how you can credib ly have a retention rate of  the devices to make it a
robust system. One of the challenges, I guess,  is that, you know, for some of our high-
country farmers, the animals are not herded  that often, or brought together in a place
where these devices could be inserted. Ce rtainly when you talk volumes, with low
numbers of labour, there are challenges around  the physical side of managing all that.
So devices that can be applied, and that have  a retention rate that is acceptable and a
reliability rate that is acceptable, is a developing area as well.
I recommend the passing of this  legislation. It has had a lo ng gestation period. It has
been fraught with debate, but it is good to see it getting to this point in the parliamentary
process.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: It is a pleasure to
follow the contribution from my colleague  Shane Ardern, and can I take this
opportunity to thank him, as chair of th e Primary Production Committee, for the work
he did in bringing this legislation back to the House. Can I take this opportunity to thank
all the previous members of the Primar y Production Committee w ho worked through
the legislation once it was finally presented to this House.
The Hon Damien O’Connor made some valuable points about the length of time it
has taken to get this legislation to this stag e, to the Committee of the whole House, this
evening. It was, in my opinion, something to  congratulate a former Labour Government
on that it started this process in 2004, not l ong after we had had a hoax scare of a foot-
and-mouth disease outbreak on Waiheke Island. But that scare did prove to us that as a
Government, regardless of which Government it was at the time, we were ill-prepared if
we had to deal with a real incursion.
I want to thank the former Minister of Agriculture, Jim Anderton, for initiating a
process, because it has not been without so me angst out there in amongst the farming
community. When the National Animal Iden tification and Tracing system (NAIT) was
first proposed, most of the industry was accep ting of the need for such a system. But
there was very vocal opposition from Federated Farmers. That has taken a long time to
dissipate. It is intere sting to note today that  as this bill passes through the Committee
stage, I understand that there will be only one party voting ag ainst it. I think we can all
figure out why there was such vocal opposition to the original legislation, and that
probably almost ends up by poi nting a finger at one partic ular personality within
Federated Farmers. But, frankly, there is a new broom that has swept through that
organisation, and Federated Farmers now willingly embraces the concept of, and
recognises the need for, the National Animal Identification and Tracing system.
When the Hon Damien O’Connor listed a num ber of other countries that are well
ahead of New Zealand in this regard, one th at he did not mention, but one that really
struck me when I had the opportunity of visiting that country, was Uruguay. That is a
country with a very underdeveloped agricu ltural system. It is using a lot of New
Zealand technology now, particularly in its da irying, and it has already ensured that it
has a complete tracing system within the cattle herd. That, for me, was a real eye-opener
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 125
as to how exposed New Zealand was, give n the fact that we did not have this
technology available, and that could well have been used against us.
There have been a couple of contributions, so  far, talking about whether we have the
latest technology, and whethe r the bill has been designe d to incorporate future
technological advances. In my mind this is a little like buying a laptop. You can put off
the day to purchase a laptop for ever, because you know that next day there is likely to
be a new model. So it is absolutely critic al that we get on with this. Technology will
develop and there will be opportunities to upda te it, but the legislation has been written
in such a way that it will be able to incorporate any such developments in the future.
Mr O’Connor raised two other questions that I want to co mment on. One was the
need to make sure that NAIT, for its completeness, recognises the owners on the
lifestyle farms. I recognise that as a challe nge. It is something that NAIT Ltd will have
to grapple with, but I do point  out that we already have a TB eradication and testing
programme, and already those lifestylers ha ve the same obligations as a large,
commercial beef farmer in that regard. To  my knowledge the level of compliance in
both commercial and lifestyle farms is really very high.
The final point I want to touch on wa s again raised by Mr  O’Connor, around the
inclusion of sheep. The legislation being pa ssed in Parliament today is only for cattle
and deer. Having said that, I ha ve no doubt that at some time  in the future, sheep as a
species will be included. Frankl y, it needs to be included if we are to have the full,
comprehensive system necessary in the event of a major outbreak of a disease. What I
think will drive the inclusion of other species, such as sheep , is actually recognition by
many good commercial farmers that  there are major technologi cal advances to be had
by better identifying the good perfor mers in your herd or in your  flock. In that regard, I
take the opportunity to acknowledge the wo rk that the Crown’s farming operation,
Landcorp, is doing in this regard. Already, despite the legislation, its staff have involved
themselves in the radio frequency ID tagging of cattle, and they have involved
themselves in the radio frequency ID taggi ng of sheep, because they want to know
about the productive traits of individuals. That gives them the ability to advance genetic
gain, to get higher productivity off their fl ock and higher productivity  off their herds. I
think it is that sort of t echnology that is becoming increa singly available to the more
progressive farmers, which, fra nkly, the less progressive fa rmers are going to have to
catch up with and utilise if they want to keep up with the pace.
Can I take the opportunity to thank the Committee for its near-unanimous support for
this legislation. I certainly do acknowledge that it is work th at was initiated by a former
Labour Government under the auspices then of the Hon Jim Sutton.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is nice to follow on from
the Minister for Primary Industries in such  a bipartisan and harmonious way, and I am
sure the previous Ministers will admire that. [Interruption] What was that?

items.speaker: Hon David Carter
items.text: It’s so you can get to the gym by 6 o’clock.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right! Do not hog the treadmill, Minister. No, it is
good to hear that, and obviously also when I look at this it does have an element of
compulsion about it, which I know is not some thing the Minister is a great fan of—the
whole notion of compulsion—but clearly in this particular  sector the Minister has
decided that it is the time for some compulsion. There has been a voluntary take-up rate
among, I think, cattle farmers of around 40 per cent, but clearly that is not enough in
order to provide the kind of comprehensive scheme that is envisaged by the National
Animal Identification and Tracing Bill. It is a pleasure to be able to stand and support
this bill and acknowledge the work not only of former Ministers, as the current Minister
has done, but of Shane Ardern and the Primary Production Committee, who, I know,
worked hard on this bill.
126 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
The Minister and Shane Ardern both talked  a lot about the foot-and-mouth situation
and the importance, I guess, of New Z ealand being able to avoid a negative
consequence through a system like this identif ication system. I want to speak briefly
about the positive opportunities that lie in th is bill for New Zealand. A little while ago,
before I became a member of Parliament, I did some work for the University of Otago,
and a project I worked on there with Sim on Upton, the former Na tional Minister, was
called Paddock to Plate. It was the notion that if New Zealand is going to market its
goods overseas and reach into new markets, we do need to be able to address, I guess,
the modern concerns that are addressed by traceability—t hat is, do we know whether
this was farmed in a sustainable way, and what do we know about the health of the herd
and the immediate environment that they are in?
There is huge opportunity, I believe, pr ovided in this bill for New Zealand to
improve its export performance by being able to  meet those concerns. It has been said
that some of the most important people to New Zealand’s primary production industries
are in fact the buyers for the big supermarket chains in the UK. If they are prepared to
say “This is a product that is sustainable. This is a product that we know has been
brought to us in a way that our consumers ar e telling us they want.”, then we will go a
long way to getting over some of those some what fictitious con cerns about food miles
and so on, which when you balance that agains t the overall sustainability of the primary
production process in New Zealand, will actua lly give you a much more sustainable
product, even if it has had to travel a significa nt distance to get there. So I believe that
this is actually part of a very important process.
My own view is that, actually, we need to go further. It is not just about the cattle or,
in this case, the deer; it is about the la nd that they graze on as well. What do we know
about that? How much do we know about th e sustainability of that land? Again,
declaring a little bit of an interest, part of the job I had involved a company that has
developed some technology. The company is called Regen Ltd, and it was part of a
company called Harmonic. They actually developed technology around measuring
effluent and looking at soil acidity content and that kind of thing. If we are truly serious
about a paddock-to-plate appr oach, we need to go right back and ask whether we are
able to give consumers in Britain w ho are buying their beef from Sainsbury’s
information all the way from the kind of land through to the cattle and how healthy they
are, right through to how they are then farm ed and produced and taken out to the shops
in the UK. We have to be able to look from paddock to plate. Traceability is an
important part of that and, in turn, this iden tification process is a significant part. But I
do believe there is great opportunity here to ac tually look at this fu rther. Equally, there
is great opportunity for New Zealand - based companies to help develop the technology,
and it is of some regret that  one of the companies that is able to do that, Sirtrack, which
grew out of Landcare Research, is no long er New Zealand - owne d; it is owned in
Canada now.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What happened to it?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Well, it is possible for Crown research institutes to sell off
their subsidiary companies. It is perhaps disa ppointing that we were not able to retain
the benefit of that in New Zealand, but, as I noted, there are other companies such as the
ones I have had some association with that are developing this technology. I know there
are numerous other companies that I have not  named today. I think it is important that
we make sure that we use this as an opport unity to support that kind of new technology.
That is the kind of developm ent that will help our economy—t o be able to say we will
leverage off what is gr eat and productive about Ne w Zealand and create new
technologies that go with that. So really those are just some  brief comments to indicate
that along with the rest of the Labour caucus I strongly support this bill, not just because
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 127
it will help us avoid the negative conseque nces of something like foot-and-mouth, but
also because it offers great positive opportu nities, in my view, for New Zealand and
companies inside New Zealand.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak during the
Committee stage of the National Animal Identif ication and Tracing B ill. The bill in its
title certainly gives us a lot of comfort in New Zealand, but as this bill progressed to the
stage that it is at now there was a lot of disquiet. Th e public debate around it emanated
right back from 2002, when Ian Corney, the then Federated Farmers chairman of the
New Zealand Meat and Fibre Producers Council, pulled together a group. It was all very
collegial early on, but as things progresse d there was that normal muddying of the
waters that happens in New Zealand, not only around farming, but around all sorts of
things. You have only got to look at the debate around the Food Bill; it does come in for
a fair bit of kicking around.
At the end of it, one has to have faith in th e process, and my faith in this process was
certainly strengthened with the work the c ontributions made by submissions and by the
Primary Production Committee.
We are at a stage now where we can comfor tably and with some level of certainty
implement this bill into law in due course, but  let us not think that it is all going to be
that easy and straightforward. The responsibil ities that will go upon those people when
this becomes law, which they will carry upon th eir shoulders, are quite significant. It is
probably a blessing in disguise that initially we are not including sheep. I say that with
some consideration, because just implementing cattle is going to be  enough for the first
3 years, in my view.
It was necessary to give this bill as it cam e forward a fair amount of consideration.
You have got to think about it working in  reverse—think about the farmer or the
shepherd working in that high country situation. When you look at some of the purposes
cattle are used for, you see they are not just  sitting in nicely flat, green paddocks in the
Waikato; they are pushing into scrub-covered hill country. There is go ing to have to be
a lot of accuracy, responsibility, and dedication to this programme to keep its integrity. I
just want to put that on record. In the winter months when you are short of grass you put
your breeding cows and your calves, and that less important stock, into those areas of
the farm to keep them open. There will be loss of tags, and there will need to be
accountability back to this legislation so that those people administering it can have
certainty that it is robust. If it is not, it is not worth the paper it is written on.
We have had the TB situation, which is righ t up there and has been controversial at
times, but we are headed in the right direction with it.
Just to give a bit of a fla vour as to where we sell our  beef, I say that 230,000 tonnes
of it goes into the United States. It goes in under a quota system, and it goes in as what
we call manufacturing beef. It is ground up and blended with all sorts of other types of
product, and we eat it in hamburgers. One sort of scratches one’s head and thinks “Well,
how do we actually use the traceability mo del around that?”. It certainly leaves
questions that have got to be asked, because  that has got to be one of the commodity
meats that is most used in the world. However, if we have got a very robust system back
here in New Zealand and we can trace that product right back th rough to the producer,
then the system has got integrity.
The dairy farming situation is reasonably simple. The average herd size in New
Zealand is about 300 cows; bear in mind that it is the same size as for deer. But when
we look at the sheep farming side of it, the economic unit for the number of sheep today
would be anything up to about 3,000 to 5,000, a nd it really would present some very
challenging situations.
128 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
The amount of meat we actually sell into Europe is 1,350 tonnes, and the majority of
that came out of the expansion of the EU. So we do not actually sell a lot of meat into
the European Union. We do sell ever-increasing amounts into Asia, however; Korea and
Taiwan are very sophisticated markets th at demand traceability and good quality food
safety.
But probably the most important thing, comi ng back to my initial comment, is the
naming of the bill. It is a tracing bill. One thing that I really see is that it bridges a lot of
gaps in our biosecurity and is just so very impo rtant. I believe that it will put us right up
at the front end of the food quality syst em, because over all our red fibre production—
our meat fibres—that we sell to the world we have the platinum level of food safety. We
have really got to keep on pushing forward so that we maintain that leadership role. We
are a small economy and if we were to be hit severely by a food safety scare it would
affect our economy considerably.
So when we look at it, why was it not intr oduced by the companies? I mean, that is
probably an argument that my politics might ha ve naturally driven. If  it is such a good
idea, why do the companies not do it? The reason why we have taken the stand we have,
and why it is going to be legislated for, is th at it is very inclusive. It has got to be
mandated by the Crown, otherwise when you ar e doing nation-to-nation negotiations it
would not have the level of credibility that one would expect.
It is a wonderful bill. It ha s had a lot of refinements. I do not believe that the time it
has taken to get to this stage has been time wasted. I think myself that the acceptance of
it out in the farming community is far better now. There is better education. There is a
lot more work to go on with, and I look forward to the third reading and its final
implementation into law. On that basis, this is very, very important  legislation and this
is a very important day for primary production. Thank you.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I rise on behalf of Ne w Zealand First to take
this brief call. Unfortunately we did not have a representative on the Primary Production
Committee last time around, so I was very happ y when I heard that the work had been
started a long time ago, in a previous Parlia ment. That was really good; we would have
had a representative there.
As New Zealanders we always pride our selves on the products we produce. Our
biosecurity is really, really important to us, and we want that high standard to continue,
like everybody else here in this House. We did have some questions about the National
Animal Identification and Tracing Bill. We  know how important our export market is,
and we want our export strategy to continue to be really successful.
We had some questions, when we had a quick look at the bill, and we are prepared to
listen to all of the comments and speeches w ith a great deal of interest. We wondered
about the additional expense to farmers, and what impact that would have on the meat
that was being exported. None of these things  are ever free, and someone always has to
pay, and usually it comes back to the farm ers. We wondered, too, about what happened
when animals lost their tags. We know that  that does happen, so who looks after that,
and how is that actually paid for?
Our next lot of questions were about the technology, but I understand that that is
included in the bill, so we will be interested to read that further, because we want to
know how that technology actually operates. It  must be successful; there is no way that
we can have technology that is so important for our export ec onomy if it is not going to
be successful.
Lifestyle farmers are an ar ea of concern to us. Having been one previously, I know
that we bought animals the right way, and I would like to think that other lifestyle
farmers would ensure that their animals, when  they were sold or sent off to market,
were actually meeting the requirements.
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 129
That brings us to enforcement. Any law that we pass here must be able to be
enforced. We really cannot afford to have a ny cutbacks in the area of enforcement staff,
if this law is to be successful. We want the process to be workable; otherwise, as
previous speakers have said, this is a total waste of time. New Zealand has a good name
around the globe; we want to continue that  good name. We wonder, too, whether or not
we could ask other countries that are e xporting into New Zealand their meat—pork and
chicken, particularly that from Asian countries—to follow the same standard that we are
following.
We are prepared to listen to this particular debate. We like the sound of what we
hear, and we want to ensure that New Zealand is a very successful exporter.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The Hon—ah—Ruth Dyson.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It has not been that long, Mr
Chairman! It was only in November that you—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I was just taking my time.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I know, I know. Mr Chairman, can I begin by congratulating
you on your re-election as an officer of this Parliament, and say that it is good to have
you in the Chair. I am sure that over the co ming term you will continue to be fair and
reasonable and allow robust debate, whether the Minister in the chair has moved that it
be wide-ranging or not, as you are regarded highly for your tolerance in ensuring that
the debates go smoothly but that everyone gets a fair opportunity to contribute.
Can I also acknowledge the Minister for Pr imary Industries, David Carter, and say
that at the end of last year we had the opportu nity to contest agains t each other, in the
Port Hills electorate this time, for the sixth time. We think we are now due to be put in
the Guinness Book of Records  for being the two New Zealand MPs who have stood
against each other the most number of times—and both been elected, one as the
electorate MP and one as a list MP. I am sure  that is a record, but  I would quite like to
hear from anyone who can be bothered research ing it, who has more interest in that bit
of research than I do, because, frankly, I have not put it as a priority. If somebody else
would like to do it, please contact me in my office, because I would be really keen to
know.
I also want to acknowledge Da vid Carter and say how plea sed I was that he, in his
turn to take a call,  acknowledged the work of previous  Labour Ministers. It is not
always the case that members of one party acknowledge the work of other parties. I
think it is important th at we do that. We should try to keep the record straight. On an
issue like this, which is to the benefit of the health and well-being of New Zealanders—
literally, as well as in terms of our ec onomy—I think it is important that we
acknowledge that representatives  of many parties have those interests at the heart of
their thinking.
It is also good to be supporting this Nati onal Animal Identification and Tracing Bill.
I note the huge amount of work that the Primary Production Committee has done to it,
including, I think, replacing the entire schedule 1A of the bill, which looks to me to be a
brand new insertion by the select committee.  So the third acknowledgment I want to
make is of the work of the select committ ee. Shane Ardern is, I know, well regarded in
the House for his chairing of select committees, but I also want to acknowledge all the
members, particularly those who are no l onger in Parliament, whether by their own
choice or by the choice of our democratic process through the voting system.
The Hon Jim Anderton was a member of this  select committee, along with my friend
and colleague from Christchurch Central Brendon Burns, Dr Ashraf Choudhary, and the
National member of Parliament Sandra Goudi e. Those four were all members of the
select committee that produced this amazing b it of work to go back to the House, and
are no longer with us to shar e in the debate. I am sure that every one of them will be
130 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
sitting beside their wireless this evening, ha nging on every word that is being said, and
ensuring that we have captured the essence of the good work they have done. I am sure
they were well supported by the officials, w ho I know are very keen for this debate to
progress.
We have heard a lot of discus sion about the reasons that th is bill is so important for
the well-being of our international reputation, and for the well-being of our livestock, in
ensuring that if there is a potential or real  outbreak of any diseas e, we do have that
robust traceability. I think the point that my colleague Grant Robertson made in his
contribution is one of the more important points that we should also focus on, and that is
the changing nature of consumer interest and the change in power that many consumers
feel. For those who eat meat—and I am not one of those people who does—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I am well balanced by my colleague from Palmerston North,
Iain Lees-Galloway, who eats more meat than one individual needs to eat in their entire
lifetime. He certainly balances up the fact that I do not share in that eating.
But people who do eat meat are more and more interested in knowing where the meat
came from and the condition of the herd it was raised in, and, as we in New Zealand
know—it is more important to us than perhaps those from any other country—are more
and more interested in the environmental de gradation that may have been caused by the
farming of the animal they eventually eat. The opportunity for better marketing of our
product, I think, is one of the by-products of this legislation.
Grant Robertson also mentioned the sale of  Sirtrack. Sirtrack was a subsidiary under
Landcare Research. It is one of the compan ies that would have benefited from this
development. We have others in New Zealand that will benefit from the development of
this legislation. But it raises for me and for Labour members of this Committee a very
important concern. Even though the Crown resear ch institutes should be able to divest
themselves of a subsidiary when they are no longer able to carry that subsidiary
through—or interested in doing that, or see it as a priority—to the next stage of the
research that it is undertaking, the fact is th at New Zealand has lost all the money that
taxpayers put into Sirtrack to develop it as a subsidiary of Landcare Research. The fact
that that information and potential econom ic benefit have now gone to Canada is
something about which we should not say “Well, that’s the way it is, because the
legislation allows it.” I agree with the point that the Crown research institutes should be
able to move on from whatever subsidiaries  they may have developed, but there has to
be a better way than what happened with Sirtrack, which was a subsidiary of Landcare
Research and is now totally owned by a Canadi an company. We have lost the benefit,
even though it was our mone y—New Zealanders’ money—that went into developing
that expertise in the first place. So this debate  is really an opportunity for Parliament as
a whole to debate how we might better progre ss the role of subsidiaries of our Crown
research institutes.
The final point that I would like to ma ke is in relation to the opposition from
Federated Farmers. I was very interested in the points that David Carter made. He said,
really, that when Don Nicolson was running the show they were an ACT empire.

items.speaker: Hon David Carter
items.text: Never mentioned his name.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: He did so, very delicately; he did not mention his name. I
cannot be bothered with that sort of game . We all know whom he was talking about.
When Don Nicolson was running the show at Federated Farmers they were a little ACT
empire, and their opposition to this legislation came primarily because it was introduced
in discussion by a Labour-led Government, and also, of course, because it had some
compulsion attached to it. I am pleased that  Don has moved on in his life, but I do think
it causes another area of consideration and conc ern, and that is that an organisation that
7 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 131
has been very well regarded as being a genuine and independent voice for the farming
community—a critical part of  our economy—was for a short period of time taken over
by one political party and no longer represented the best interests of the farming
community or of the New Zealand economy as a whole. I think that is of concern, and
that sort of outing—for want of a better term—might well have been better raised at the
time of Federated Farmers’ opposition to this legislation, rather than later.
This is a good bill. I want to acknowledge  the Labour Ministers who introduced this
debate in the first place, and to support the fa ct that the National Government has
carried it on. The work that the select committee has done has been extraordinarily
robust and very detailed. It not only had submissions from the general public—
obviously, people who were interested; I thi nk 15 or 16 organisations actually made a
submission, according to the select comm ittee’s report back—but also sought
independent and expert advice. That is a very good process.  It should be commended to
other select committees as a way of ensuring that when we get legislation back to the
House like this we can have some confidence that the best eyes and ears in the country
have had their say and had their input, and that we are looking at robust legislation.
It will give us more international credib ility—that is the primary point of it—but it
does offer us an opportunity to say what cons umers of our products in the future will be
looking for, and also, most important, not onl y how we track the animal back to the
herd, the condition, and the e nvironment but how we as a nation make sure that what
they learn when they track that product b ack to the source is good news. We do not
want them hearing that the animal they are proposing to eat has co me from a herd that
destroys our environment. That is the next big challenge for this Government.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak very briefly on this
bipartisan bill, the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill. Some years ago I
was living in south-west Fran ce at the height of the ma d cow epidemic, and it was a
great pleasure to be ab le to go into a char cuterie and boucherie in the south-west, in the
patte d’oie of Auch, and know exactly what farm the meat that I was purchasing was
coming from. Was it near Jegun or Fleurance or St Lary? It was a very, very useful tool.
It is a very important tool for us as a marketer of dairy products and of meat globally.
It applies at this stage only to cattle and deer, but the meat industry alone is worth
something like $5 billion. This is a bill that tracks the location of animals from birth to
death or live export from New Zealand, so it gives that important security to consumers,
whether they be in Korea or Taiwan—where they are enjoying our grass-fed beef more
and more—or anywhere else in the world. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: This is a short call, I
should think, just to underscore Labour’s position on the National Animal Identification
and Tracing Bill. It is very pleasing to see a bill that was initiated by the Labour
Government as long ago as 2004 finally making swifter progress through the House
than it was in the last term under the Na tional Government, be cause this is so
fundamental to what New Zealand is all about.
Many speakers have discussed our intern ational reputation, the more discerning
markets that we are sending our products into in the 21st century, and the need, really, to
catch up with the rest of the world on this issue. As the previous speaker, Dr Calder,
pointed out, other countries in Europe have  been doing this for some time. For a long
time, internationally, it has been easy to identify the ex act source of different foods, and
when you think just how important food is  to our economy in New Zealand and how
important our reputation is when trying to get things into those markets, it is really
important that we get this legislation through. So it is a pity that it has kind of stalled for
a while, but good that we are finally going to be moving on.
132 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 7 Feb 2012
Given that time is short and I understand that there is another member from the
Green Party intending to take a call, I am happy to take my seat at this point.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The member must call; you call out “Mr
Chairman” to get my attention.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chairman. I would like to
acknowledge the Primary Production Committees that over the years have worked so
hard on the National Animal Identification an d Tracing Bill. I have watched it from the
side—unfortunately, I have not been able to be a member of the select committee until
this point—and other members of Parliament for the Green Party have followed this. I
think we may have had a slightly different position if I had been there; we may have had
some further amendments.
In the spirit of consensus, we will be s upporting this bill at this point, but I will
suggest that because of what we see as ra ther Draconian powers, which are put both to
the National Animal Identification and Traci ng organisation and the Minister, this may
come back before the House at some time if it seems to go for a walk in terms of
individual farmers, and particularly the smallholders.
It is fantastic that we have something that has a high level of traceability. I have done
a lot of work in the organic sector, and tr aceability is paramount. It is absolutely
paramount for the consumer to be able to  know where their food comes from. One of
my previous colleagues from this House, who has now retired, pointed out to us that this
is really a paddock-to-plate situation. We  think of things lik e country-of-origin
labelling, which we would look at. Here we have a bill that says  “Hey, we will track
every last movement of an animal in this  country.”, but the consumer in New Zealand
does not have any idea, in so many instances, where thei r food from other countries
comes from.
There is a concern with the wide-ranging powers as well, because they are so
discretionary. I am hoping that for farmer s who do not want to use the low radio
frequency identification tags because some  consumers will not want products from
animals that have been exposed to electromagnetic radiation—right or wrong, and I will
not go down that track, but from a consumer perception point of view they may well not
want it—there will be options for farmers, rather than something that may be decreed by
a larger, industry-based Crown organisation.
There are huge powers given to an as yet not actually fully identified organisation.
We have got a fair idea, and the papers that I have been able to see pretty well spell out
the sector organisations and wh at their percentage of owne rship relative to the Crown,
or the contribution, will be—

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It seems like a long time ago, but before the last
Parliament rose I was reflecting on the title and commencement clauses of this bill, the
Road User Charges Bill. I was observing that the title of the bill is the Road User
Charges Bill 2010, and now we are in 2012. Howeve r, I mean, I think I predicted rather
unkindly that the chairperson of the Trans port and Industrial Relations Committee from
the last Parliament, Mr David Bennett, woul d not be back, and certainly would not be
back in his role as chair, so I do want to congratulate him and say that I said that with all
kindness in my heart, David Bennett, because I really thought you would be a Minister
should the National Government be re-elect ed. So I do congratulate you on taking on
the role of the chair of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee again, and I
look forward to playing my usual really he lpful role, particularly when it comes to
industrial relations. I think we are going to have a very interesting time.
So in debating the title of the bill and the commencement date, I wish to reiterate that
Labour does have a problem with two parts of this bill. We have addressed that in the
second reading and we have addressed it thr ough the Committee stage. That is because
the changes to gross vehicle weights does disadvantage many operators, and we
continue to hear from them and I am sure other members have. There is real fear about
the impact of increased costs on what is already a struggling sector.
The problem is that operators do not know what is ahead. They are rightly fearful
because this bill does enable changes to be made and charges to be made by regulation,
so they have no idea. So although the title might  be relatively straightforward, in that it
134 Road User Charges Bill 7 Feb 2012
is called the Road User Charges Bill, it does hide some mischief th at I think will be
visited on many transport operators.
Worse still, the commencement clause provid es for this bill to be enacted, still
leaving the industry in the dark about what the actual costs are going to be or what the
increase in costs is going to be, because of  the provision in the bill that provides for
charges to be set by regulation. We had many examples of that in the select committee,
and we have, as I have said, discussed th at during the second reading and during the
Committee stage of this bill. And I was hoping that over the—

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you, Darien, for those very
kind words. The Transport and Industrial Re lations Committee approached this issue in
a very committed and universal way in that we were genuinely looking at the issues that
arose for truck drivers and other users, a nd we were looking for a solution that was
viable but also a solution that brought th e industry along with the Government in
making change. I think lessons had been learnt  from the last time there was a road-user
charges bill, when demonstrations resulted  from the industry not being part of the
consultation and not feeling al igned with the Government ch anges. So the Minister and
the Government made sure and en sured the role of the industry  in the way that this bill
was handled. I would like to thank memb ers of the Opposition who were on that
committee for the way that they assisted in that process, as well.
This bill, the Road User Charges Bill, has a very simple title, as you would expect,
and it is commonly called “RUC”, for those non-transport believers. Essentially, it is a
change in the system whereby vehicles will be accountable to pay their road-user
charges by moving to one based on the ma ximum permissible on-road weight. The
problem we had in the past is that drivers and companies often had to estimate the load.
There were a number of compliance costs involv ed in that. It was hard to enforce and
led to difficulties as people challenged what  they perceived the weights to be. It was
something that was a more difficult process than it needed to be. Now this process here
moves it to a much simpler regime, which everybody will understand and it will be very
visible to people as they engage in this indus try. It is one where th e actual costs, as the
Opposition has said, will be determined throug h regulation, but that is the only way it
can be done. You cannot expect this Parliament  to set the costs here. That is why we
have regulations, and this is a prime ex ample of an opportunity where regulations
should be used and are being used by the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: We know what he got up to.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Maybe there were some regulati ons that were needed then, but
in essence this is a good bill. It is one that is necessary for the industry. It is something
7 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 135
that the industry has been s upportive of. There is never goin g to be anything perfect in

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia ora an ō tātou. Firstly, let me acknowledge the
new Minister of Transport, Mr  Brownlee. It is a complicated  area, transport, but with
the experience of his parliamentary years, the skill, and the Job-like patience he is
showing to his task in Christ church, I am sure that with the minimum amount of effort
he will eclipse the deeds of Mr Joyce on this point.
We actually support this bill, but there are a number of points that unfortunately I
will be unable to make as I am no longer likely to grace the committee David Bennett
chairs, the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. My services have been called
on by Shane Ardern in the primary produce sector . We need to get back to that sector
and strip the red tape that this Government has unwisely allowed to grow, like some sort
of noxious weed, through that part of the economy. But that is for another matter.
Yes, modernisation of the road-user char ges system is importa nt, but why it is
important is because that is the basis of  the revenue we actually rely upon for the
ongoing upkeep and advancement of the infrastructure that we call our transport system.
There are a couple of areas. Consultation, unwisely by the Government, has been
deprecated and diminished in status in this legislation. Now really, what one of the most
sophisticated transport operators in the country actually wanted—Toll New Zealand—I
hope Mr Brownlee does have the opportunity to go and meet with the chief executive
officer of Toll, who I have found to be a ve ry non-partisan chap. He spreads the tickets
for rugby around on a very fair and even basis. I am not entirely sure whether or not we
are going to reach the threshold as to whether they have to be declared in this irksome
process—which has become more and mo re petty—otherwise known as pecuniary
interest. But that is another matter. That is another matter.
I would say that Toll transport, and I think it is a proxy for a host of other companies,
is bothered by the fact that, ye s, subsidiary legislation will be used—that is, regulatory-
making powers—but there is no duty on the Minister to go through essentially our
justiciable process of consultation with the affected parties prior to the promulgation of
the regulations, and that is not unreasonable.  So that was an area that we pushed quite
extensively in our—I would not call them debates—discussions and differences of
opinion in the select committee. But by and large the select committee, when it dealt
with this bill, because it is partly techni cal and partly political , found a lot of common
ground. We actually did find a lo t of common ground. The thing to bear in mind is that
there was no overwhelming evidence put before us that the current system was creaking,
to the point of collapse. There was a sense from the bureaucrats that there was a case for
modernisation. There was a case that as  the technology improved and people could
actually rely upon more efficient ways to ensure that they we re being legal, we should
not stand in the way of this process of actually modernising how we charge revenue,
collect revenue, from the heavy haulage fleet, in particular, within the country.
Now we need to be mindful—and we call upon the Minister—in this policy, as it
becomes law and as it moves through the proce ss of subsidiary legislation, that where it
is evident that either there ar e egregious omissions or it is  actually not working how the
bureaucrats thought it might wor k, there is a willingness an d a level of courage on the
part of the Minister to actually improve matters as it goes along. Far be it for me to want
136 Road User Charges Bill 7 Feb 2012
to spare the Minister the a gony, but no one actually wants to  see what Minister Annette
King faced in 2008, as I recall, wh en she increased the costs of road-user charges. It led
to something akin to a large truck strike in places like Whangarei, and other large urban
areas were congested as people were enrage d about the way in which the costs were
changed at that particular point in time.
So let us be confident, as we move through th e latter stages of this, that this bill does
not represent inadvertently an additional im post on our transport fleet, because, rest
assured, that will add an intolerable burden on the tradable sector. It will decrease the
efficiency in terms of price and quality of service in respect of our exports, and it may
also have the effect of chasing more Kiwis out of this industry as they think about going
to Australia, where unfortunately they are able to earn better amounts of money, etc.
There is an additional area where we were criticised as a committee. People felt that
the larger firms, with their vested interest s and their ability to absorb cost through a
larger, essentially, armada, or a fleet of vehicles, would actually slowly but surely
marginalise the smaller firms and put them out of business. That is not good. No firm
actually wants to see a system, and no citi zen should want to see a system, where it
becomes calcified, it becomes inefficient, and the large players have the ability to game
the market. So I think it is important that the smaller firms—after all, that is the genius
of competition; the smaller firms—that are a wee bit more nimble, a little bit more
flexible, hold the larger ones to account. We need to bear in mind that during the
process where we received lobbying, we received advocacy, and we received
submissions, there was a conc ern that the smaller, perhaps undercapitalised, firms
would not be able to make the process or the transition.
I do not think it is unreasonabl e that those of us who ar e parliamentarians on this
committee, or who will be coming on to this committee, are mindful not only of the
large powerful vested interests but also of th e smaller firms. In particular in the areas
where I hail from, where there is forestry, aquaculture, and a host of pastoral industries,
not all the firms in those areas are large, nati onally spread enterprises. It is important
that we have a view about the importance of competition, the importance of innovation,
and ensure that as this modernisation system begins to bite it does not have the perverse
impact of actually reducing the ability of  some firms to stay in business as a
consequence of an ill-conceived and poorly executed new bout of red tape.
Far be it for me to apply red tape to Gerry  Brownlee in relation to what the man has
already got to deal with in Christchurch, and I am sure I speak for my colleagues on this
side of the Chamber. I personally wish the man well in expediting the process to help
our fellow citizens down in that part of Aot earoa, but please, I make a plea. When we
implement changes of this nature, let us ensu re that we hold our bureaucrats to account,
and that as the process unfolds where they find examples that the policy is developing
and creating anomalies and poor results, we have got the courage to change it and
ensure that our transport fleet remains efficient and competitive, because that is going to
have a significant impact on our ability to pay our way in expanding the tradable sector
or growing our international revenue. Thank you.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I want to highlight in these closing stages
a group of people who will be severely disadva ntaged by the passage of the Road User
Charges Bill. A number of them made subm issions to the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee and their concerns have not been alleviated, and they fear that
with the passage of this legislation the provisions that shift the charging of the road-user
charges from a nominated weight to a gross we ight will threaten the viability of their
businesses. In the case of  one of the submitters, th e New Zealand Motor Caravan
Association, it believes that a substantial number of the 40,000-odd members who travel
around this country in motor caravans are going to be paying substantially more because
7 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 137
they typically have vehicles that have a heavy gross weight  and those vehicles are very
rarely, if ever, laden to their full capacity.
In its submission it points out that t ypically a vehicle of a mass of about 19,600
kilograms would currently be paying $121 for 1,000 kilometres and under these changes
it will be up for an increase of about $330 on top of those char ges—according to the
submission by the Motor Caravan Associati on. That is an outrageous increase—270
percent. It believes there is no justification for it and this will weigh very heavily on, as
I said, the 40,000-odd individuals who are members of the New Zealand Motor Caravan
Association.
There were also a number of submitters, principally small-business owners, who
submitted that this change would have the effect of making their businesses no longer
viable, and I want to read the Committee one or two quotes from the submission by
Southern Trucking Ltd, which operates four si x-by-four tractors and two eight-by-four
truck and trailers around the country: “If this law passes, the company that my wife and
I started with one truck 7 years ago and ha ve poured our heart a nd soul into will no
longer be viable.”

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Off to Aussie!

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Yep, that is right. Off to Aussi e; off to Aussie. McLean Road
Services, which specialises in transportin g large loads like fibreglass swimming pools,
which are up to 5 metres wide, around the country has large vehicles to do this, but they
are never fully laden. Therefore, the impact of this change, which will hit it up for road-
user charges calculated on the gross weight of the truck, wi ll amount to, it  believes, a
huge increase. I quote from Don McLean, the proprietor: “Our margins are thin now,
and if I have to pay RUCs for the GVM, it probably won’t be viable.”
Finally, Mike Hermansen says: “The method currently [proposed] would
disadvantage operators carrying lighter loads and would … negate the use of multi axle
units that operators have currently in their fl eets, these units have been specifically built
with more axles to be easier on our roads.  If you [move] to gross weights these units
will be disadvantaged and operators will no longer use them.”
So it is a great shame that these objections were not listened to by the majority on the
select committee. The Government has ridden roughshod over the concerns that
Opposition members on the committee rais ed throughout the process through all
readings to this point. The Government has fa iled to take on board those concerns, and
the passage of this bill will impose a terrible burden on many small businesses around
this country that cannot sustain the kinds of costs that this bill will add to their bottom
line. So I do not believe that the Governme nt and the majority on the select committee
have adequately considered the consequences, albeit unintended, of this change—

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I feel I need to respond to
Phil Twyford’s concerns. Firstly, I w ill acknowledge that Labour members are
supporting the Road User Charges Bill, so obvi ously they will be speaking from a very
genuine and concerned perspective. But one of  the things I would point to is Appendix
1 of the consultation document that went out for consideration by all parties who pay
road-user charges. The example that th e member gave us was of a 1,960, I think,
kilogram vehicle, where I think the suggestio n was that the road-u ser charge was going
to go from $121-odd to something in exce ss of $450 by the time you add two things.
That would be a rate per 1,000 kilometres, mean ing that in that case someone would be
paying close to 50c per kilometre. That is patently ridiculous and not something that is
going to happen.
The consultation document gives the example of a vehicle of up to 4 tonnes, twice
the weight of the vehicle th at Mr Twyford was using as an example. Currently that
vehicle would pay somewhere between  $44 and $49 per 1,000 kilometres. The
138 Road User Charges Bill 7 Feb 2012
consultation document gives a range—remember, it is up to 4 tonnes, so there will be
various gross weights below that. The new range is somewhere between $45 and $87
per 1,000. That is a long, long way from the $460-odd that the member was speaking of.
The mid-point, I guess, in that range is something like about $60, which represents a
gross increase of about $11 per 1,000 for people in that category. I am just working off
the bands that I have put here. They are certainly not rates that  are struck at this stage,
but they are substantially less than the very big figures that the member gave before.
I think the issue of gross laden weight and trucks is really the problem with the
mileage. If you are just charging on a mileag e rate, that truck is  doing some wear and
tear on the road at all times that it is on the road, whether it is at its gross laden weight
or not. If we are going to have efficiency in  transport, something that the Green Party
certainly requires of us as a point of policy, then having some road-user charges that
actually encourage inefficient use is not particularly helpful. I think also that even at the
upper end, I would like to say—so you might  have vehicles up to 44 tonnes—the
increases in the road-user charges are not likel y to be anywhere near as substantial as
the member spoke of. In that case, for the current ranges be tween $250 and $409,
depending on the weight that they put on to  that vehicle, under the gross system it
would be around about $276. That is encourag ing efficiency, as you get bigger units
able to take larger loads.
I think the Transport and Industrial Re lations Committee has done a good job in
considering all of these aspects, and I appreciate the efforts that the committee has made
to get a good bill. No one likes passing bills that  increase charges. This, I think, is a bill
that may increase some charges, but, by and la rge, it will improve the efficiency of that
large chunk of the transport system and also make it much fairer for those who
participate in it at all levels.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.
