items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I move, That the Electronic
Identity Verification Bill be now read a first time.  At the appropriate time I intend to
move that the bill be re ferred to the Government Administration Committee for
consideration and that that committee report finally to this House on or before 29 June
2012. This is an important bill. It is part of  the Government’s framework to put tools in
place that make it easier for individuals to in teract with government, and at a lower cost
for those individuals and for the agencies concerned.
Specifically, the purpose of the Electronic Identity Verification Bill is to regulate and
enhance the operation of the igovt identity verification service. Once it is fully
operational, individuals will be able to use th at service to verify their identity via the
internet for interactions wher e it is necessary for an agen cy to know who it is dealing
with. Those might, for example, be transact ions involving the paying out of money or
the exchange of personal information. Curr ently for those types of transactions,
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 139
agencies usually require individuals to provide multiple documents as evidence of their
identity, such as passports and drivers’ licen ces. Individuals have to bear the cost and
the time burden of applying for and supplying  those documents, and individuals whose
identities have been wrongly used can face si gnificant inconvenience, distress, and cost
to rectify matters. There are costs for ag encies to check, c opy, and return those
documents. In addition, the use of false, lost , or stolen identity documents can impose
considerable further costs on agencies. Another bill before this House, the Identity
Information Confirmation Bill, will go a long way to combat the risk of fraudsters
presenting false identity documents to agenci es. While that bill will help with face-to-
face transactions, the current bill and the iden tity verification service within it provide a
complementary role for the online environment.
The igovt system will provide agencies with  a ready-made, secure process to support
the provision of online services that woul d not otherwise be possible because of the
potential fraud risks involved. It will allow individuals to avoid repeatedly having to
provide physical documents to multiple agencies in order to  use online services, should
they choose to use the service. The igovt identity verification service has been operating
successfully but in a limited form since the end of December 2009. Individuals have, for
example, been able to use the service for the online ordering of certificates and copies of
records from the Births, Deaths and Marriages registry, which requires proof of identity.
In this way the identity verification service use has to date been limited to a small
community of eligible indivi duals for a single type of tr ansaction. It is now time to
expand the service for use by all members of  the public and for the widest possible
range of services so that individuals, gove rnment, and businesses can all realise the
benefits that internet technologies offer. The Electronic Identity Verification Bill will
enable this to happen.
The bill will enable individuals to choose to verify their identity via the internet with
approved agencies with appropriate contro ls and safeguards while also providing
operational flexibility for the service to be developed over time to respond to changing
technology. It is important that this significant Government service, as it is expanded, is
duly authorised by legislation. The bill wi ll ensure that the service can operate
effectively and that appropriate safeguards are put in place and maintained. It is vital
that the bill is progressed quickly. This will ensure the best use of the investments being
made to develop the service and individual agencies’ online services that will rely on it.
Clause 4 of the bill is part icularly important. It sets out the principles around which
the service’s operation is based. Those principles emphasise that the use of the service is
optional and that individuals have control ove r the personal information that the service
holds. Individuals will not be required to jo in the service. If they do choose to do so,
they can decide whether or not to use it for any particular transaction, and agencies are
expected, therefore, to ensure that i ndividuals can still access their services by
presenting other forms of evidence of ident ity, should the individual  wish to use that
option. The bill does not impose any mandatory obligation on New Zealanders.
Individuals can cancel their membership of  the service at any time. The identity
verification service provides authorised  agencies only the minimum amount of
information necessary to verify  an individual’s identity thro ugh a record referred to in
the bill as an electronic identity credential. The credential may be provided to an agency
only with the individual’s consent. An individual may check the information before it is
sent, correct it or update it as necessary, a nd monitor where the information has been
sent. An individual’s identity is verified using an identifier, or code, that is unique to
each authorised agency, and this prevents  the unauthorised sharing of information
between agencies.
140 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012
The bill will allow anyone to use the servic e once his or her identity is verified to a
high standard comparable to that used for the issuing of New Z ealand passports. That
may occur, for example, through checking that an individual’s identity information,
which includes his or her phot ograph, is consistent with information held in other
official records. The bill authorises information-matching programmes and other
processes for that purpose. Children will be able to apply, but those under 14 will need
their parents’ or guardians’ consent.
The bill also provides a number of other safeguards that will ensure the service
operates securely and protects people’s privacy. Those protections are vital. If the public
loses trust in the service, it will fail. The first key protection in the bill is that it provides
that agencies must be author ised through regulations to use the servi ce. Those agencies
may be in the public or the private sector s. Approved agencies must adhere to the
standards for the use of the system. Secondl y, the bill strictly regulates access to
photographs and other personal information he ld by the service. Thirdly, the Privacy
Commissioner will be able to require reports on the general operation of the service,
rather than just reactively dealing with comp laints about privacy breaches that may be
associated with the service. I am pleased that the Privacy Commissioner and her staff
have been closely involved in the development of the service and this bill, and that this
involvement will continue. Finally, the bill cr eates specific offences and penalties to
deter abuse of the system. Courts will have the ability to ban offenders from using the
service and to determine the validity of a ny transactions that have been undertaken
using false information. Agencies will be notified if a false electronic identity credential
has been used for their online services so that they may take immediate action.
This is an important bill. It will enable individuals and agencies to realise the benefits
of being able to easily verify individuals’ identity information via the internet for a wide
range of services. There will be appropriate  safeguards in place to ensure the service
continues to be secure, protects people’s privacy, and is easy to use. I commend the bill
to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Can I begin my contribution on the
Electronic Identity Verification Bill by congratulating you, Mr Assistant Speaker
Robertson, on your re-election to the esteemed position of an officer in this House. I say
that I look forward to your reminders and support of us adhering to the Standing Orders,
which you know more diligently, I believe, than  any other officer of the House whom I
have known about, and also to the engagi ng way that you respond to members during
often quite difficult times. Your persona is  appreciated, I think, by all members in the
House.
I also want to commend the Hon Amy Adam s for what I would imagine is her first
piece of legislation, even though I also want to acknowledge her predecessor, Nathan
Guy, because he actually did a lot of the wor k—not all of it. I thi nk it is an important
occasion when a Minister has her first bill introduced in the House. I can assure you that
the select committee to which you alluded and to which you want  to refer it, the
Government Administration Co mmittee, will give it rigorous attention and will ensure
that it comes back to the House with every single detail considered and every concern
not only looked at but also addressed, and th at the entire House wi ll have confidence in
the robustness of the legislation.
Labour certainly agrees with the point of this legislation and supports its progress.
No doubt there will be some issues that arise in the select committee—I do not recall
any legislation that has not had that happen—but in terms of the principle, I think it is a
really good bill. Basically, as the Minister outlined, it stops people needing to provide
often quite frustrating amounts of identification to a variety of different agencies. We all
know that to carry numerous amounts of pa perwork around with you is a pain in the
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 141
neck. Actually, it is quite dangerous, as  well. I do not think people should be
encouraged to carry their passport with them  all the time. Certainly, overseas it is a
habit that people are strongly advised agains t doing. You do not walk  around the streets
of some city with your pass port in your pocket, but in Ne w Zealand that is what we
require of many people—to bring in your pa ssport, or get it photoc opied, and then you
have to go through the added ta sks of getting a justice of the peace, a lawyer, or a
member of Parliament to witness that that  document is a genuine copy of the original.
So you have another round of paper filling to do.
This bill seeks to get rid of that requireme nt by having a little box that is controlled
by the Department of Internal Affairs und er the management of New Zealand Post,
which I am very pleased to hear about, and if an individual chooses to put information
in that little box, they can then—again, thei r choice—have that information shared with
the agencies that they have authorised in order to provide the level of identification that
is needed. I think it is a great  idea. I do hope that it leads us on to further thinking and
courage about how better the internet can be used to provide access to information,
access to services, and access to voting and whatever, because so often that robust
verification of identification has been the barrier.
I do not know whether it is common in ot her countries, but I th ink in New Zealand
we still have a lot of anxiety about wher e things go when you put information on the
internet. I know a large number of people w ho still will not buy th ings online because
they are so nervous about putting their credit card numbers into a computer because
then they vanish off the screen and they  do not know where they go. Someone else
might get them and the next minute they wi ll get a huge credit card bill. Actually, it
happens when you just leave your credit card on the counter by mistake, as well.

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: That’s just your children.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: That is right, or you leave your  wallet somewhere where your
children might get access to it. I do think ther e is an anxiety about where information
can go. I particularly noted the point that Minister Adams made during her introductory
speech that if the public loses faith in this process, then the whole service will fail, and I
do think that is a very important point. We have to be very careful if this bill is referred
to our select committee that we listen to the concerns the public have and make sure that
we can provide them with the level of confidence they require, because this is not a
service that should fail. We need the confid ence of the public and therefore we need the
robustness of the service.
We do have the absolute clarity within the legislation—I actually think it is a very
well-drafted bill—that consistently throughout the process it is the individual’s choice
about what information is stored and whic h agencies that information can then be
shared with. So that is, for me, a primary poi nt to make known to the public. This is not
information that can be gleaned from other documents or other sources and compiled on
your behalf; it is only when you have authorised it yourself that you will be able to have
that then shared with agencies, and then it is only agencies that, again, you have
authorised. You cannot have any unauthorised exchange of information.
I heard some debate over the dinner hour about this legislation, where people thought
that it actually allowed for data sharing betw een agencies, which would be of benefit to
the particular agencies. For example, some Work and Income information may be of use
to the Housing New Zealand Corporation, the Inland Revenue Department, or some
debt-collecting agencies. There is information that if it was shared could be of use. And
I know, from the discussion we had over the dinner hour, that some people thought that
this would allow that, and that is something th at I will be seeking absolute clarification
of during the select committee process. My re ading of the bill says  that that is not
possible. If that was a sort of side advantag e, then I think we would have to be very
142 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012
upfront with the public. But the Minister is agreeing with my point; it is not enabled by
this legislation, and I am very pleased to see her nodding about that point.
The other advantage in this le gislation to me currently—and , again, it might be just
part of the progress of the way we do thi ngs in New Zealand—is that this does not
replace other ways of providing identification. So if you just do not trust the internet, or
if you do not want to do it  for whatever reason, you ca n still get your passport
photocopied and validated and send the photoc opy with the signature saying it is the
correct copy off to whichever agency you have to provide that verification of
identification to. So this is a progressive c hoice; it is not eliminating the current ways
that we do things. I think that is a very good point, as well.
I was delighted to hear the Minister’s ent husiasm for the involve ment of the Privacy
Commissioner in this work. I do think it is very important that the Privacy
Commissioner keeps on top of these issues. The ability to require the chief executive of
the Department of Internal Affairs to report on any aspect of this service to the Privacy
Commissioner should, again, give  New Zealanders confidence that the information will
not be misused.
I also noted that New Zealand Post was an exclusive agency for the operation of this
service, which is—well, I think it is fine ac tually, but it does s eem to go against the
grain somewhat, and I wondered whether th e Minister had any particular reason.
Perhaps the deputy chair of the select committ ee to which this bill is being referred
might be able to glean some words from her about whether having New Zealand Post in
that position as the exclusive agency wa s a considered decision, whether it just
happened to be that New Zealand Post was the most appropriate or up and able to do it,
or whether it was because New Zealand Post has been working this system, this service,
since the operational trial began in December 2009.
I certainly hope that we will be able to get some assurance that New Zealand Post
will not be next on the block to be sold off, as well, because if it was, that would cause
the public huge concern and would, I know, be  of worry to the Mi nister, because then
the public would lose faith if a private agency had all this information stored and
perhaps was able to potentially make money out  of it. We want to avoid those sorts of
things, and the best way to do  that, of course, is for the Government to not sell State
assets.
The final point I want to make is that th is has been operating since the end of 2009. I
agree with the bill and with the comments in the explanatory note and also in the
regulatory impact statement, wh ich looked at the alternatives: do we need to have a
legislative framework, are there alternative regu latory processes, or could we just have
it operating as it has been under trial with a non-regulatory option? I want to commend
the regulatory impact statemen t; I think it is very considered  and robust, and it is the
sort of quality this House needs. I agree with the verdict of the regulatory impact
statement that we do need a robust regulator y framework. I look forward to the debate
in the select committee, and certainly offer Labour’s support for this bill to the next
stage.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: May I begin as the previous speaker did by
congratulating you, Mr Assistant Speaker Robertson, on the position that you hold as
returned Assistant Speaker to the House. I am sure many other members will enjoy the
careful and considered way you fulfil your responsibilities, so congratulations on that.
I am particularly pleased to follow the Hon Ruth Dyson on this particular bill, the
Electronic Identity Verification Bill, particular ly as she spoke so positively and in such
a considered way about this bill. It is not new to this particular committee, the
Government Administration Committee, it is new to me because I am a new member of
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 143
the committee. I think it bodes well for the pa ssage of this bill  through the select
committee to hear such a positive approach being taken by both sides of the House.
I am very pleased to be taking a call on the Electronic Identity Verification Bill,
which is the latest step in National’s progra mme of better public se rvices. This is an
excellent step forward for online Government  services, and for all the reasons so far
canvassed by Minister Adams and by the Hon Ruth Dyson, it augurs well for the future.
The world of technology moves very qui ckly, and occasionally Governments are
accused of not keeping up with that changing world. That criticism cannot credibly be
levelled at this Government. We are ro lling out high-speed broadband to schools,
homes, and businesses across the country a nd we have improved our cyber security.
Under the new Minister, the Hon Amy Adam s, our communications and information
technology infrastructure will continue to gr ow as New Zealand begins to benefit from
the transformative effect of what we have achieved thus far in this area. It is appropriate
that as we are transforming New Zealand with  some of the highest broadband speeds in
the world we also establish online Government services that match the best in the world.
This bill establishes the Electronic Identity Verification Service. The service will be
responsible for issuing individuals with an  electronic identity for use across multiple
Government agencies with an online presence.  It does away with the need to verify
one’s identity repeatedly, of ten with original hard-copy documents or copies of those
documents, when dealing with multiple Government departments. As a practising
justice of the peace in a rural area I can sympathise with the comments made by the Hon
Ruth Dyson about the difficulty people have in obtaining verifica tion of copies of
passports and other things—it puts them to so me considerable degree of trouble to get
these things done in a rural situation.
The bill’s objectives are achieved by aut horising the Electronic Identity Verification
Service to create electronic id entity credentials. These credentials will contain limited
core identity information about  an individual. Th e core information can include the full
name, the gender, the date of birth, and th e place of birth of the individual. The
electronic identity credential will ensure that a Governme nt agency with an online
presence can identify individua ls with a great degree of accuracy, which is necessary
when dealing with sensitive Government serv ices. This is particularly the case, for
example, when dealing with those services related to identity, such as the issuing of
passports.
By centralising the verification of online se rvice users’ identities, we will not only
provide a high degree of effi ciency for both the users them selves and the Government
agencies they deal with, but also provide a consistent level of security across agencies.
This whole-of-Government approach to iden tify verification is in line with National’s
goal of providing better public services.
The Hon Ruth Dyson did ask that I take th e opportunity to canvass with the Minister
why we are using New Zealand Post in particular. Basically, it is a matter of providing a
contract, which New Zealand Post has cont ested for and has secured. It gives one
measure of control, so that we do not lose measurements of efficiency by having
random providers, and also it is a national organisation, and most people have access to
a post office service within a reasonable distance from where they live. Basically, those
were the contributing reasons for that choice.
I would like now to focus on the principles se t out in this bill, in clause 4. These are
the principles that must be taken into acc ount by every participating agency. I concur
with previous speakers when I say that it is very comforting to see the degree of
preparation that has gone into the drafting of this bill, because it has not avoided what
we could call public perception issues, which are going to be a feature of this sort of
thing.
144 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012
Again, I find myself agreeing with previous  speakers who say that there will be
public apprehension, particularly, perhaps, amongst people who are a little older and not
au fait with modern technology. I think that most of us, if re ally pressed, would find it
hard to give an absolute assurance of the net being a very secure sort of organisation.
Indeed, most of our institutions would caution care when using it. But basically it is the
controlling principles that will decide on th e protocols that control this service, and
these are the principles that must be take n into account by every participating agency.
These principles provide a strong defence, in  my mind, against any kind of misuse of
this new important tool.
When considering an online service that  involves the Government collecting
personal information about individuals for use across multiple Government agencies,
one’s first concern must be for the security  and appropriate use of that information.
Information is power. Once somebody has it, it  cannot simply be taken away. So this
bill has been structured from the point of view that in receiving that information there
are safeguards over its use. I am pleased to see that any concern on that score is well
and truly put to bed by the strong safeguards in this bill.
I will quote from clause 4, “Pri nciples”, if I may: “(d) an  individual’s consent to the
supply of his or her personal information to  a participating agen cy must be obtained
before the Service can supply th e information to the agency and, even if the consent is
obtained, the Service may supply only the mi nimum amount of personal information
that is necessary for the agency to act as part of a given transaction or series of
transactions:”.
The safeguards in these principles are comprehensive. They clarify that at no time
will an individual be forced to use this service. Nobody can be forced or coerced to
apply for an electronic id entity credential and nobody can  be forced to use it.
Importantly—and I think this is important—no Government agency can make this the
only way in which to access its services.
The system is a good one. It will provide a high level of convenience to the users of
Government services. However, there will of  course be individuals  who prefer not to
make use of it, for all sorts of reasons. The principles of this bill make it absolutely clear
that that decision is at their discreti on and will not prevent them from accessing
Government services.
In addition, individuals are entitled to check the information on them held by the
Electronic Identity Verification Service and to view the usage of their electronic identity
credentials. This is the level of service you  can expect from most privately run online
services, and it is good to see that this bill will ensure that people can expect that level
of service from their Government-run services.
When dealing with online information, secu rity of information is of the utmost
importance. Safeguards in this bill are comprehensive and they seem to me to be an
appropriate level of security for the informati on that will be held. I am sure this is an
area that will be thoroughly scrutinised when it comes before the Government
Administration Committee, and I too look forward to working on it there.
The Electronic Identity Verification Bill br ings our online Government services into
the 21st century. It does so in a way that comprehensively safeguards the security and
the privacy of those who use those services, and for those reasons I fully commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in the first reading of
the Electronic Identity Verifi cation Bill, but before I begin my contribution may I also
take the opportunity to c ongratulate you, Mr Assistant Speaker Robertson, on your
election as an officer of this Parliament. I look forward to you continuing your role as a
fair and effective officer of this House. We  have all had great experiences with you in
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 145
the role, and it is very nice to know that you are continuing in that. I would also like to
congratulate the new Minister, Amy Adams, and I congratulate her on introducing her
very first bill as a Minister in this Parliame nt. As my colleague Ruth Dyson said, it is a
pretty special moment. I also acknowledge the work that has gone before, but well done,
Minister.
Labour, as my colleague has said, supports this bill’s referral to the Government
Administration Committee. I know that the process in the select committee will be
really robust. I think that th ere will be a lot of interes ting submissions, and, hopefully,
we will be able to return a bill that everybody can continue to support in this House.
I was a member of the Government Administration Committee in my first term in
Parliament, and this is not the first time that  committee has dealt with issues of identity.
I was on the committee when we did the chan ges to accessing online information about
births, deaths, and marriages. I remember how  controversial that was—on all sides of
the argument, actually—and how distrust ful people were about anybody collecting
information, particularly Government depart ments. So I think th e committee has a big
job ahead of it. There is no doubt  about it—issues of identity are extremely sensitive. It
is understandable, because it is part of our uniqueness. It is part of who we are as human
beings, and it is extremely personal to ev ery single one of us. The history of our
families and our whānau, and our personal information, is something that we all hold on
to and hold dear.
It used to be the case that it was paper ba sed, and I really do not want to part with
any of that paper-based information that I st ill hold from my forebears, such as birth,
death, and marriage certificates. Of course, our drivers’ licences are still paper based, as
are our passports, although I will acknowle dge the work of the former Labour
Government and the Hon Rick Barker, as th e Minister of Internal Affairs, and the
progress we have made with our passports. In  fact, I just got my new one. It is very
good; it is very nice. I like the black cover and the fern. It is very beautiful, and also it is
somehow reassuring to know it has that el ectronic tag in it so that it cannot be
duplicated. Somebody cannot obtain my passport and duplicate it.
Technological developments are altering  access to personal information quite
radically. It has become a valuable comm odity—unfortunately, often to be bought and
sold, combined, sorted, profiled, mined, an d sometimes abused, meaning that the
opportunities for the misuse of that information have multiplied. There have been many
stories about identity fraud, and the State’ s role in this is that it has special
responsibility for the personal information th at it holds. Actually, it holds personal
information about almost every New Zealand citizen in one form or another. And so
what this bill will do is enable a wide r sharing of that information through the
Electronic Identity Verification Service, where individuals will have the option of
verifying their identity online and in real time to participating agencies, including, in the
future, the private sector.
Now, it seems like it is an inevitable ch ange, as technology ove rtakes us, and many
people will welcome the ability for an online service. It is optional and I acknowledge
that, and it should stay that way, but sadly I do not think it will. If we think about the
development of call centres, fo r example, and if we think about the services that are
provided through public services, for example, we now have to spend quite a lot of time
on the end of the phone going through a whole lot of diffe rent numbers, pressing
buttons, and so on, and sometimes speaking to people in different countries. It is now a
requirement. I read something the other day that said that the ordinary person now
spends something like 14 hours a year on the end of the phone going through the
various—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: That’s on hold?
146 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: That is on hold—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: That’s just the IRD.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: That is just the IRD. But cons ider that. We are time poor as it
is, and here we are now obliged to follow those processes because it does save money, it
is more efficient, and so on, and there are people on the end of  the phone maybe in
India, maybe in other countries, maybe in the Philippines. But, you know, that is the
way our lives have changed. So although we can say it is optional at the moment, my
fear is that it will not stay that way. It is just the inevitability of the change that we are
seeing in technology.
I do want to give a caution. I am glad th ere are protections in this bill, for the
moment, but let us keep in mind the peopl e who actually have no idea about how to go
about doing something online. It is not nece ssarily because they are older; sometimes
that is the reason. Some people do not even have access to a computer, and some people
do not even have access to a phon e. So we have got to remember this, as we go into
these things, and remember that not only are many of our families time poor, but they
are also technology poor. They are communications  poor, so we have to bear that in
mind. For those people, putting something in the envelope and walking down to the
Post Office, because they probably do not have  a car because they cannot afford one, is
the only option that they have. It is the cost of living issue, and I just really, as I said,
caution that we keep in mind that not everybody is able to move with the times, with the
fast pace of technology, as this bill indicates we will be doing.
It is really important in this bill that there is provision for ensuing that there are
protections against fraudulent applications and criminal activity. I think it will be easier
if it is online. I think there are far more security checks in that than in being able to copy
someone’s birth certificate as people used to be able to  do, and probably still can, and
then reinvent themselves as another person. I probably should not talk about that too
much. I mean—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Where is David Garrett?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: That is right. We have had an unfortunate example of that in
this Parliament, and we know what distress that caused. It really did cause enormous
distress to that family. It was a very sad story, actually, on all counts.
But whether we like it or not the internet, as a service delivery channel, is continuing
to grow in importance. Statistics New Zeala nd reported that in the 12 months to the end
of December 2009 around 2.68 million New Zealanders used the internet, and that
number continues to increase. Now, I w ill own up and say I have got much more
comfortable about online access to some of th ese things. It took me a while to trust
internet banking, and I am still a bit iffy about it. I still do not really believe that it is
secure; however, it is conve nient. Often convenience, in  the end, overtakes one’s
requirement to be cautious.
I am glad about many things in this bill.  I think of the “Principles”, which the
previous member referred to, and also, in Part 2, the admini strative provisions. Part 3, I
think, will receive a great deal  of attention because it is ar ound the intersection with the
Official Information Act and the Privacy Act 1993. That is a while ago, you know, but it
has become a really important part of the New Zealand culture and expectations around
privacy of our information and privacy ar ound the way we are treated, and how our
information is used. I think all of those thi ngs will receive a great deal of attention and
scrutiny in the select committee.
The challenge in this legislation is to pr eserve the benefits of online transfers,
including easy access for those who require it in the public interest, while minimising
the risk to individuals, preserving the option— so that it is not compulsory—in the long
term, and making sure that the contest between access and convenience ensures an
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 147
obligation on the State to protect personal info rmation. I suspect that this bill will have
to visit all of those debates when it gets to the select committ ee. I look forward to
hearing about it, but we are happy to support it to the select committee. Thank you.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker Robertson. Ng ā mihi
nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. It is a pleasure to rise to take a call on the Electronic Identity
Verification Bill. I would also like to sh are the best wishes of this House, so
congratulations to you, Mr Assistant Speak er Robertson; congratulations to Amy
Adams, the new Minister for Communica tions and Information Technology; and
congratulations to all members in the House who were elected at the last Parliament.
I also want to thank the o fficials. It has been surpri sing that Labour has not taken
credit for this in the debate I have heard, but it did do a lot of work in the years it was in
Government in getting this process with igovt, the process towards getting this
legislation started. So I would like to ac knowledge Labour members’ work and also the
officials who have worked with them over a number of years for this bill.
It is an important and emerging issue we ar e discussing in this Parliament in 2012.

items.speaker: We are quite right
items.text: we are talking about our lives, we are talking about our memory, and
we are talking about our da ta. One has only to look at  Facebook to see that that
company did not get rich just by selling ad s or subscriptions; it got rich because it
managed data. It managed to package, compile, and share data in such a way that it is
one of the wealthiest companies in the worl d. I think its share offer will be immensely
huge.
The Greens share with the other parties their support for this legislation’s referral to
the select committee. What I would like to talk about is the im portance of it around
easing the relationship with Government depa rtments. I note in the regulatory impact
statement there is a quote that there are over $300 million in tangible economic benefits
to the nation. That is good. I would love to ask one of the officials what they estimate
the time savings could be for people us ing this system around the country. I am
prepared to wager any member in this Chambe r that the time-savings from this bill, for
a minuscule sum of money, will  be much more considerable  than the $19 billion the
Government is currently borrowing to spend on motorways, literally saving only
minutes of Kiwis’ time across the country.
So we see the potential. We see the benefits. That is why we are supporting the bill to
the select committee. But, like the other part ies, we do think there are valid concerns,
and we will be asking some questions at the select committee. So this bill effectively
sets up an online passport. I think it makes se nse. I think it is common sense. You have
a mishmash of different log-in requiremen ts for different Government departments.
Like Darien Fenton, I cannot remember half of my passwords. I have to keep getting
them to email them to me, because there are just so many when you are engaging with
Government departments, let alone all the other services that people use online for work
or for pleasure. So we see the common sense.
I have been very interested to follow ove r the years the progre ss of igovt, which is
currently the contractual-only service preced ing this legislation—the trial that is
effectively making this legislation relevant and, I would say, desirable. But I would also
note that there are only 400-odd people on igov t at the moment—the Minister might be
able to correct me—and I would love to see more people using this service.
I have also got some concerns because I ha ve to write to the Minister of Internal
Affairs just to go to the National Library. I asked him more than a year ago whether I
could have a briefing from officials, because I am interested in this and I would like to
engage constructively, but to no avail—Minister Guy would not let me have a briefing.
So to look at the detail, it is important that we as legislators get our heads around this
issue. Technology is shaping lives in ways we cannot even imagine, probably in the
148 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012
next 5 to 10 years, and certainly longer. Mo re and more of us are engaging with our
Government online; more and more of us e ngage with the Government only online. As
Chris Auchinvole said, the Government is embracing t echnology. I think they have
done some good things, but I also think it is maybe a bit of an ex aggeration to portray
ourselves as world leaders in the technologica l field. We have got Skynet, the copyright
infringing and file-sharing law, and we are engaging with the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade
Agreement negotiations recently signed in Tokyo, and the punitive rules in the Trans-
Pacific Partnership.
Look, you know, I do not think we are embraci ng technology as we could be. I do
not think we are world leaders in this, but th is is one area where we certainly could be.
Take the Inland Revenue Department—it was only  last year that this Parliament passed
a law, the Education Act No. 4, that let stude nt loan borrowers go online to check their
balance. In 2011 this Parliame nt was not passing such legi slation. Take the legislation
just before this bill, the Road User Char ges Bill. At a time when we could be using
digital electronic technology, we are instead going down the absolute opposite path and
getting average weight-based models of calculating road-user charges.
The stuff we are talking about in this Parlia ment is topical. We have just seen in
America and all around the world that lit erally 7,000 websites, I think it was—4.5
million people—signed Google’s petition in 1 day. We saw the two Houses, the House
of Representatives and the Senate, in the US fully step backwards from the punitive
copyright legislation there—the Stop Online Piracy Act and the Protect IP Act. We have
seen the Megaupload arrests where we have had 70 police officers flying in on
helicopters to catch someone in relation to  alleged copyright infringing. And, to the
right side of the ledger, we are seeing the Government invest a considerable sum in
ultra-fast broadband, which the Green Party supports the intent of.
I think what we have seen in terms of  the Skynet legislation, debates in New
Zealand, and the stop online piracy and protect IP debates in Ameri ca, is that it is no
longer OK—as a popular blog post also points out —for us as legislators to not know
any more. It is not a badge of honour to pr etend we do not use computers and we do not
know how to engage—it is not OK any more. We have to get on top of our game, I
think these are salutary lessons, and I look forward to engaging with the other members,
the officials, the submitters, and the select committee.
So we will be supporting this legislation to the select committee. We think it is
common sense. We think there are some defi nite inefficiencies—we could be engaging
with other departments—but also there ar e some tremendously exciting opportunities
that flow out from this legislation. Take th e last election: we sa w the lowest-ever level
of youth non-enrolment in our country’s histor y. I heard anecdotally of people around
the country who would have enrolled and w ould have liked to vot e but had to send in
the blasted form via a fax machine from overseas. We heard of people who would have
loved to do it online, in between checki ng Facebook, or Twitter, and to enrol online.
There is no framework or legislative allowance for that.
I would like to see this law look at how we take this unique identifier to understand
the potentialities not only fo r our economy and society but also for our democracy. So
what we see with that change, which I thi nk would be desirable in our future, is a
challenging of the central tenet, which we have  talked about in the clause 4 debate in
this Parliament, which is that we should not  worry about privacy concerns. Everything
is taken care of in clause 4, “Principles”. At  the moment the main protection is the fact
that it is only opt-in for people to have their data saved, but, if we are going to unleash
the powers of this legislati on, obviously we are going to have to look at a mandatory-
type system in the future and what the privacy implications are there.
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 149
So we see that people cannot opt out in every circumstance when it comes to this bill.
People cannot opt out when it comes to statistical analysis. As Ruth Dyson aptly put it,
there is a digital divide. We still need to  make sure people have options. We cannot
replace every type of communication or valid ation with the Government. It has been
good to see that the Privacy Commissioner has been involved in the drafting of this
legislation. I think we might want to inves tigate in the select committee actually going
slightly further than what this bill out lines, which is that currently the Privacy
Commissioner can go to the chief executive of  the Department of Internal Affairs and
ask for a report. I wonder whether we should write into the legisla tion, or through an
Order in Council, a regular reporting requirement, given that this is the front line of both
the privacy and the new technological developments in New Zealand.
The regulatory impact statement talks of the risk of function creep, which I think is a
definite risk. When we look at the Privacy Commissioner’s website, principle 12 of the
privacy principles says categorically—and it is going to be intere sting to ask her how
she is going to deal with it—that the Gove rnment is not allowed to give people one
personal number to use in all their dealings with Government agencies. There is a whole
bunch of questions around privacy, around th e sharing of information between
Government departments, and around what I belie ve is a flagrant overuse of Orders in
Council by this Government to pass regulations.
These are all questions the Green Party looks  forward to raising with officials and
submitters and the other parties in the select committee process. We urge Kiwis to get
out there, make a submission, and find out more about it. I think there is a whole host of
subsidiary issues, which I think would be valid to raise on the select committee. There
are questions around the need for a time line for those Orders  in Council to be
broadened by the Government, and there are some questions  around what the scope of
those fees is going to be, for the full costing.
I think we have got to ask the officials flat out whether they are confident we can
avoid cyber-security or hacking threat s, given having one unique repository for
information does make us vulnerable. We ha ve seen Governments fall victim to that
recently. As a historian, in the interests of fu ture archivists, what are we going to leave
as a legacy, given that so many of us found out about our families around the world
because those paper forms, those parish books, still exist and we can still access them?
So I think there is a whole bunch of important  questions. This is the front line of the
privacy and the technological debate in this country, and the Green Party looks forward
to constructively engaging with all the parties in Parliament. Kia ora.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: I stand in support of  the first reading
of the Electronic Identity Verification Bill. Ov er the course of each year individuals are
likely to have to visit or deal with severa l agencies to undertake various transactions
that require their identities to be verified.
The Electronic Identity Verification Bill will regulate and enhance the operation of
the igovt identity verification service. Once fu lly operational, individuals will be able to
use the service to verify their identity via the internet for interaction where it is
necessary for the agency to know who it is d ealing with. The ID is in electronic form
and is made up of four pieces of informa tion about the person that can be used by
logging into a service and givi ng consent for use of your ID. Instead of providing a
document that contains a lot of other inform ation, such as a passport, it reduces the
amount of detail about yourself.
Since the early 2000s it has been recognise d that there would be inefficiency and
inconsistency if each Government agency developed its own identity verification
system. The Electronic Identity Verification Service was developed as a shared service
to provide members of the public with the option of providing th eir identity to the
150 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012
different Government agencies. Complying wi th the evidence of identity requirements
of these transactions adds cost, travel and transaction time, and inconvenience for
customers and processing costs for the ag encies. Detecting and acting upon fraudulent
applications and criminal act ivities committed through the use of false, lost, or stolen
identity documents can impose cost and additional requirements on agencies and
individuals who identify information as being wrongly used.
The scope of the Electronic Identity Verification Bill will set clear parameters and
provide adequate penalties to deter and punish abuse of the system and ensure
compliance with the Privacy Act 1993, especial ly in relation to the disclosure of
personal information. An individual has the ch oice to decide whethe r to apply for an
electronic identity. This is, in fact, a record kept in electr onic form that contains unique
detail personal to that very user. The fo llowing details should be given to provide a
person’s unique code and validate personal information, such as full name, sex, date of
birth, and place of birth. This electronic id entity is personal to each individual and
cannot be transferred. Significant benefits ha ve been estimated. Individuals who choose
to use this service will have potential re duction in compliance costs, travel time,
transaction time, and risks associated with id entity crime. I fully support this bill and
look forward to the select committee process. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: Firstly, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch,
congratulations on your appointment to your role. We know that the Speaker’s role is in
a very capable pair of hands, and we l ook forward to worki ng with you over this
parliamentary term. We would also like to c ongratulate the Minister of Internal Affairs
on her first bill. We know it is a big moment, and we hope it is the start of many more
of these moments.
On behalf of New Zealand First I rise to  support the Electronic Identity Verification
Bill to select committee. We are looking fo rward to the chance to discuss the bill
further, and to hear the public  debate on this particular issu e. We know that the internet
is a huge concern for many, many members of the public, and the fact that the
information can be hacked into, and can be accessed by unauthorised persons, is a really
big fear, I think, for everybody. Of course, mo re and more people are actually working
online. But again, it is an option; it is not compulsory, which we are pleased to see in
this bill.
We note that the public has to  have confidence in any serv ice of this nature, so we
are going to look forward to canvassing it furt her. Security, to us , is of the utmost
importance. We are pleased to see that there has been a trial alrea dy, because it is only

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I intend to take only a fairly brief call on
the—

7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 155
