SENTENCING (AGGRAVATING FACTORS) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I move, That the Sentencing
(Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill be now read a second time . Let me first extend
my thanks to the Law and Order Committee for its work on the Sentencing
(Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill. The committee received 11 submissions on the
bill and has recommended that it proceed without amendment.
This bill demonstrates the Government’s support for front-line law enforcement staff.
It helps to protect our police and correc tions officers by explicitly denouncing those
offenders who commit offences against these of ficers while acting in the course of their
duties. Without this amendment, the courts are not under any obligation to consider the
fact that an offence has been committed against a police or corrections officer as an
156 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 7 Feb 2012
aggravating factor in sentencing. The current  law includes a number of offences that
apply specifically to police and corrections officers. However, when an assault on a
police or corrections officer is serious, the offender is charged with a generic offence,
such as attempted murder or wounding with intent to injure. Generic offences do not
specifically recognise that the victim in a pa rticular case was a police or corrections
officer acting in the course of his or her duty. The absence of a specific aggravating
factor in section 9 of the Sentencing Act mean s this fact does not have to be considered
by the courts at all when an offender has been convicted of a generic offence.
This bill creates a specific aggravati ng factor for offences against police and
corrections officers, making it mandatory for ju dges to consider the fact that the victim
was a police or corrections officer as an a ggravating factor in sentencing. The bill sends
a strong signal that assaults against police and corrections o fficers will not be tolerated.
We know the number of assaults on police a nd corrections officers has increased over
the years. The Government believes the role  of police and corrections officers as the
first line of defence for the public is deserv ing of enhanced protection. This bill ensures
that our police and corrections officers are gi ven the level of State protection that they
deserve.
Police and corrections officers have a legal obligation to deal with dangerous people
in dangerous situations. Th is obligation is unlike that  applicable to any other
occupation. Where staff in other occupations  can walk away, police and corrections
officers must move forward to deal with  dangerous situations on behalf of the
community, as our front line of defence.  Our police and corrections officers are
responsible for keeping our communities sa fe from the most dangerous people in
society, so it is important that the Governme nt reciprocates by taki ng a firm stance on
assaults against our front-line officers a nd that the Government expressly denounces
this abhorrent behaviour.
This bill demonstrates this firm stance. This bill shows that the Government is taking
assaults against our police and corrections offi cers seriously, by requi ring the courts to
specifically consider this as an aggravati ng factor in sentencing offenders. I commend
this bill to the House.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: The Sentencing Act contains a number of
instructions from Parliament, which is th e supreme lawmaking body in our system, to
the judiciary as to how that branch of Government should carry out one of its most basic
responsibilities: the sentenci ng of convicted persons. Section 7 of the Sentencing Act
sets out the purposes this Parliament tells the courts they ought to observe in carrying
out the act of sentencing. Section 8 sets out the principles that the courts are to take into
account when sentencing or otherwise dealing with offenders. Section 9(1) lists factors
that judges are to take into account as aggr avating ones when dealing with the exercise
of sentencing. I want to list some of the aggravating factors that are currently in the Act,
so that members have a clear understanding of the context of what is being done by this
amendment.
The first aggravating factor is  the actual or threatened us e of violence in the conduct
of the offence, or the actual  or threatened use of a weapon. The offence, if it involves
unlawful entry into, or unlawful presence in, a dwelling place, will be aggravated. If the
offence was committed while the offender was on bail or still subject to the sentence of
the court, that will also be an aggravati ng factor. The extent of any loss, damage, or
harm resulting from the offence, particular cruelty in the commission of the offence, the
abuse of a position of trust or authority in re lation to the victim, or the vulnerability of
the victim by reason of his or her age or hea lth, or because of any other factor known to
the offender, are also aggravating factors that a judge must take into account in
sentencing.
7 Feb 2012 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 157
Clause 5 of the Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill will add a new
aggravating factor to section 9(1), and I am going to read th e aggravating factor that we
are contemplating here. We heard the Minister of Justice refer to it briefly in her speech.

items.speaker: It is
items.text: “that the victim”—presumably, the victim of the offence in question—“was a
constable, or a prison officer, acting in the course of his or her duty:”. So that is
expressly said to be a factor that the courts  must take into account. This is in response
to, we learn from the regulatory impact statement, a 13.9 percent increase between fiscal
years 2004-05 and 2008-09 in assaults on police officers, and a 56.3 percent increase in
assaults on corrections officers over the same time.
Labour did not oppose this amendment on its first reading, and our members listened
carefully to the evidence at the Law and Order Committee. We will not oppose this bill
at its second reading, because it seems to us  that it is a measure that can do little harm.
But the question we really need to be asking ourselves at this juncture is whether the bill
will do any good. It stands to reas on that if there has been a marked increase in assaults
on police and corrections officers over the last  5 or 6 years, then we have a problem.
But we also need to not ignor e the evidence, and th e evidence is this. There are already
a number of specific offences that exist on the statute book in respect of violence
against uniformed service persons in the poli ce or the corrections se rvice. For example,
there is already a maximum of  14 years’ imprisonment for using a firearm against any
police, traffic, or prison o fficer. It is already the case th at there is a maximum of 3
years’ imprisonment provided for the aggravated assault of a constable in the execution
of his or her duty. Under the Summary Offen ces Act it is already the case that 6
months’ imprisonment is prescribed for assa ults on a police officer, and elsewhere in
the Summary Offences Act there are special provisions for resisting a police officer, a
prison officer, or a traffic officer, with a maximum penalty of 3 months’ imprisonment.
There is already a special regime in place. We put it in place to punish, in particular,
assaults on front-line responders, and yet we still have this big increase in assaults on
them. That would tend to tell us that whatev er appears in the law relating to sentencing
is not a big deterrent to t hose who choose to assault po lice officers or corrections
officers. The regulatory impact statement actually recognises that this is to be an Act of
this Parliament that leads us very close to window dressing. I am going to read what is
said in the regulatory impact statement: “T he proposed amendment will not require the
court to take any specific action in terms of  the type or severity of sentence imposed.
The court will be required to take this f actor into account—along with other specified
and unspecified aggravating factors—in arri ving at the appropriate  sentence to be
imposed in a particular case. Because judge s’ assessment of aggravating and mitigating
factors are not amenable to empirical anal ysis and the proposed amendment does not
entail specific action by the court, no monitoring or evaluation of the proposed
amendment is possible. As noted above, th e Government has decided to undertake the
proposed amendment to the Sentencing Act. The narrow and specific nature of the
proposal has restricted the range of options that can reasonably be considered.”
The problem here is that the Minister has seen a practice that she rightly wishes to
condemn. Nobody can support an increase in assaults on front-line responders. But then,
as so often happens in this Parliament, the response that has been employed is suspect.
It is not evidence based. In fact, we know th at there is no way to tell whether or not all
the parliamentary time that we are now devo ting to this measure will make one jot of
difference to the safety of police or correctio ns officers. When we are in that situation
we just need to ask ourselves why we ar e doing this: whether it is all about responding
to particular interest groups and particul ar folk on a certain end of the political
spectrum, or whether we are actually sincere in trying to legislate for a solution.
158 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 7 Feb 2012
There are other questions about this bill. What about other first-line responders, like
nurses and ambulance officers, w ho are also in danger of a ssault in their workplace?
Why not provide for them in this sort of legislation? I think it would be an appropriate
thing to consider amendments of that nature in the Committee of the whole House if this
bill proceeds to that point.
I think it is fair to say that as far as the cynicism inherent in this measure is
concerned, the Government knows what it is  doing. This legislation has hardly been
rushed through the House. It had its introduction on 13 October 2010 and it has wended
its leisurely way through the processes of the Parliament since then. Clearly, the
Government does not feel there is any urgent need to move in this way. And that has
been, sadly, typical of the Key Government ’s approach to law and order—engage in
window dressing and engage in legislation that sounds good on talkback radio and in
sound bites, but that makes no difference to safe ty on the streets. If we want any further
evidence of that we can think of the three-strikes legislation, we can think of the stalled
alcohol law reform legislation—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Would Labour repeal it?

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Labour will repeal it; that is  right. Labour will repeal all
non - evidence-based measures that do not make  one jot of difference to public safety.
The three-strikes legislation, the stalled al cohol law reform—all these measures have a
common genesis. They are done because they are something that can be rehearsed in
public and there can be chest-b eating about it, but ac tually there is very little difference
that is made to law and order in the end. Now, at the same time, important measures,
like those defining the search and surveilla nce powers of our police, languish on the
Order Paper. We have a new Minister of Ju stice, and she has the opportunity to make a
new beginning. Sadly, but perhaps not surprisingly, we are not seeing it.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise and speak on the
Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill. I must take issue with my colleague
across the floor Charles Chauvel, making the comments he did about this Government’s
record on law and order. In 1854 William Ho ward Russell, reporting on the Russian
cavalry’s advance on Balaclava, spoke: “They dashed on towards that thin red line
tipped with steel.” In 2008, under the previo us Government, for the Russian cavalry
read the assorted miscreants, recidivists, and gang members of the small villages, towns,
and cities of New Zealand. The thin red line is now tinged with blue and made up of
men and women armed with little more than  their courage, their hope, and wooden
batons against the relentless  tide of crime. That was th en, in 2008, and this is now.
Since then we have had an excellent Minister  in charge of measures of law and order
and corrections in the form of the Hon Judith Collins, and huge gains have been made.
I can speak from the heart on this, having been based in Manurewa for 3 years. It is a
wonderful, diverse community, full of people hard-working and ambitious for
themselves, with a small number who lack  a sense of purpose and a feeling of
belonging, who become, regrettabl y, the object of the long arm of the law. It has to be
said there are many more long arms of the law in Manurewa since this Government has
been in power. In fact, there are 300 more uniformed men and women—300 more
uniformed men and women—in Manurewa, Manukau, and the Counties-Manukau
Police District, where crime has been shown to have fallen significantly. There are 300
more spread around the rest of New Zealand in our small towns and villages and urban
centres, such as New Plymouth; in  places like Otago, Dunedin, and W ānaka, where my
colleague Jacqui Dean is base d; and, of course, in our gr eater urban centres such as
Auckland and Christchurch.
This Government has done an enormous amount for law and order. Some of the tools
that our police have got  since 2008 include Tasers and poli ce safety orders. I have been
7 Feb 2012 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 159
out with the police on a number of occasi ons in Manurewa. May I commend those men
and women in the Counties-Manukau team who go out there, risking their lives day and
night, to protect our community.
This is one of the reasons this bill applies only to police and corrections officers,
because it is our Government’s view that it is the police and corrections officers who
cannot hide behind anyone else. Nurses do a wonderful job. I have worked as a doctor at
accident and emergency myself, and I know what it is like on a Saturday night when the
drunks come in. I know what it is like on a Saturday night when  the drunks come in,
and the nursing staff and the medi cal staff in our hospitals do an outstanding job. But if
they get into trouble, who do they call? They call the police. It is the police who have to
take the brunt of this unbridled aggression and appalling behaviour day in and day out.
That is the reason that this is yet anothe r layer of protection this Government is
affording our men and women in the thin blue line.
This is a denunciatory piece of  legislation. This says it is  not appropriate to assault
the custodians of law and order—those pe ople, those men, those women who time and
time again go out there and put their lives on  the line to keep us safe. I commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I am actually very
grateful to that member, Cam Calder, for his contribution to this debate, because he has
actually spelt out in his contribution exactly why the top priority for this Government in
this area should have been the alcohol law reform bill and why this Sentencing
(Aggravating Factors) Amendmen t Bill will not make the ex tent of difference it could
make if, in fact, it was extended to first re sponders such as nurses in our emergency
departments and other staff in that area.
But more important, and they have not been mentioned yet, are our ambulance
officers. They too are confronted with a situation, and, yes, they may call the police. But
the purpose of this is ac tually to state the abhorrence, as  the member said, of the act of
committing a criminal act against an individual who is acting in the course of their duty.
A first responder in an accident situation wi ll, in fact, be an ambulance officer more
often than not. They will be there before the police are there, and they are the ones who
are subjected to outrageous attacks on occasio ns, as well. And if the purpose of this
legislation is as the member said—and I think th is is the purpose of th e legislation; it is
not to act as a deterrent, and thereby pot entially reduce the number of assaults on
anyone concerned; it is designed simply to st ate this Parliament’s abhorrence of such
attacks being made on people in  those positions—then there is  no reason not to include
people who work for our ambulance services and people who work at the front line of
our health services. They are much more likel y to come into contact with this kind of
behaviour than any group othe r than, obviously, the police a nd the corrections officers
themselves. So I think it would be a very good thing for us to expand this.
Now I did see that the Justice and Electoral  Committee considered this as an issue,
and its response to it was that the bill itself was to recognise the legal obligation of first
responders to dangerous situations. Well, I ac tually think that that language applies
equally to our ambulance officers, in par ticular, but to emergency staff at our
emergency departments as well.
The other thing that I would just mention in relation to this is that when the select
committee looked at this, it felt that there wa s potentially a problem with the scope of
the legislation and whether there was suffic ient scope in the purpose of the law to
recommend an amendment to extend it beyond th at. I think the solution to that lies in
this House, because, of course, when it come s to the Committee stage it would be very
easy for the Minister of Justice to move, or  seek leave of the House, that any out-of-
scope amendments extending the coverage of th e legislation could be dealt with in the
160 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 7 Feb 2012
Committee stage. I certainly could speak fo r the Labour Opposition in saying that we
would be very amenable to such an amen dment. I think it would send a very powerful
message if the House took that approach to our ambulance officers, and to other staff as
well. And if the reason is genuinely that th e select committee felt that it could not go
beyond the scope of the legislation as introduced, well then, the remedy lies in the
House’s hands. That is someth ing that I would ask the Minister to perhaps look at over
the next wee while before we get to the Committee stage of the bill.
The second issue that was looked at in se lect committee was the question of creating
a reciprocal aggravating factor. Now, I actua lly agree with the position that the select
committee came to on this. As for the purpose of the legislation in sending a message in
terms of how we feel about this kind of be haviour—that in itself—I do not think it is
appropriate to reverse the obligation, when that obligation already exists, in fact. So I do
believe that the select committee came to the right point of view on that.
Now I want to turn to the regulatory im pact statement. Those of you who know me
know that I love regulatory impact statements . I think they are the most important part
of the legislative process. I have been wo rking very hard on ensuring that we have a
really good process around regul atory impact statements, and I know a good regulatory
impact statement when I see one and I know a very poor one when I see one. I am sorry;
this one fits into the very poor category. But that is because of the brief that the officials
were given. I will just run through the re gulatory impact statement, because I notice
some new members in the House and they will not have heard my speech before—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: They will be invigorated.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: They will be invigorated by it—absolutely. My normal
speech goes something like this: the purpose of th e regulatory impact analysis is to one,
state the problem; two, identify all of the options for addressing the problem; three,
undertake detailed analysis—and that means risk, opportunity, cost, and benefits, so you
really do have to undertake the analysis with all of the options on the table—consult
with relevant stakeholders, and then recomm end a particular course of action. The final
point, which people do not always  remember, is to follow it up with a process for the
analysis of the efficacy of what you have done—so that you are actually looking back
over a period of time, seeing how the change  has actually been implemented. Now, that
is a very good process.
Unfortunately, this statement has not done  any of them, except for stating the
problem and the solution in one sentence, whic h is that there has been an “increase in
the number of assaults on police officers and prison officers over the past five years and
a spate of serious incidents in recent months, [therefore ] the Government has decided
that the Sentencing Act 2002 shoul d be amended to ensure that  the fact that an offence
is committed against a law enforcement offi cer will be taken into account as an
aggravating factor at sentencing.” So all of the in-between steps have been left out of
the process, and with regard to that final one  about analysis of its impact afterwards, it
says here: “Because judges’ assessment of aggravating and mitiga ting factors are not
amenable to empirical analysis and the pr oposed amendment does no t entail specific
action by the court, no monitoring or evaluation of the proposed amendment is
possible.” It is not even difficult; it is just not  possible. So it fails on that final point, as
well. We have had a statement of the pr oblem, gone straight to the solution, and
unfortunately I think we have missed a bit of an oppor tunity to do something a little bit
more than this.
I am not opposed to the concept of setting out in the Sentencing Act another
aggravating feature—I am not, at all—but I do not want anyone to think that the
aggravating features in the Sentencing Act are in any way a method by which we reduce
the offending concerned, because in actual f act it does not work like that. Usually when
7 Feb 2012 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 161
we are talking about assaults, we are talking about things that are done on the spur of
the moment. We have heard of alcohol invol vement, which is why I think the Alcohol
Reform Bill would have been a better priority for us to be dealing with tonight. So there
are not any occasions that I can think of where people in the circumstances of being
engaged in an assault say “Gee, I wonder what sentence I’ll get for this if I get caught?”.
That is the problem with the concept of it not reducing the problem. I think there has to
be more than this; it cannot just be this to deal with the underlying issue.
When we look at how the High Court regard s assaults on police officers, again the
regulatory impact statement is a great source of valuable information. This is how the
High Court has described an attack on a police officer. The Hi gh Court has said it is the
“equivalent to an attack on the community b ecause our police are the representatives of
the community in the matter of law and orde r in society. They are society’s frontline
…”. The Court of Appeal has emphasised the gravity of using serious violence against
police officers and upheld dete rrent sentences in a number of cases. That was done on
an ongoing basis. That case dated back to 1985. So if we had had the problem definition
and the analysis done in between, then we might  have actually identified that in fact the
law already allows the courts to take this matter into account, and they usually do. In
fact, that has been the problem of the pr ocess—nobody has identified for us when they
did not take it into account, or whether they allowed a mitigating factor that this would
not allow. This does still allow mitigating fa ctors; it is only one of the aggravating
factors to be considered, and that is why it is  very difficult to monitor. So I think that
this whole legislation could have been improved, and it can still be improved.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am pleased to speak on this bill, the Sentencing
(Aggravating Factors) Amendm ent Bill, for the first time and to state the Greens’
continuing support for the bill, despite the fact that, somewhat like the Labour Party, we
do not see any particular need for it in the form that it has been presented in. My
esteemed colleague Keith Locke spoke during the earlier reading of this bill. With his
departure to greener pastures, I have inherited the task. It  took, of course, remarkably
little time to read the bill in its entirety—a very few number of paragraphs and one
substantive clause. It is undoubtedly the shorte st piece of legislation I have read in my,
admittedly limited, experience.
There seems to be no particular justificati on for this bill. Our reason, essentially, for
supporting rather than opposing it is that to oppose it could be seen to oppose what is
basically judicial practice of the time. Th e judiciary does acknowle dge that assault on
police or prison officers is a serious matter and is  treated as if it is an aggravating issue,
and for that reason I guess we are continuing to support this.
The Crown Law Office, in its review of the bill, was quite unequivocal, and I quote:
“New Zealand sentencing decisions take into account the fact that a victim of an offence
was a police officer or a prison officer, acting in the course of his or her duty, as a
matter of established practice. The Bill confirms the common law position.” This bill is
almost superfluous, so clearly there is oppor tunity within it to make it do something
useful, to make it do something better.
Mr Chauvel has already listed some of the existing aggravating factors mentioned
specifically in the Sentencing Act. These incl ude the actual or threat  of use of violence
and the threat or use of a weapon, and clearly these are appropriate to be referenced in
sentencing legislation. People have the right to the security of their person. It is a basic
tenet of our law that people ought to feel secure in themselves and to be safe from
assault upon them.
The aggravating factors include unlawful presence in a dwelling place. Again, people
have a right to feel secure in their own homes and in the places where they live and
work, and if that security is lost, that is a significant issue. That is an important thing,
162 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 7 Feb 2012
and it is a fundamental role of  the State to protect the secu rity of the person in their
home. In that sense, clearly, these aggravat ing factors already identified are somewhat
generic and less specific, and that is as appropriate as one would want it to be.
The list is clearly not definitive or exhaustive in the existing legislation. There has
been no specific reference to date to police or corrections officers. It is acknowledged
that police and prison officers do put themselv es in harm’s way. Judges take that into
consideration, and we can demonstrate th at through case law and through simple
observation. In fact, the case law quoted by the Crown Law Office goes back to at least
1980 and up to the early or mid-2000s. It is current practice, it ha s been practice for
quite some time, and it is questionable that we really need to take this step.
The judiciary do their best to protect poli ce officers. They are not loath to impose
quite significant sentences on people proven guilty of assaults on police or prison
officers, but we must also bear in mind that  length and severity of  sentence are not in
any degree proven to be deterrents for poten tial offenders. The Police Association itself
supports this view in its submission. It states  there that it can see that simply adding
longer or tougher sentences is no t a deterrent, particularly to  violent crimes, which, as
has been pointed out, are typically irra tional, spontaneous actions. People plan
burglaries; they plan to deal in drugs or other illegal activity. Vi olence, particularly
against police or corrections officers, is often a reactive, spont aneous action. You can
have the longest, toughest sentences in the world; it will make not a blind bit of
difference in that moment when somebody offe nds against an officer. So let us not
delude ourselves or be under any illusion that these sorts of measur es that this bill
would put in place will actually make our communities safer and our police and prison
officers safer.
I would add to that that in my belief—I sa y now and we have said consistently over
the last several years—a lot of the actions of this Government, the former Government,
have actually made our prisons and our streets more dangerous. I think of things like the
“three strikes and you’re out” legislati on, like double-bunking, and like the imposition
of tougher penalties and more severe terms for inmates in our prisons. Those have all
contributed to making the job of our corr ections officers more dangerous. Words on
paper will not remedy that. In that sense, this will not be particularly effective.
The Justice and Electoral Committee—it must be conceded that I did not sit on that
committee, and I am sure the House will be th rilled, as we are, that the Greens are now
in sufficient numbers that we will have sitting members on every select committee and
will be able to participate; we are very happy about that—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: We’re delighted for you.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: Indeed, I am sure you are! Thank you. The select committee
did deal with these two issues. I made comm ent on the notion of reciprocal aggravating
factors and this situation affecting other people in the public sector. The notion of
reciprocity is suggesting that given that police are in a uni que position, we could say, if
they are to be uniquely protected, then they  should also bear unique responsibility, shall
we say. It was captured quite well by the C ouncil for Civil Libertie s in its submission,
where it said, and I quote: “… if offences against police officer and prison officer are to
be elevated to the status of ‘aggravating f actors’, then it is l ogical that offences by
police officers and prison officers are also elevated to the same status.” There is perhaps
an implied suggestion in the existing aggravating factors th at a person in a position of
authority—a person in a position of trust—oug ht to be treated more severely by the
courts, and, clearly, that does encompass police and prison officers, but we do think that
there is an argument to be made that there ought to be that recipr ocity. Given that the
specific rights of police and corrections officers are to be embedded in law, then it
seems reasonable that the unique responsib ilities of those roles also should be
7 Feb 2012 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 163
acknowledged in this law. That is somethi ng that we will be bringing to the Committee
stage of this conversation.
The matter of other public sector officers of  various forms, and the vulnerability of
some of those people who are providing a ve ry significant public service, we think
could also usefully be acknow ledged in this legislation. We could start with nurses,
ambulance drivers, doctors, and people worki ng in emergency departments at hospitals.
We could think of people working in mental health services, and things as basic as noise
control officers and animal control officers. I would make a special case for an example
like fisheries officers. The penalties for people offending against fisheries legislation are
very, very severe and can i nvolve significant loss of prope rty, vehicles, boats, and dive
gear, and loss of liberty at the extreme. Fi sheries officers are often working in very
isolated situations against people who have  considerable motivation, dare I say, to
respond potentially violently against being rest rained or arrested by a fisheries officer
and taken to task by them.
So I would suggest that there are cases where these sorts of aggravating factors ought
to specifically cover some of these other public servants who ar e often doing a very
difficult job in very vulnerable situations —situations where they  are vulnerable to
violence against them—and, even in small communities, to violence or threats of
violence that could affect their family and their social life. I do think that if we are going
to look at amending this part of the bill, we should think a little more broadly.
I think I will end my contribu tion there, except to say that, yes, we will continue to
support this legislation. In its current form it does no particular harm. It could be
amended to do some positive good, and we do look forward to suggesting some
amendments, some additions to it, at the Committee stage. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am pleased to stand in
support of this Sentencing (Aggr avating Factors) Amendment Bill and note that parties
on the other side of the House likewise ar e supporting it. I do want to say that we
continually hear the comment that none of this legislation will act as a deterrent to those
activities. There are times when a judgment from a court is not actually just to serve as a
deterrent but as a protection to  society, particularly if some body is prepared to assault a
police officer or a corrections officer. We n eed to question whether that person ought to
be at liberty to continue or to assault members of the public, because assaulting a person
in that level of authority shows that they have no regard at al l to the rule of law. Let us
not be mistaken—this bill is not about a soft  counselling session to create a deterrent,
but about a protection. It is sending a signal. We are writing a line in the sand to say that
the protection of our men and women in unifo rm—who represent the rule of law in our
society—is something we take with the utmost seriousness. To think that this legislation
is unimportant, I believe, is a travesty of the purposes of th is House, which is to protect
our society.
I am sure that each of us here in this House know men and women in our
communities who are police officers or corrections  officers. Let us not forget that they
are our friends and our neighbours. They ar e sportsmen and women, they are coaches,
they are sons and daughters, mothers and fa thers, family members, and brothers and
sisters. They are people like us who want to make a contributi on, not only in their
vocation but as contributors to our soci ety. Their job, unlike anyone else’s in our
community, pits them against the most viol ent in our communities, something that none
other is required to do.
I would like to read out what th e Police Association printed in its Police News at the
end of last year, because this tells the stor y of two of its officers who received bravery
awards. These are constables in Christc hurch. Let me read: “Constable Wardle was
speaking after receiving an New Zealand Po lice Association bravery award along with
164 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 7 Feb 2012
his colleague former constable Marty Stil es. The two officers were involved in an
incident in the Christchurch suburb of Ph illipstown in July last year, during which
Senior Constable Bruce Lamb was shot in the face, his police dog, Gage, was killed and
his colleague, Constable Mitch Alatalo, was shot in the leg. Constables Alatalo and
Wardle were conducting a routine search unde r the Misuse of Drugs Act, during which
the aggressive manner of one of the occupa nts led them to call for backup. Constable
Stiles and dog handler Senior Constabl e Lamb, and his dog Gage, responded. The
occupant refused to come out  of his room. When Senior  Constable Lamb opened the
door, the man opened fire with a rifle, shoot ing him through the face. His next shot
killed police dog Gage. The gunman then cam e to the doorway and opened fire again,
this time hitting Constable Al atalo as the officer retreated , escaping from the house …
While under fire, Constable Stiles grabbed his fallen colleague, Senior Constable Lamb,
by the belt and dragged him back down the ha llway towards safety. At the same time,
Constable Wardle (then acting as Sergeant), confronted the gunman with a Taser. As he
did so, the gunman aimed at Constable Wardle  and pulled the trigge r, but the firearm
jammed. The officer fired the Taser, but it failed to incapacitate the offender. To buy
enough time for Constable Stiles to evacu ate the wounded Bruce Lamb, Constable
Wardle reloaded the Taser and continued to challenge the offender, who briefly
retreated before again following the officer s out of the house and down the drive while
pointing his rifle at them. Constable Ward le provided cover for his colleagues while
they retreated. Following the officers’ retreat, further armed police arrived. The offender
rearmed himself with a higher powered rifle, and was ultimately arrested by the Armed
Offenders Squad.”
This is the reason why this legislation is  before the House, because these men and
women are facing life-threateni ng situations that can happe n any moment of any day.
As a Government we stand by our men and women in uniform , who are there to protect
the citizens of this nation. National is deli vering on our promises to take action on
violent crime. We have passed 18 new laws to make families safer in their homes and
communities. We have made sentences toughe r and strengthened bail law. We have
boosted the number of police on the streets a nd given them new tools to tackle crime,
while improving services for victims. We ar e proud of the stance that we are taking.
Thank you.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Z ealand First I rise to
support the Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill. It is absolutely essential
that our police officers, our prison officers, a nd other staff who work in related roles in
these areas are safe and are al ways as safe as possible in their workplace, and that any
offence that is committed against them w ill be taken into account at sentencing. The
Government and the courts must take this  seriously. Any workplace safety issue is
viewed very, very seriously a nd the same must apply here. We  do not like to hear that
the number of assaults on police officers and prison officers is increasing at the rate that
it has done; figures suggest a 33 percent increase over the 2004 to 2009 period.
It does raise a number of questions. Will the amendment make any difference? We
are saying that hopefully it will, because it is highlighting the issue to the public. But we
ask what about the other related areas—for example, the mental health workers, the
doctors, and the psychologists who are employed in the prison service? They are not in
uniform but they do need protection. This could be one bill where they actually are
provided that protection. We would gladly support an amendment to that effect.
Training is another area that  actually makes us question what is happening in that
area. We need to ensure that police and co rrections staff have th e best training they
possibly can get. It needs to be robust, it needs to be vigorous, and it should be good
enough to equip them to carry out their roles in the safest possible manner. If there has
7 Feb 2012 Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill 165
been this increase in assau lts on police and corrections officers, then that should be
good reason to ensure that police recru itment and Department of Corrections
recruitment is not being deferred, and that the number of these people in these services
remains high. We will be looking very carefu lly at the figures over the next wee while
to ensure that they actually are.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: Bring back Ron Mark.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: We are bringing back a strong law and order focus.
We will be looking very closely at these bills that the Government is actually
pushing through and passing to ensure that they  do meet the criteria of our particular
law and order policy. New Zealand First has al ways prided itself on the strong stance it
has taken in the law and order area, and we will be continuing to do that. We will be
supporting appropriate legislation in this area. At this point in time, I know that my time
is nearly up. New Zealand First will suppor t the second reading of the Sentencing
(Aggravating Factors) Amendment Bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It gives me huge pleasure to speak in the
last dying minutes of tonight about the Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amendment
Bill. You know, we had a police officer in Ōāmaru who was going about his business
late on a Friday night, and these scumbags , these local little scumbags, thought they
would beat him up when he stopped them to have a look at their brake lights, which
were not working properly. Do you know wh at these scumbags did to this police
officer? They beat him into the gutter. Do you know what this lone police—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member, but the time has come for me to leave the Chair.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

7 Feb 2012 Members Sworn 79 
TUESDAY, 7 FEBRUARY 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MEMBERS SWORN 
Charles Chauvel, Hon Annette King, and H on Maryan Street were presented to the 
Speaker, made the affirmation required by law, and took their seats in the House. 
VISITORS 
Sweden—Committee on Environment and Agriculture, Riksdag 
Mr SPEAKER: I have much pleasure in informing the House that representatives of 
the Committee on Environment and Agriculture from the Swedish Parliament, the 
Riksdag, led by Deputy Chairperson Mr Beng t-Anders Johansson, are present in the 
gallery. I am sure members would wish that the delegation be welcomed. 
MOTIONS 
Queen Elizabeth II—Diamond Jubilee 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I seek leave that th is House congratulates 
Her Majesty the Queen on the occasion of the diamond jubilee of Her Majesty’s 
accession to the Throne. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Prime Minister is seeking leav e. Is there any objection to that 
course of action being followed? There is no objection. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I move, That this House congratulate Her Majesty the Queen 
on the occasion of the diamond jubilee of  Her Majesty’s accession to the throne . On 6 
February 1952—60 years ago yesterday—Queen Elizabeth II ascended to the throne 
and became New Zealand’s monarch. She was only 25 years old—younger, in fact, than 
any member of our Parliament today. In her speech as she ascended to the throne she 
promised to follow the example of servic e and devotion provided by her father, King 
George VI. For six decades the Queen has kept that undertaki ng. These have been 
decades during which the concept of the Brit ish Empire has receded and the importance 
of the Commonwealth has come to the fore . The realms over which Queen Elizabeth 
reigns have had their times of prosperity, al ong with times of tur bulence and challenge. 
And over 60 years New Zealand has orientated  itself on the world map differently: less 
the Antipodes and all that that implies, more a modern and assertive nation with a 
central role in the Pacific. We have developed our own dist inct sense of identity. We 
value the things that make us unique, that  make us Kiwis. We are a nation of many 
different peoples sharing a common belief in peace, progress, and a fair go.  
The dignity, wisdom, and assurance that the Queen brings to her role as New 
Zealand’s head of State supersedes maps and distances. Throughout the changes of the 
past 60 years her status as our  Sovereign has given many of us a sense of stability and 
confidence. Her role is a link with syst ems of constitutional government that have 
histories much longer than our own, and with traditions that move and inspire us.  
In my time as Prime Minister, I have been  fortunate enough to meet Her Majesty on 
a number of occasions, and I can say to memb ers of this House, and, indeed, to New 
Zealanders, that she has a great care, concern, and passi on for, and intimate knowledge 
and love of, this country, and, in my view, has done a wonderful job as the monarch of 
New Zealand. I know that in this Parliament there are a ra nge of views on the future of 
the monarchy in New Zealand. I respect thos e views are sincerely held, while at the 
same time maintaining my own belief as bot h Prime Minister of New Zealand and as a 
80 Motions 7 Feb 2012 
citizen of this realm that the monarchy con tinues to be both relevant and meaningful. 
Sixty years of service, and counting—let us warmly congratulate the Queen of New 
Zealand. 
DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) : On behalf of th e Labour Party, I 
join with the Prime Minister and other members of this House in paying tribute to, and 
thanking, Queen Elizabeth II, who marks the 60 th anniversary of he r ascension to the 
throne. New Zealand stands alongside many other Commonwealth countries in 
congratulating Her Majesty on  this, her diamond jubilee. I also welcomed the Prime 
Minister’s announcement earlier that New Zealand will host the Prince of Wales and the 
Duchess of Cornwall later on, in November this year, and I know that will be welcomed 
by many New Zealanders.  
I understand that Queen Victoria was the only other queen to have reigned as long as 
Queen Elizabeth II, so it is appropriate that Parliament marks this occasion. Her reign is 
perhaps best described by the United Nati ons Secretary-General, Ban Ki-moon, who 
said that “in a churning and ch anging world” she is “an anchor for our age.” Her reign 
has been one of an unwavering commitment and dedication to service. It is a 
commitment that has spanned the service of 14 New Zealand Prime Ministers and 12 
British Prime Ministers, and, as the Prime Minist er just remarked, it is sobering that the 
weight of responsibility of the monarchy fell on her at the age of only 25. Perhaps most 
famously for New Zealand is our link to that coronation 60 years ago, when Sir Edmund 
Hillary conquered Everest and said that that feat was, in fact, a coronation gift. No one 
can doubt her dedication to Commonwealth countries. In our darkest hours she has 
stood by us. Her words of support, for example,  in Canterbury were very well received, 
and her grandson’s visiting and saying the words “kia kaha” to Cantabrians perhaps best 
acknowledged the stoic resolve of Cantabrians at that particular time. She is the first 
monarch, in fact, to have ever visited New Zealand, and she has visited 10 times in her 
60-year reign.  
I had the privilege of meeting Queen Eli zabeth at Buckingham Palace some 15 or 16 
years ago, and it is an honour I will not forg et. I have enormous respect for her work 
and her service.  
We acknowledge, of course, that over the last 60 years much has changed in New 
Zealand, and there will inevitably be some discussion about our future constitutional 
arrangements. But that is a debate for anothe r day. Today is a day to  mark her reign of 
service, commitment, and dedication, and on behalf of the Labour Party I congratulate 
Her Majesty. 
Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) : The Green Party pays tribute to our head of 
State, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth of Ne w Zealand. As the sec ond - longest serving 
Sovereign, the Queen has played a most si gnificant and important role in the world 
through an extraordinary 66 years of tumultuous world history. She has honoured the 
institution of the monarchy th rough the natural dignity of her person and the grace with 
which she has discharged her duties. She has honoured this country in the genuine 
interest she has displayed in our history, our  culture, our sporting prowess, our military 
sacrifices, our changing demographic charac ter, and our hopes and aspirations for the 
future.  
When the Queen was crowned in 1952, Sir Edmund Hillary was yet to conquer 
Mount Everest. Back home, ha lf of New Zealand homes did not have a fridge, and one 
in five did not have a flus hing toilet. No home had televi sion. The idea of standing on 
the moon remained in the realm of heroic pla nning, if not science fiction. So times have 
changed considerably sin ce our Queen ascende d the throne as a young woman. We 
celebrate her 60 th anniversary with a respectful me ssage of gratitude and personal 
affection shared by all New Zealanders.  
7 Feb 2012 Motions 81 
No discussion about the New Zealand m onarchy occurs today without attention 
being naturally given to the nature of the institution of the head of State. We remain in a 
small minority of nations that share the same head of State with others. There are many 
who advocate a transition soone r or later to a republican institution—one based here in 
our own soil. There are others who are comfor table with the status quo and wish it to 
continue. Her Majesty will not be unaware of  the somewhat desultory debate in the 
country along these lines. The Green Party does not have a formal position on this 
matter, and now is not the time to explore it. But equally it is inappropriate, even as we 
pay tribute to our respected monarch, not to  acknowledge the future  challenge we face 
as a nation on this matter. Let us send a message from this Parliament of Aotearoa New 
Zealand to Her Majesty thanking her for he r gracious service and wishing her a long 
and fruitful life ahead. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First): New Zealand First wishes to be 
associated with the previous sentiments and to say that we agree with them in their 
entirety. New Zealand is one of only nine countries with an unbroken line of democracy 
these last 150 years, and the Queen being our head of State may be one of the 
significant reasons why we have that proud cl aim, which so few countries can boast as 
we do. Hence we send her our heartfelt congratulations. 
HONE HARAWIRA (Leader—Mana) : T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Huri rauna t ēnā 
tātou katoa. E tautoko ana i ng ā mihi atu ki te Kuini. I te mea hoki ka huri au ki te reo 
Pākehā, kia mōhio tūturu ai tātou, he aha pū ngā whakaaro kai roto i taku ngākau. 
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker, and to us throughout. I endorse the accolades to the 
Queen and immediately turn to English so that we understand fully  what the thoughts 
within me are.] 
On behalf of the Mana movement I congrat ulate the Queen on achieving this historic 
milestone, and I urge this Gove rnment to invite her to reaffirm her commitment to Te 
Tiriti o Waitangi as a guide to how this Gove rnment might act in all matters pertaining 
to the indigenous people of Aot earoa and the lands and resources  that it holds on behalf 
of all New Zealanders. Tēnā tātou katoa. 
Hon JOHN BANKS (ACT—Epsom) : The ACT Party is glad to be associated with 
this motion. This weekend marked the 172 nd anniversary of the sign ing of the Treaty of 
Waitangi. Rather than a day of national celebr ation, it has continue d to be a time of 
angst and controversy. We contin ue to be lost in a mire of conflicted identity. The last 
time I attended Waitangi was in 1990, the year  the Queen suffered an offensive affront 
to her dignity as our head of State when  she was assaulted on the Treaty grounds. I 
vowed that day that I would not return unt il the behaviour improved. Two decades later 
the behaviour of many of those remains the same. It is my hope that 6 February can 
become a day when all of us can peacefully  celebrate the greatness of our country and 
can recognise the important ro le that both the Crown and M āori have played in the 
development of our nation.  
The sixth of February also marks the 60th anniversary of the Queen’s ascension to the 
throne. Today offers an opportunity for this  Parliament to celebrate the Queen and 
everything her reign has meant to the country over the past six decades. Her 
commitment to the Commonwealth and the sense of duty with which she has carried out 
her role is to be applauded. Her reign ha s brought a common thr ead of stability and 
unity to our young country, and as a nation we  should not be in any great haste to 
change such an important link to our past . The Queen has kept her solemn coronation 
oath to govern the people of New Zealand ac cording to our laws and customs. Fourteen 
New Zealand Prime Ministers have served her, and she has always fulfilled her duty 
without becoming embroiled in the politics of  the day. She embodies the principle that 
82 Motions 7 Feb 2012 
constitutional monarchy is power constrai ned and upholds democratic government in 
New Zealand through the notion that policy is determined, finally, in this House.  
Today this Parliament—this country—gives praise and thanks, congratulations, and 
warmest best wishes to Queen Elizabet h II, Queen of New Zealand, on her 60 th year on 
the throne. Long may she live in good health, happiness, and contentment. 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader—United Future) : On behalf of United Future I 
want to join with others who have spoken in tribute to Her Majesty the Queen on the 
occasion of the 60th anniversary of her ascension to the throne. 
It is sobering to realise that when that event occurred very few members of this 
House were actually alive, Winston Churchil l was the Prime Minist er of Great Britain, 
Harry Truman resided in the White Hous e, and Stalin was still carrying on his 
murderous ways in Russia. Sidney Holland wa s our own Prime Minister. So much has 
changed, when one reflects upon those people and the character of their times, and yet 
the one thing that Queen Eliz abeth has been able to provi de through thos e intervening 
60 years to the present has been a sense of continuity, a huge measure of dignity, and, in 
many senses, that portrayal of common sens e and common wisdom that has held her 
own country together in times of great crisis, and, I think, has been a beacon of hope for 
many around the world. It never ceases to  amaze me that republics like the United 
States, for instance, give the Queen perhaps the warmest welcome of all when she visits 
there, and I think that says a lot about her and her character. 
As a republican, I acknowledge this is not the occasion to delve into that debate in 
any sense; this is the occasion to mark 60 years of service, commitment, and dedication 
to her people by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, and to wish her and her family well as 
they celebrate this occasion and look forward to the future. 
Motion agreed to. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economy—Government Priorities and Challenges 
1. SIMON BRIDGES (National—Tauranga) to the Minister of Finance: What are 
the Government’s priorities for the economy in its second term? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government intends to get back 
to surplus and manage the Government’s fina nces very well. We in tend to continue to 
develop a more competitive economy, because we  have to earn a living in the next 10 
years, rather than borrow it as we did in the last 10 years. The Government intends to 
rebuild Christchurch, and our final top prior ity is to improve public  services across the 
board so New Zealanders get better service for the same or fewer resources. 
Simon Bridges: What challenges does New Zealand’s economy face? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The fundamental challenge is the same now as it was 2 or 3 
years ago, which is to rebalance this ec onomy from excessive resources in the non-
tradable sector to the tradable sector. Much of the growth of the last 10 years was built 
on borrowed money going into an uncompe titive domestic economy. In the next 10 
years we have to earn our living by investing in a competitive export sector. 
Simon Bridges : How does the Government intend to tackle the economic 
challenges? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: In the same considered and balanced way as it did in its first 
term of office. But I think New Zeala nders share with the Government the 
determination to make real progress over the next few years so that we can have more 
jobs and higher incomes. 
7 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 83 
Hon David Parker: Did the briefing he received as incoming Minister from his chief 
economic advisers in Treasury project that under his Government’s economic settings, 
New Zealand’s net international liabilities would increase by nearly 10 percent of GDP 
over the next 5 years—an increase of approximately $25 billion? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: That may have been their projection; I would have to go and 
check. We, of course, want to continue with the significant improvement in recent years 
in our net international liab ilities. I am somewhat more optimistic than Treasury 
because I think New Zealanders have learnt the lesson that more borrowing and 
excessive borrowing are not the way for them to  get better incomes, and if they refrain 
from excessive borrowing and get into higher savings, the prospects of that projection 
coming to pass are less. 
Simon Bridges: What signs of progress has he seen in the economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Just to give a couple of signs, the economy has grown for 
nine of the last 10 quarters, and the forecas ts for growth in this economy are stronger 
than in the US, Europe, and quite a numb er of other develope d countries. Secondly, 
some of the more detailed changes the G overnment is making are bearing fruit. For 
instance, on 1 April there will be a $600 million reduction in ACC levies because the 
Government in the last 3 years applied itself to turning ACC round. That is an example 
of what can be achieved with public services. 
Economy—Prime Minister’s Statements and Relationship with Māori Party 
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement “National will deliv er a strong, stable government—and build a 
stronger economy with less debt and more jobs”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
David Shearer: Does he take seriously th e question of whether the M āori Party will 
continue to be bound to his G overnment for confidence and supply; and if so, is he 
confident that they will? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes, I am confident they will. 
David Shearer : Has he discussed with M āori Party co-leader Tariana Turia her 
comments in relation to section 9 of the Stat e-Owned Enterprises Act that she is “not 
one prone to idle threats”; and if so, what was the result of that discussion? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, not specifically in relati on to that comment, but I think 
what the co-leader of the M āori Party was saying is that they take that issue seriously. 
The Government is going through a 2-week  consultation process, and I am very 
confident we will come out with an elegant solution at the end of it. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : In the negotiations for the formation of the Government, 
did the Māori Party raise that issue in those discussions—yes or no? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. 
David Shearer: Does he stand by his statement of  this morning that “they are bound 
with us for confidence and supply, which is  effectively the Budget, and the mixed-
ownership stuff doesn’t flow through the Budget”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, I do, insomuch that they are not bound by the mixed-
ownership model legislation, which will fall outside of the Budget. 
David Shearer: Did he read the Government’s B udget papers, which show that the 
next 5 years’ capital budgets rely on the sale of public assets? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, and that is probably one of the reasons why we have 59 
MPs and the Labour Party has very few. And that is because New Zealanders want less 
debt, more productive assets, and an economy that is going to function, not a load more 
debt, as Phil Goff was promising and, I have no doubt, David Shearer is, as well. 
84 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Feb 2012 
David Shearer: How will he make a Treaty clause apply just to the Crown’s share of 
the State-owned enterprises, when the actions  of the privatised State-owned enterprises 
will affect both the Crown and private shareholders alike? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The Treaty is a compact between the Crown and M āori, and 
what the Government will be aiming to do is to  spell out that very clearly in the section 
that will then apply to the mixed-ownership model. 
David Shearer: Does he accept that his determination to push ahead with asset sales 
is creating instability in his Government? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Not in the slightest. I accep t what it will do is deliver a 
country that has less debt than it would under Labour, a Government that will deliver 
for New Zealanders something to invest in other than failed finance companies—which 
were overseen by the previous Labour Government—entities that will deliver well. I say 
to that member the same thing I used to say to Phil Goff: “If you don’t like the mixed-
ownership model, put up your policy to buy b ack the bit of Air New Zealand we don’t 
own.”  
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I ask the Prime Minister, if the M āori Party campaigned 
against asset sales, and if United Future was committed to ensuring that water was 
regarded as a strategic asset, then where does he get his majority from to make the 
assertions he is making around the country of having public support? 
Mr SPEAKER: Before I call the right honourable Prime Minister, obviously he is 
not responsible for what either the M āori Party or ACT campaigned on. But the latter 
part of the question can be answered. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As part of the confidence and supply agreements put together 
between National, ACT, and United Fu ture, we secured support for the mixed-
ownership legislation. That is 61; that is a majority. 
State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Ownership of Shares 
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister for State Owned 
Enterprises: What steps, if any, has he taken to  ensure that should the Government sell 
49 percent of Mighty River Power, Meridia n, Genesis and Solid Energy, “New Zealand 
investors will be at the front of the queue  for shareholding, and that there will be 
widespread and substantial New Zealand share ownership”? 
Hon TONY RYALL (Minister fo r State Owned Enterprises) : Ministers have 
made this requirement of widespread New Zealand investment a fundamental part of 
every step of the process to date. Both th e scoping studies and Crown advisers have 
confirmed that there is sufficient domestic demand to meet the Government’s 
objectives. As part of any share float the G overnment has the ability to determine what 
type of investors are allocated shares, and we will use this ability to ensure widespread 
and substantial New Zealand shareholding. These proposed share floats are important to 
ensure public debt remains under control, a nd we certainly do not want to reach the 
level of debt as in some countries such as Britain, where they are having to lay off 
700,000 public servants. 
Dr Russel Norman: How will he ensure that New Zealanders are at the front of the 
queue when New Zealand’s trade and invest ment agreements state that New Zealand 
investors cannot be given preference over foreign investors? 
Hon TONY RYALL : The Government is quite clea r that those agreements do not 
override the Government’s ability in respect  of the allocation policy to make those 
decisions. 
Dr Russel Norman : What advice has he received regarding the ability of the 
Government to give preference to New Zealand investors, and advice that the 
agreements we have do not prevent him doing that? 
7 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 85 
Hon TONY RYALL: We have received advice that those agreements do not prevent 
the Government from ensuring widespread and substantial New Zealand ownership of 
the mixed-ownership model companies. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove: What is he going to put in place, if anything, to stop buyers 
of shares from onselling those shares to overseas interests? 
Hon TONY RYALL : I think what is quite clea r is if you look at the mixed-
ownership model as it applie s at the Port of Tauranga, which is a mixed-ownership 
model type approach, we have actually got  New Zealanders buying out foreigners. I 
think the fact that we have  good quality investments will give New Zealanders that 
opportunity— 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. That was a specific 
question. It simply asked— 
Mr SPEAKER : I hear the member. To save time, the honourable member may 
repeat his question. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove: What actions, if any, is he goi ng to put in place that would 
stop buyers of shares in these State-owned enterprises from onselling those shares to 
overseas interests? What specific actions will he take, if any, to stop that happening? 
Hon TONY RYALL : The Government is not proposing that it would take any 
action that would stop ordinary people having a right to decide to whomever they sell 
their shares. The problem is that the part y opposite does not think working people are 
good enough to own shares, and on this side of the House, we think they are. 
Dr Russel Norman: Will the Minister release the advice he has received, as stated in 
his earlier answer, that the Government has no restrictions on giving preference to New 
Zealand buyers of shares in these companies? 
Hon TONY RYALL : The member is entitled to ma ke an Official Information Act 
request for that information, and I am sure we will consider it in due course. 
Dr Russel Norman: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was not asking whether I 
could make an Official Information Act request; I was asking whether the Minister 
would release the advice. 
Mr SPEAKER: I think, in fairness to the honourable member, the Minister made it 
clear that without such a request he proba bly would not, but with such a request it 
would be looked at. I think that is a reasonable answer to the question asked.

ELECTRONIC IDENTITY VERIFICATION BILL 
First Reading 
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister of Internal Affairs) : I move, That the Electronic 
Identity Verification Bill be now read a first time.  At the appropriate time I intend to 
move that the bill be re ferred to the Government Administration Committee for 
consideration and that that committee report finally to this House on or before 29 June 
2012. This is an important bill. It is part of  the Government’s framework to put tools in 
place that make it easier for individuals to in teract with government, and at a lower cost 
for those individuals and for the agencies concerned.  
Specifically, the purpose of the Electronic Identity Verification Bill is to regulate and 
enhance the operation of the igovt identity verification service. Once it is fully 
operational, individuals will be able to use th at service to verify their identity via the 
internet for interactions wher e it is necessary for an agen cy to know who it is dealing 
with. Those might, for example, be transact ions involving the paying out of money or 
the exchange of personal information. Curr ently for those types of transactions, 
7 Feb 2012 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 139 
agencies usually require individuals to provide multiple documents as evidence of their 
identity, such as passports and drivers’ licen ces. Individuals have to bear the cost and 
the time burden of applying for and supplying  those documents, and individuals whose 
identities have been wrongly used can face si gnificant inconvenience, distress, and cost 
to rectify matters. There are costs for ag encies to check, c opy, and return those 
documents. In addition, the use of false, lost , or stolen identity documents can impose 
considerable further costs on agencies. Another bill before this House, the Identity 
Information Confirmation Bill, will go a long way to combat the risk of fraudsters 
presenting false identity documents to agenci es. While that bill will help with face-to-
face transactions, the current bill and the iden tity verification service within it provide a 
complementary role for the online environment.  
The igovt system will provide agencies with  a ready-made, secure process to support 
the provision of online services that woul d not otherwise be possible because of the 
potential fraud risks involved. It will allow individuals to avoid repeatedly having to 
provide physical documents to multiple agencies in order to  use online services, should 
they choose to use the service. The igovt identity verification service has been operating 
successfully but in a limited form since the end of December 2009. Individuals have, for 
example, been able to use the service for the online ordering of certificates and copies of 
records from the Births, Deaths and Marriages registry, which requires proof of identity. 
In this way the identity verification service use has to date been limited to a small 
community of eligible indivi duals for a single type of tr ansaction. It is now time to 
expand the service for use by all members of  the public and for the widest possible 
range of services so that individuals, gove rnment, and businesses can all realise the 
benefits that internet technologies offer. The Electronic Identity Verification Bill will 
enable this to happen.  
The bill will enable individuals to choose to verify their identity via the internet with 
approved agencies with appropriate contro ls and safeguards while also providing 
operational flexibility for the service to be developed over time to respond to changing 
technology. It is important that this significant Government service, as it is expanded, is 
duly authorised by legislation. The bill wi ll ensure that the service can operate 
effectively and that appropriate safeguards are put in place and maintained. It is vital 
that the bill is progressed quickly. This will ensure the best use of the investments being 
made to develop the service and individual agencies’ online services that will rely on it.  
Clause 4 of the bill is part icularly important. It sets out the principles around which 
the service’s operation is based. Those principles emphasise that the use of the service is 
optional and that individuals have control ove r the personal information that the service 
holds. Individuals will not be required to jo in the service. If they do choose to do so, 
they can decide whether or not to use it for any particular transaction, and agencies are 
expected, therefore, to ensure that i ndividuals can still access their services by 
presenting other forms of evidence of ident ity, should the individual  wish to use that 
option. The bill does not impose any mandatory obligation on New Zealanders. 
Individuals can cancel their membership of  the service at any time. The identity 
verification service provides authorised  agencies only the minimum amount of 
information necessary to verify  an individual’s identity thro ugh a record referred to in 
the bill as an electronic identity credential. The credential may be provided to an agency 
only with the individual’s consent. An individual may check the information before it is 
sent, correct it or update it as necessary, a nd monitor where the information has been 
sent. An individual’s identity is verified using an identifier, or code, that is unique to 
each authorised agency, and this prevents  the unauthorised sharing of information 
between agencies.  
140 Electronic Identity Verification Bill 7 Feb 2012 
The bill will allow anyone to use the servic e once his or her identity is verified to a 
high standard comparable to that used for the issuing of New Z ealand passports. That 
may occur, for example, through checking that an individual’s identity information, 
which includes his or her phot ograph, is consistent with information held in other 
official records. The bill authorises information-matching programmes and other 
processes for that purpose. Children will be able to apply, but those under 14 will need 
their parents’ or guardians’ consent. 
The bill also provides a number of other safeguards that will ensure the service 
operates securely and protects people’s privacy. Those protections are vital. If the public 
loses trust in the service, it will fail. The first key protection in the bill is that it provides 
that agencies must be author ised through regulations to use the servi ce. Those agencies 
may be in the public or the private sector s. Approved agencies must adhere to the 
standards for the use of the system. Secondl y, the bill strictly regulates access to 
photographs and other personal information he ld by the service. Thirdly, the Privacy 
Commissioner will be able to require reports on the general operation of the service, 
rather than just reactively dealing with comp laints about privacy breaches that may be 
associated with the service. I am pleased that the Privacy Commissioner and her staff 
have been closely involved in the development of the service and this bill, and that this 
involvement will continue. Finally, the bill cr eates specific offences and penalties to 
deter abuse of the system. Courts will have the ability to ban offenders from using the 
service and to determine the validity of a ny transactions that have been undertaken 
using false information. Agencies will be notified if a false electronic identity credential 
has been used for their online services so that they may take immediate action.  
This is an important bill. It will enable individuals and agencies to realise the benefits 
of being able to easily verify individuals’ identity information via the internet for a wide 
range of services. There will be appropriate  safeguards in place to ensure the service 
continues to be secure, protects people’s privacy, and is easy to use. I commend the bill 
to the House.

this new important tool.  
When considering an online service that  involves the Government collecting 
personal information about individuals for use across multiple Government agencies, 
one’s first concern must be for the security  and appropriate use of that information. 
Information is power. Once somebody has it, it  cannot simply be taken away. So this 
bill has been structured from the point of view that in receiving that information there 
are safeguards over its use. I am pleased to see that any concern on that score is well 
and truly put to bed by the strong safeguards in this bill.

supply of his or her personal information to  a participating agen cy must be obtained

that is necessary for the agency to act as part of a given transaction or series of

The safeguards in these principles are comprehensive. They clarify that at no time

apply for an electronic id entity credential and nobody can  be forced to use it.

Government services.

appropriate level of security for the informati on that will be held. I am sure this is an

Administration Committee, and I too look forward to working on it there.  
The Electronic Identity Verification Bill br ings our online Government services into 
the 21st century. It does so in a way that comprehensively safeguards the security and 
the privacy of those who use those services, and for those reasons I fully commend this 
bill to the House.
